decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
Dear authors, thank you for your submission and for engaging in detailed discussions with all reviewers. Since some reviewers were unavailable to quickly reply when the authors were allowed to respond, we hope that the comments below will help improve your work.

The stability score is defined in A.3.2 as the percentage of molecules that are charge neutral. This is indeed a natural heuristic for molecule generation and prediction, because a non-neutral molecule might exist under special ambient conditions, which requires a proper experimental confirmation in a wet lab. For this basic charge neutrality (called stability), the proposed MotiFlow achieves 92.6%, less than the QM9 baseline of 95.2% in Table 1.

On the second dataset GEOM, there is no reported stability at the molecular level, but the paper reported the VxC score (validity by RDKit and connectivity to guarantee a single molecule after adding chemical bonds under standard conditions) of 81.2% on MotiFlow, which is significantly less than the baseline of 99% on GEOM.

For canonical frames and comparisons, the paper mentioned the "rotation matrix, computed via the Kabsch algorithm". This algorithm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabsch_algorithm) essentially uses ordered points. If atoms are not ordered, the same approach leads to exponentially many permutations. Even if we take chemical elements into account, the simple molecule of benzene C6H6 has (6!)^2>500,000 possible permutations of atoms of the same chemical element.

Though the authors included "novelty" as "percentage of sampled molecules not present in the training set" in some responses, this word did not appear in the paper. The previous paragraph shows why quantifying the novelty of 3D molecules was highly non-trivial and was solved in general position by a distribution of pairwise distances at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0196885803001015 and for all unordered clouds by Lipschitz continuous invariants and metrics in polynomial time at https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023/html/Widdowson_Recognizing_Rigid_Patterns_of_Unlabeled_Point_Clouds_by_Complete_and_CVPR_2023_paper.html

Uniqueness was defined in lines 734-735 as "the percentage of valid samples that possess a unique SMILES string". Unfortunately, the SMILES string depends on many choices and is unsuitable for uniqueness. Here is the quote from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Molecular_Input_Line_Entry_System: "The resultant SMILES form depends on the choices: of the bonds chosen to break cycles, of the starting atom used for the depth-first traversal, and of the order in which branches are listed when encountered."

Without proper comparisons of 3D molecules, one can easily generate millions of differently looking molecules through atom reordering and perturbations. In a similar case, the Nature correction at https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09992-y/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9992_MOESM1_ESM.pdf crossed out almost all the words "novelty" and "discovery" because nothing novel was discovered.

Potentially, the most impactful contribution is the exposure of disconnected entries in the training datasets QM9 and GEOM, while MotiFlow reported even lower percentages (92.6% < 95.2% on QM9 in Table 1 and 81.2%<99% on GEOM drugs in Table 2). Since the charge neutrality and connectivity of generated molecules should be easy to verify, the authors are encouraged to report all failures in their update. This exposure of past mistakes should lead to corrections of the QM9 and GEOM papers, similar to the Nature 2023 paper above.

Reviewer fQUj summarized the concerns as "Limited performance on small molecules".

our_title: Self-Supervised Flow Matching for Scalable Multi-Modal Synthesis

match.matched_title: Self-Supervised Flow Matching for Scalable Multi-Modal Synthesis

submission.title: Self-Supervised Flow Matching for Scalable Multi-Modal Synthesis
submission.abstract: Strong semantic representations improve the convergence and generation quality of diffusion and flow models. Existing approaches largely rely on external models, which require separate training, operate on misaligned objectives, and exhibit unexpected scaling behavior. We argue that this dependence arises from the model's training objective, which poses a denoising task with little incentive to learn semantic representations. We introduce *Self-Flow*: a self-supervised flow matching paradigm that integrates representation learning within the generative framework. Our key mechanism, *Dual-Timestep Scheduling*, applies heterogeneous noise levels across tokens, creating an information asymmetry that forces the model to infer missing information from corrupted inputs. This drives learning strong representations alongside generative capabilities without external supervision. Our method generalizes across modalities and enables multi-modal training while following expected scaling laws, achieving superior image, video, and audio generation.
submission.tldr: We propose Self-Flow, a self-supervised flow matching paradigm that unifies representation learning and generative modeling in a single framework
submission.lay_summary: Despite the dominance of diffusion and flow models in visual and multi-modal generation, they remain paradoxically dependent on external engines for global semantic understanding.  This reliance suggests a fundamental limitation: standard local denoising objectives provide little incentive for models to develop a global structural understanding. To address this, we introduce __Self-Flow__, a self-supervised framework that _unifies representation learning and generative modeling within a single pipeline_. Our framework works by creating an information asymmetry across tokens, forcing the model to infer corrupted inputs from cleaner surrounding context. This process naturally drives the emergence of strong internal representations alongside generative capabilities. Because Self-Flow operates without external models, it _generalizes seamlessly across diverse modalities including images, video, and audio, and follows expected scaling laws_, offering a path toward _world models that are both perceptually grounded and semantically rich_.

reviews.summary: The paper proposes a self-supervised flow matching paradigm to eliminate the reliance on external representation models for training generative models. The authors introduce dual-timestep scheduling, which applies heterogeneous noise levels to input tokens, creating an information asymmetry. A student network is trained to denoise the input while simultaneously matching the features of an EMA teacher network that processes a less noisy version of the same input. Experiments show the superior scalability and multi-modal generalization of the proposed method.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

+This paper study a highly relevant and timely problem of the scaling bottlenecks and cross-modality limitations of external representation alignment.

+Integrating a masked-autoencoder-style self-distillation objective natively into the continuous-time flow matching framework via Dual-Timestep Scheduling is an elegant and structurally novel approach.

Weaknesses:

-The key claim of the paper is that self-supervised alignment (Self-Flow) outperforms external alignment (REPA). However, the comparison is fundamentally confounded. Self-Flow introduces two components: DTS and an EMA Self-Distillation loss. REPA uses Standard Scheduling and External Distillation. Figure 2b explicitly demonstrate that DTS alone improves vanilla flow matching. Therefore, more detailed ablation should be conducted.

-The mask is sampled randomly token-by-token. In continuous modalities like images and videos, local spatio-temporal redundancy is exceptionally high. A heavily noised token is highly likely to be adjacent to a "clean" token. Consequently, the student network can minimize the representation loss trivially by performing local spatial/temporal interpolation, bypassing the need to learn the "global semantic connections" you claim it learns.

-The transition to multi-modal joint training relies on manually tuned, static modality-specific loss weights. For a framework claiming to be a unified, scalable paradigm, relying on brittle hyperparameter tuning to balance modalities undermines the "elegance" of the approach.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: Please see the Weaknesses.
reviews.final_justification: Thanks for your response. After carefully reading the comments, I will keep my original score.

reviews.summary: This paper presents a self-supervised training framework that incorporates representation learning directly into flow matching models. The key idea is a dual-timestep scheduling strategy, where tokens are perturbed with different noise levels to induce information asymmetry between the student and teacher models. As a result, the student is encouraged to predict the representation of a more informative teacher token from its more heavily noised counterpart. Experiments show that this approach consistently improves performance across image, video, audio, and multimodal generation tasks, while eliminating the need for external representation encoders.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

1. The paper is technically solid, with experiments across image, video, audio, and multimodal generation that consistently support its main claims.
2. The proposed method is simple, effective, and well motivated. In particular, eliminating the need for an external representation encoder and making the pipeline more scalable constitute significant contributions.



Weaknesses: 

1. The novelty is somewhat incremental, as the proposed method is closely related in spirit to prior ideas in the self-supervised learning literature, such as self-distillation, masked prediction, and asymmetric corruption. Compared with SRA, the method also appears to use very similar hyperparameter settings(layer index), which further limits the sense of methodological distinctiveness.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Have you explored multi-layer feature alignment in Self-Flow, rather than using only one student-teacher layer pair for the representation loss? I’m curious whether aligning multiple layers improves representation learning or instead interferes with generation.

2. I am particularly interested in whether the method remains effective in a much larger, product-scale regime with sufficiently large models and long training schedules. Based on the current results, many of the baselines do not appear fully converged, so it is difficult to tell whether Self-Flow genuinely raises the  upper bound of the baseline or mainly provides faster optimization in the non-converged regime.
reviews.final_justification:
The additional clarification on the hyperparameter selection logic, the multi-layer alignment results, and the new 1B-scale results addresses my main questions well. I think the idea of inserting representation learning into generative models is quite interesting, and I look forward to seeing how this direction performs at even larger scales.

I will keep my initial positive score.

reviews.summary: This paper introduces Self-Flow, a self-supervised flow-matching framework that integrates representation learning directly into generative training via Dual-Timestep Scheduling and an EMA teacher–student objective. The method eliminates reliance on external encoders (e.g., DINO), resolves scaling pathologies observed in external alignment, and generalizes cleanly across image, video, audio, and multi-modal generation. Empirical results consistently outperform both vanilla flow matching and state-of-the-art alignment methods.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

- **Strong motivation and problem framing**  
  The paper clearly identifies fundamental limitations of external alignment, including scaling failures and modality mismatch, and supports these claims with targeted experiments.

- **Conceptually elegant solution**  
  Dual-Timestep Scheduling is simple, intuitive, and well-motivated. It avoids the train–inference gap that plagues masking-based or diffusion-forcing approaches.

- **Unified generative + representation learning**  
  The method integrates self-supervision directly into flow matching without auxiliary pretraining stages or architectural changes.

- **Excellent empirical coverage**  
  Results span ImageNet, text-to-image, text-to-video, text-to-audio, and multi-modal generation, with consistent gains.

- **Self-supervised method to outperform external alignment on ImageNet**  
  This is a notable and nontrivial result.

- **Compatibility with semantic latent spaces (RAE)**  
  Demonstrates robustness to autoencoder choice and latent representation type.

### Weaknesses and limitations

- **Limited theoretical justification**  
  The paper relies heavily on empirical evidence to justify why heterogeneous token-wise timesteps do not bias the learned flow. A short theoretical discussion or controlled ablation would strengthen confidence.

- **Insufficient clarity on timestep handling**  
  The treatment of token-wise timestep embeddings is implicit. Explicit clarification would improve reproducibility and reader understanding.

- **Additional hyperparameters**  
  The method introduces masking ratio $R_M$ and loss weight $\gamma$, but sensitivity analysis is limited.

- **Computational overhead**  
  The EMA teacher and dual forward passes increase training cost. While justified by performance gains, a cost–benefit discussion would be helpful.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Does heterogeneous-noise training mismatch the uniform-noise generation trajectory?
2. How is the non-scalar time input handled with heterogeneous noise?
reviews.final_justification: I really appreciate this paper, which introduces a self‑supervised flow‑matching framework that removes the need for external encoders (e.g., DINO), resolves the scaling pathologies associated with external alignment, and generalizes cleanly across image, video, audio, and multimodal generation. The authors have addressed all of my concerns through clear theoretical justification and comprehensive ablation studies. I strongly recommend this paper for acceptance.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes **Self-Flow**, a self-supervised flow matching framework that integrates representation learning directly into generative training. The authors introduce Dual-Timestep Scheduling, which applies heterogeneous noise levels across tokens to induce information asymmetry and encourage semantic inference. The method removes the need for external models and generalizes across modalities. Experiments show improved performance in image, video, and audio generation while following expected scaling behavior.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
- **Strengths**
	- The paper is well written and easy to follow.  
	- The motivation is clearly articulated, and the proposed solution is well justified and convincing. 
	- The method is novel, and the experimental results convincingly demonstrate its effectiveness.
- **Weaknesses**
	- In Sec. 3.3, the connection between the two intuitive solutions and the final proposed method is not sufficiently clarified. While the proposed strategy is conceptually related to Solution #1 (masking a subset of tokens with $t=1$), its relationship to Solution #2 (assigning independent random timesteps to all tokens) is much less evident. The specific insight or motivation that Solution #2 provides for the final design is not clearly articulated.
	- It is unclear whether training the teacher model with the generative loss $\mathcal{L}_\text{gen}$​ would be a feasible or beneficial alternative.
	- Compared to approaches that rely on external models, the computational efficiency and memory usage of the proposed method are not explicitly analyzed.
	- In Sec. 3.4, the text refers to Fig. 3(b); however, Fig. 3 does not contain a subfigure labeled (b).
	- In Eq. (6), the notation $h_θ$  appears inconsistent with earlier definitions, where $f_θ$​ was introduced, suggesting a possible typographical error.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and the interesting points for discussion. We address the questions raised in the review below.

### __Q1: Ablations:__ 
Please note that the ablations requested in the review are included in Fig. 10(a) (albeit with slightly different terminology). For example, w/o $\mathcal{L}_{{rep}}$ denotes an ablation where we keep only DTS, and remove the representation loss, w/o masking refers to the mirror ablation where we keep the representation loss but remove DTS. We enclose the same ablation study presented in the paper with only the ablations referred to in the review in the [following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/ablation.pdf) for the reviewer’s convenience. We additionally include vanilla flow matching for compatibility with Fig. 2(b) referenced in the review. As can be observed, both components have a noticeable impact on the performance of our method, and the full benefit of it can only be obtained by combining the two. This relation is expected, since __DTS serves as the basis to create the asymmetry required for effective representation learning__. Thus, the two are fundamentally tied to each other.

While the use of an EMA teacher is the common practice in self-supervised methods, we additionally enclose an ablation comparing the performance of Self-Flow with and without it in the [following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/EMA.pdf). As can be expected, the non-EMA variant begins with a lead since EMA catches up gradually with the student in earlier training. As EMA catches up, it obtains a slight advantage over non-EMA. Notably, this advantage is not very significant, indicating that our method’s advantages stem from DTS and the self-supervision more than the use of an EMA checkpoint.


### __Q2: Masking effectiveness in continuous modalities:__
The need to learn the "global semantic connections" depends on the value of the masking ratio, $\mathcal{R}_M$. We invite the reviewer to explore our interactive visualization at [this link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/), which directly illustrates the effect of different masking ratio ($\mathcal{R}_M$) values on token masking patterns. The image and video experiments employ $\mathcal{R}_M = 0.25$ and $\mathcal{R}_M = 0.1$ respectively, where under $s \ll t$, the majority of tokens are heavily noised, fundamentally limiting the extent to which local interpolation can be exploited.

Furthermore, the video generation results show very strong gains, with a margin of nearly 2 FVD points over REPA (Table 3), demonstrating the effectiveness of Self-Flow for domains with high redundancy.

### __Q3: Multi-modal joint training:__ 
Please note that our experiments are conducted on a __wide-range of weights__, which were not manually tuned but automatically computed based on the data size and batch size per modality (see Appendix D). The considered weights include extreme weightings that favor each modality specifically (i.e., $w_I \gg \lbrace w_V, w_A \rbrace, w_V \gg \lbrace w_I, w_A \rbrace, w_A \gg \lbrace w_I, w_V \rbrace$) (L. 313 rightmost column - L. 370 leftmost column). The reference in the text for "we employ modality-specific loss weightings" just means that we test extensive variations where the weights across modalities are different. Fig. 6(a) interestingly shows that even with extreme weightings that favor each modality specifically, Self-Flow is still able to __improve generation quality across all modalities__ (L. 368-370). Furthermore, in Appendix D (specifically Fig. 15, Tab. 6), we enclose __all results for all considered weights after 1M multi-modal training steps__ (5 combinations), and show that all modalities improve under any weight selection, demonstrating robustness. 

We are happy to address any remaining questions.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the careful and detailed review, and for the intriguing questions. We address each point below.

### __Q1: Novelty and methodological distinctiveness:__
Below, we address the relation between Self-Flow and two types of methods that do not employ external alignment: (i) methods that incorporate an explicit self-supervised objective (ii) methods that rely solely on the model’s learned features.

__(i) Self-supervised generative methods:__ We agree that Self-Flow draws inspiration from established self-supervised principles. However, we believe that the contribution lies in the ability to integrate an explicit self-supervised framework *within* the generative framework, which is a non-trivial endeavor. As demonstrated in Section 3.3, creating information asymmetry in a way that preserves natural generative behavior is a delicate balance. Naïve approaches such as full masking or Diffusion Forcing severely degrade generation quality (Fig. 2(b)) due to train-inference mismatches (L. 185-191). Furthermore, other attempts to integrate self-supervised objectives into the generative framework (e.g., MaskDiT [1], SD-DiT [2] via masking) have fallen short of outperforming external alignment (L. 93-107, rightmost column). Self-Flow creates effective information asymmetry through Dual-Timestep Scheduling, enabling a seamless combination of representation learning and generation.

__(ii) Internal feature-based methods__: First, to address the reviewer’s point on the choice of layers for alignment, we wish to clarify that this is not unique to Self-Flow or SRA, but is rather a property shared across all feature alignment methods in this family. For instance, REPA (Yu et al., 2024) uses the same student layer ($l=8$ in a depth-28 model) and demonstrates the same behavior of feature evolution across layers. This convergence in layer selection stems from the natural evolvement of semantic features in diffusion transformers: empirically, semantic understanding begins to emerge at around $30$% of the network depth, and features are most semantic around $70$% of the depth (Yu et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025). We therefore believe this similarity is expected and method-agnostic, and does not diminish the distinctiveness of any individual method.  
Importantly, the fact that SRA and Self-Flow share layer selections yet produce significantly different results (e.g., on ImageNet: FID of 7.27 for SRA vs. 5.72 for Self-Flow, compared to 8.3 for flow matching, Tab. 1) is evidence that the layer choice is not the source of our gains. Rather, the improvement stems from the explicit self-supervised framework introduced by Self-Flow, which goes beyond reliance on the model's naturally learned features.

### __Q2: Multi-layer alignment:__ 
Preliminary results of combining multiple student layers ($l=4,8,12$) for the best teacher layer ($k=20$) on ImageNet are included in [this link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/multi_layer.pdf). As can be seen, this combination causes a slight degradation in Self-Flow performance. We hypothesize that aligning several layers at once encourages the model to form uniform features across layers, which harms generation. This is consistent with Fig. 4(b), which shows that even when using $l=8$ for alignment, features continue to evolve naturally (i.e., improve) across the network up to around layer 18, suggesting that the natural progression of features across layers is important for generation quality. However, implementing such a combination is an interesting direction for future research.

### __Q3: Results at convergence/ larger scale:__ 
We thank the reviewer for this question. The results reported in the paper present the performance until the baselines plateau. In the [following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/convergence.pdf) we show the effect of continued training beyond the number of steps reported in the paper compared to the most competitive baseline, REPA (for image generation, we show Fig. 1(a) from the paper, as the baseline already plateaus). As can be observed, additional training does not result in performance gains. 

To further illustrate Self-Flow scaling laws, we added a 1B parameter scale to Fig. 7 from the paper in the [following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/scaling.pdf). Notably, __the 625M parameter Self-Flow is able to outperform the 1B parameter REPA, a model with nearly twice the number of parameters__.
While training production scale models using all baselines is beyond the scope of this work, we believe the results above, combined with our 4B multi-modal results (supp website), demonstrate promise and robustness at scale.

We are happy to answer followup questions.

References:
- [1]  Fast training of diffusion models with masked transformers, Zheng et al., 2023
- [2] SD-DiT: Unleashing the power of self-supervised discrimination in diffusion transformer, Zhu et al., 2024

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the thorough and positive review, and for the insightful questions. We address each point below.

### __Q1: Effect of heterogeneous timesteps on learned flow:__
**Theoretical discussion:** We show that a pointwise minimizer of the dual-timestep (DTS) objective, $L\_{DTS}$, is also a pointwise minimizer of the conditional flow matching (CFM) objective, $L\_{CFM}$.

Let $p(t)$ denote the timestep pdf as in Sec. 3.3. The dual-timestep forward process is:

$$
\\begin{aligned}
t, s &\\overset{\\text{iid}}{\\sim} p(t) \\\\
m\_i &\\sim \\text{Bernoulli}(R\_M), \\quad i=1,\\dots,N \\\\
\\tau\_i &= m\_i s + (1-m\_i) t \\\\
x\_{\\tau,i} &= (1-\\tau\_i)x\_0 + \\tau\_i x\_1
\\end{aligned}
$$

With slight abuse of notation, let $\\tau(t, s, m) \\mapsto \\tau$ and $x\_\\tau: (x\_0, x\_1, t, s, m) \\mapsto x\_\\tau$ also denote the functions constructing the timestep vector and forward process. Then:

$$
L\_{DTS}(f) = \\mathbb{E}\_{x\_0, x\_1, t, s, m} \\left\\Vert f(x\_\\tau(x\_0, x\_1, t, s, m), \\tau(t, s, m)) - (x\_1 - x\_0) \\right\\Vert^2
$$

We ask if a $f^\\star \\in \\arg\\min L\_{DTS}$ also minimizes

$$
L\_{CFM}(g) = \\mathbb{E}\_{x\_0, x\_1, t} \\left\\Vert g((1-t)x\_0 + t x\_1, t) - (x\_1 - x\_0) \\right\\Vert^2
$$

where we generalize $L\_{CFM}$ to vector timesteps by replacing $t$ with $\\tau(t, 0, 0)$.

By the law of total expectation, we split $L\_{DTS}$ into a homogeneous and heterogeneous component:

$$
\\begin{aligned}
L\_{DTS}(f) &= P(m=0) \\mathbb{E}\_{x\_0, x\_1, t, s} \\left[ \\left\\Vert f(x\_\\tau(x\_0, x\_1, t, s, m), \\tau(t, s, m)) - (x\_1 - x\_0) \\right\\Vert^2 | m=0 \\right]+ \\\\
&\\quad\\; P(m\\neq0) \\mathbb{E}\_{x\_0, x\_1, t, s} \\left[ \\left\\Vert f(x\_\\tau(x\_0, x\_1, t, s, m), \\tau(t, s, m)) - (x\_1 - x\_0) \\right\\Vert^2 | m\\neq0 \\right] \\\\
& \\eqqcolon P(m=0) L\_{hom} + P(m\\neq0) L\_{het} \\\\
\\end{aligned}
$$

When $m=0$, we have $\\tau\_i=t$ for all $i$, so $s$ drops out:

$$
L\_{hom} = \\mathbb{E}\_{x\_0, x\_1, t} \\left\\Vert f(x\_\\tau(x\_0, x\_1, t, 0, 0), \\tau(t, 0, 0)) - (x\_1 - x\_0) \\right\\Vert^2 = L\_{CFM}
$$

Since $P(m=0) = (1-R\_M)^N > 0$, the homogeneous loss part $L\_{hom}=L\_{CFM}$ has a positive weight in $L\_{DTS}$. Moreover, the regression target, $x\_1 - x\_0$, does not depend on $(t, s, m)$, so all loss contributions for a given input $(z, \\tau)$ (including those from $L\_{het}$) impose the same optimal value. Hence, a pointwise minimizer of $L\_{DTS}$ must also minimize $L\_{CFM}$, i.e. $f^\\star \\in \\arg \\min L\_{CFM}$.

**Controlled Ablation:** For a controlled ablation, we compare a model trained with DTS to a model trained with the vanilla conditional flow matching objective (CFM).
Both models are evaluated on held-out data using the CFM objective under homogenous timesteps. The [results](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/stratified_dts.pdf) show that the model trained with DTS achieves a lower CFM loss. This indicates that DTS enables better learning of the flow. See also Fig. 2(b) of the paper showing the same comparison in terms of FID.

### __Q2: Timesteps with heterogeneous noise:__
In standard flow matching, a scalar $t$ is broadcast to all tokens as a shared conditioning signal via adaLN modulation. With DTS, we extend this to a per-token timestep tensor $\\tau \\in \\mathbb{R}^{N}$, which introduces no new parameters. Upon publication, we will make the SiT-XL implementation, as shown [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/selfflowrebuttal/DTS_visualization/refs/heads/gh-pages/model.py), available.

### __Q3: Sensitivity of masking ratio and loss weight:__
__Masking ratio:__ The submission included results across masking ratios in Supp. Fig. 12, but the sensitivity analysis was not explicitly highlighted. We now make this explicit, with results across masking ratios (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5) in [this link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/masking_ratio.pdf). Across all three metrics, every masking ratio variant of our method outperforms all baselines, demonstrating that it does not require careful tuning to achieve gains. A judicious choice of masking ratio can boost performance further. E.g., increasing the ratio from 0.05 to 0.5 yields gains on 2 out of 3 metrics. The masking ratio controls the amount of clean context, and is therefore related to the redundancy of the domain, see also [this interactive demo](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization).

__Loss weight:__ All experiments use the same loss weight $\gamma=0.8$ without adjustments across modalities. This was determined by an initial sweep on ImageNet. The results are included in [this link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/gamma_ablation.pdf). Increasing $\gamma$ from 0.2 to 0.5 to 0.8 is helpful, until the point where $\gamma$ overpowers the generative loss, which causes a slight degradation.

### __Q4: Computational overhead:__
Please see the answer to Q3 of Reviewer y2Qe.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the positive and constructive feedback, and the interesting points for discussion. We address each question raised in the review below.


### __Q1: Connection between solution #2 and Self-Flow (Section 3.3):__
The relation between Dual-Timestep Scheduling (DTS) and solution #2 (Diffusion Forcing) is that both constitute different methods of introducing information asymmetry to the flow matching paradigm. Creating such asymmetry is a key challenge in combining generation and representation learning (L. 150-160, rightmost column). There are two common approaches in the literature to achieve this: __masking a subset of tokens (masked autoencoding)__ or __assigning a different noise to different subsets of the sequence (Diffusion Forcing)__. We explore both alternatives and show empirically that they lead to severe degradation in generation quality (Fig. 2(b)). DTS is designed to avoid this failure mode, while still inducing the asymmetry needed for representation learning.

### __Q2: Training the teacher with the generative loss:__ 
Please note that the teacher is an EMA version of the student (Fig. 3, L. 195-196, rightmost column). Therefore, the teacher is indeed trained with the generative loss and the representation loss combined, as it is updated using the student weights. While it is possible to consider a teacher that was trained solely using the generative objective, employing an EMA teacher is the common practice across representation learning frameworks (e.g., DINO, JEPA), as it allows the teacher and the student to share a representation space where a feature reconstruction loss is meaningful. Additionally, training an entirely separate teacher would incur significant computational costs for an additional backward pass.

### __Q3: Computational efficiency:__  
- __Compute efficiency:__ Unlike external alignment, Self-Flow scales with the model size, enabling healthy and predictable scaling laws. Fig. 7 in the paper measures compute efficiency using FLOPs, which is the standard approach to estimate computational efficiency in the literature (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024), and demonstrates that __Self-Flow achieves significantly better performance given the same computational budget (FLOPs)__. Following the review, we added a 1B parameter scale to Fig. 7 in the [following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/scaling.pdf). As can be observed, __the 625M parameter Self-Flow is able to outperform the 1B parameter REPA, a model with nearly twice the number of parameters__. Furthermore, the performance gap between Self-Flow and REPA widens monotonically as a function of training FLOPs across all model sizes (depth=8 through depth=28), meaning that __every additional unit of compute invested in Self-Flow yields strictly greater returns than the same compute spent on REPA__.

- __Runtime analysis:__ In terms of wall clock time, let $T$ be the time for a single forward pass. A backward pass takes roughly $2T$, and the additional pass through $70$% of the teacher layers adds $0.7T$, resulting in $\sim3.7T$ vs. $3T$ for vanilla flow matching ($\sim$23% increase). The cost for external alignment is a constant independent of $T$, and its relation to the generative model’s runtime depends on the model size and external encoder selection.
- __Memory usage:__ Self-Flow employs an EMA variant of the student as the teacher, which requires additional storage proportional to the size of the student. However, we emphasize that (i) maintaining an EMA variant is standard practice in generative training, as it typically performs better than the vanilla model. As evidence, all baselines considered in this work employ an EMA model for their evaluations, including external alignment methods. (ii) We enclose results of Self-Flow without an EMA teacher in [the following link](https://selfflowrebuttal.github.io/DTS_visualization/EMA.pdf), which demonstrate that a non-EMA variant of Self-Flow is nearly identical to the full method in later training steps, further indicating the stability of our method.

### __Q4: Figure and notation typos:__ 
We thank the reviewer for pointing these out, we will make sure to fix these in the final version of the manuscript.

We are happy to answer followup questions.

References:
- [1] Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers, Peebles & Xie, 2023.
- [2] Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis, Esser et al., 2024.
- [3] SiT: Exploring Flow and Diffusion-based Generative Models with Scalable Interpolant Transformers, Ma et al., 2024.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment: This paper received overall recommendations of 3, 4, 5, and 5. This paper introduces a self-supervised flow matching framework, which natively integrates representation learning into generative training via Dual-Timestep Scheduling to eliminate reliance on external encoders. The method achieves superior scalability and generalization across image, video, audio, and multi-modal generation tasks. During the rebuttal, the authors addressed the reviewers' concerns by providing a mathematical proof that aligns their objective with standard conditional flow matching, and by presenting strong 1B-parameter-scale results demonstrating significant compute efficiency over strong baselines like REPA. Although one reviewer maintained a weak reject score for spatial redundancy and ablation clarity, the authors' detailed interactive visualizations and extensive baseline comparisons sufficiently addressed these concerns. Given the impressive empirical performance and potential to influence scalable multi-modal generative modeling, this paper is recommended for acceptance.

our_title: Consensus is Not Verification: Why Crowd Wisdom Strategies Fail for LLM Truthfulness

match.matched_title: Truthfulness Does Not Scale Like Reasoning: Why Polling Fails as a Proxy Verifier

submission.title: Truthfulness Does Not Scale Like Reasoning: Why Polling Fails as a Proxy Verifier
submission.abstract:
Pass@$k$ and other methods of scaling inference compute can improve language model performance in domains with external verifiers, including mathematics and code, where incorrect candidates can be filtered reliably. This raises a natural question: can we similarly scale compute to elicit gains in truthfulness for domains without convenient verification? We show that across five benchmarks and models, surprisingly, it cannot. Even at $25\times$ the inference cost of naive sampling, polling-style aggregation yields no consistent accuracy gains over single-sample baselines and often amplifies correlated errors. We find that under uncertainty, models are better at predicting what other models will say within model ensembles than at identifying what is true, revealing a separation between social prediction and truth verification.  Across models and benchmarks, aggregation fails to provide a robust truth signal because language model errors are strongly correlated.  The source of correlation goes beyond any individual benchmark: we show that even when conditioned on out of distribution random strings and asked to produce pseudo-random outputs, different models produce correlated outputs. Confidence-based weighting provides no benefit because self-reported confidence fails to reliably distinguish correct from incorrect answers. 
These results delineate a boundary for inference-time scaling: in verified domains, additional samples provide more candidates for a verifier to filter; in unverified domains, additional samples merely reinforce correlated errors.
submission.tldr: Polling language models does not reliably improve truthfulness in domains without external verification, because models tend to agree with each other more than they agree with the truth.
submission.lay_summary: Many AI systems answer questions by generating several possible answers and then choosing the one that appears most often. This can work well for problems like math or programming, where answers can be checked. But many important questions do not have an easy way to verify the answer. We study whether asking many language models, or asking the same model many times, can make AI answers more truthful in these harder settings. Across several question-answering and forecasting tasks, we find that it usually does not. The models often agree with each other, but this agreement does not reliably mean they are correct. In many cases, the models make the same mistakes. Our results suggest that agreement among AI systems should not be treated as proof that an answer is true. It may still be useful as a warning sign that a question needs extra checking, such as looking up evidence, using tools, or asking a human. But for questions without a clear way to verify the answer, simply polling more AI systems is not enough to make them trustworthy.

reviews.summary:
**Context:**
The wisdom-of-crowds hypothesis states that aggregation (averaging) of independent judgments often outperforms any single individual. This is based on the assumption that errors in human crowds are weakly correlated and can be erased through aggregation at scale. This paper sets up an empirical evaluation to test what one might call the "wisdom-of-llms" hypothesis, where repeated samples from a language model or multiple language models form an inner crowd. If errors from distinct LLMs are also only weakly correlated, then aggregating them might serve as a proxy for verification (eg to answer factual knowledge questions). 

**Experiments**:
To test this, this paper picks several existing LLMs (GPT-OSS, Qwen, Gemma) and implements traditional aggregation strategies (majority voting, confidence, popularity). Data comprises four benchmark datasets spanning Q&A and commonsense reasoning. 

Findings contradict the "wisdom-of-llms" hypothesis and show that models agree with each other more reliably than they agree with the truth labels. Authors hypothesize that correlated errors may be due to (i) shared training data and objectives between existing models, (ii) architectural similarities, (iii) aligned inductive biases. This leads authors to conclude that in the absence of truth labels, aggregation of LLM results does not improve truthfulness, but rather merely reinforces shared misconceptions.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- Results are directly relevant to multiple AI/NLP-related subfields. Obviously to inference-time scaling, as they extend prior results on auto-verifiable instances (e.g., math problems) to verifier-absent domains (e.g., fact-checking). But they are also relevant more generally to literature on LLM-based ensemble methods (e.g., juries of LLM-as-a-judge, LLM annotators). There may be an upper-bound to improvements from running a task by multiple seeds of the same LLM or by multiple LLMs.

**Weaknesses:**
- No statistical testing of correlations
- Authors say that "polling-style aggregation yields no consistent accuracy gains over single-sample baselines and often amplifies shared misconceptions" (see Abstract). What about whether it also amplifies shared truths? What part of the correlation is strictly from the wrong answers? When LLM predictions correlate on right answers it's not a problem. The real issue is correlation on false positive and false negative predictions. This could be simply investigated by running the same correlation analysis but separating samples where aggregation yields correct vs incorrect answers. This important question is not investigated by the paper. 
- The 0-100 self-reported confidence setting is not rigorous imo. It may be completely random and brings little value. In my own empirical work I have found that LLMs are very inconsistent when picking from even more than 5 labels, let alone a discrete interval of size 100. Did you experiment with a smaller discrete interval? Optionally with language labels similar to Likert scales or confidence scales in human-annotation tasks (e.g. "Low confidence" to "High confidence")
- The temperature interval T ∈ {0.7, 1.0} is not justified enough. Why not T ∈ {0.6, 1.0}, T ∈ {0.3, 1.0} ? A robustness check with a comprehensive interval would make results more convincing. 
- The quality of some figures is very poor (Figure 4, Figure 5)
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
- Why didn't authors test for statistical significance of the correlation results? 
- see other questions in the "Weaknesses" subsection
reviews.final_justification: **EDIT:** After acknowledging authors' rebuttals, I updated my score from "Weak Accept" to "Accept" for reasons I explicit in my rebuttal acknowledgement (see my answer to authors' rebuttal below).

reviews.summary: This work investigates whether scaling inference compute, such as using self-consistency or majority voting, can improve LLM truthfulness. They specifically consider the domains that lack external verifiers, and show that while self-aggregation are effective in verifiable domains like mathematics and coding, the authors demonstrate that these strategies fail to consistently improve accuracy on factual or reasoning benchmarks. The cause is that LLM errors are strongly correlated; thus polling multiple models or sampling a single model multiple times does not cancel out noise, but rather amplifies shared errors.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
The presentation and readability of this paper is excellent. The authors maintains a highly structured and logical flow to present the challenge, idea and empirical results. 
The message they try to convey is very clear, i.e., social prediction (internal consensus signals) does not imply truth verification. 
The authors show the existence of a structural correlation by introducing the zero-knowledge baseline of random ASCII strings.  

For the weaknesses, please refer to Key Questions and Limitations.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. If internal signals like confidence primarily track expected consensus, how can they be effectively repurposed to trigger tool use or external retrieval instead of being used for answer selection?
2. What specific training methodologies could potentially promote epistemic diversity and break error correlations within model ensembles?
3. How does the error correlation manifest in long-form Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning? Do models exhibit correlated errors at the early stage of reasoning or will converge to the same wrong answer a the end? 
4. Breaking shared priors is exactly what advanced inference-time alignment is supposed to do. How does the inability to scale truthfulness without external verifiers impact the development of inference-time alignment algorithms? 
5. When an LLM is fed with absolute garbage, like the 32-char random string, it defaults to positional biases or tokenizer artifacts. Therefore, in my opinion, proving that models share correlated errors when completely confused does not automatically extend to highly complex, expert-level tasks. It will be great to study how this correlation is baked in during the pre-training phase or post-training?
reviews.limitations:
1. The evaluation relies heavily on binary response formats, e.g., Com2Sense, HLE and BoolQ dataset. While I understand the reason why the authors choose this settings to ensure that vote shares and predictions are well-defined for the baseline algorithms, this artificial constraint limits how directly the findings can be applied to open-ended generation tasks, which is exactly where the hard algorithmic work begins.
2. While the authors include the forecasting benchmark (Predict-the-Future), it is relatively small with only 100 questions, which limits its validity.
3. The paper tests temperature variation and basic ensemble methods, but they ignore more advanced inference-time interventions that actively force epistemic diversity—such as contrastive decoding, diverse beam search, or using an extra reward model. 
4. In real-world application where there is not external verifier (the entire focus of the paper), "truth" is rarely a clean binary. By forcing complex, unverified domains into a strict binary, the paper strips away the nuance of partial correctness, contextual validity, or valid but conflicting reasoning paths. If an ensemble cannot agree on a strict binary "truth", can their aggregated reasoning paths reliably highlight the uncertainty or controversy of a topic, and use it to trigger external verifiers?
reviews.final_justification: I am maintaining the score leaning reject. While the authors identify a valid boundary condition and correlation wall, the contribution remains narrow and passive. By restricting the scope to naive polling for binary outputs, the paper ignores modern inference-scaling methods (e.g., CoT) and lacks the empirical breadth needed to address true process-level reasoning.

reviews.summary: This paper examines whether polling strategies like self-consistency lead to higher accuracy as the number of samples scales. They examine this across 5 aggregation strategies, on 4 benchmarks (commonsense reasoning, Humanity's last exam, BoolQ, and forecasting), and using multiple models across a range of sizes. The paper generally finds that models tend to agree with each other, rather than providing a ground-truth signal via consensus. This finding is robust to changes in temperature.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths 
- The authors evaluate a wide variety of models and aggregation settings to support their claims.
- Much of the paper is clearly written.
- The paper provides further empirical evidence for something that is part of the "folk knowledge" of LLM use.

## Weaknesses
Weaknesses

My main problem with the paper is that the main findings are both not surprising, and not novel. To expand a bit more, based on the list of conclusions in L091-109:

1. The finding that polling saturates has been shown in a number of previous papers, including https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05120 (TMLR), https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12147 (EMNLP 2025). I don't see how this paper's findings fundamentally differ from these papers, which should have been discussed as related work. 

2. Explanation of why aggregation methods reflect consensus: this seems like an accepted notion in recent work, it's not clear how this explanation is novel.

Another fundamental issue with the paper is that the authors only test direct answer settings; sample-and-aggregation methods like SC generally work better with CoT, where it's been argued that sampling marginalizes over CoT paths. Not evaluating CoT at all is a major oversight.

These alone I think make the paper below the bar for publication. Some other issues I noticed as well:
- The claim that SC only works in math because of external verfication (L194, right side) strikes me as odd. What exactly do the authors mean by external verification? There are many instances (including the original SC paper) of SC being applied to math without external verifiers. 
- The last parts of the paper look a bit rushed in terms of presentation.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: Based on the weaknesses above, I think this paper needs to engage more with the existing literature on sample-and-aggregate strategies for LLMs.
reviews.final_justification: The rebuttal did not substantially change my assessment, and so I'll maintain my score.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for these helpful suggestions. 
### Statistical Testing
On statistical testing, we did quantify uncertainty for the correlation analyses using bootstrap confidence intervals and error bars. This was a deliberate choice rather than an omission: paired/bootstrap CIs are a standard nonparametric tool for ML/NLP system comparison, are applicable to arbitrary metrics, and a 95% CI excluding 0 corresponds to the usual 0.05 significance criterion. That said, we agree that making this more explicit, or adding paired permutation or sign tests, would improve clarity, and we will incorporate this in the revision.
### Segregation by Correctness
We reran the correlation analysis, segregating the data by majority correctness.  We found that the correlation matrices look extremely similar for both majority correct and majority incorrect models, suggesting that correctness is not a factor influencing the correlation matrix.  If it were then it would potentially provide a signal for measuring correctness from answer aggregation.  Thus, the thesis of the paper stands.

### Confidence Reporting
Regarding self-reported confidence, we used the 0–100 format because it is a common baseline in the LLM confidence literature and enables direct comparison to prior confidence-based aggregation methods; recent work on confidence-informed self-consistency explicitly evaluates both binary verbal confidence and verbal 0–100 confidence, which is where we borrowed our experimental settings from [1]. At the same time, we agree the scale itself matters: very recent evidence suggests 0–100 confidence is often heavily discretized and that coarser scales can perform better, so exploring Likert-style or smaller discrete scales is a valuable follow-up.

### Temperature
For temperature, our choice of T∈{0.7,1.0}T \in \{0.7, 1.0\}T∈{0.7,1.0} was meant as a simple, standard robustness check rather than an exhaustive search. These are common LLM decoding settings, and prior empirical work finds that varying temperature within 0.0–1.0 often does not significantly change problem-solving accuracy [2], making this a reasonable first comparison range. Higher temperatures often degrade performance, and lower temperatures reduce diversity, which is not ideal in an aggregation setting.  We agree that a denser sweep could be informative and will note this as future work.  
Finally, we agree that Figures 4 and 5 can be improved and will replace them with higher-resolution versions in the revision.

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.05221
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05201

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and thoughtful feedback. We are glad the paper’s core message came through clearly. Below we clarify the scope of our contribution and address the main concerns.

Our paper makes a boundary claim about self-aggregation without external verification. In this setting, multiple samples from models sharing similar priors do not reliably improve truthfulness, because errors are often correlated. Empirically, across verifier-absent benchmarks, no aggregation rule consistently outperforms strong single-sample baselines. Additional samples rarely change the plurality answer (2.9% of question <-> model pairs), suggesting that aggregation is not introducing the independence required for crowd-wisdom effects.

1. We think this is right, and it aligns with how we intended the results to be interpreted. The key distinction here is between selection and control - our results show that consensus is unreliable as a selection mechanism for truth. At the same time, it can serve as a useful control signal for deciding when to defer, retrieve, or escalate. We will clarify this distinction more explicitly. 

2. We agree this is  promising. Our results don’t rule out reducing correlation, they show that naive methods of aggregation are insufficient. Approaches that introduce genuine epistemic diversity, external grounding, or explicit verifiers fall outside the regime we study - and are consistent with our interpretation of what is required for truthfulness to improve.  Our results on random strings suggest that how one prompts an LLM is extremely important: cross correlations could be reduced by varying prompting methods.  One could also reduce variance of group polling signals by doing correlation-based reweightings of model participant responses.  

3. We agree these methods are important, and this point helps clarify the scope of our claim. We think that the key point here is that diversity in outputs doesn’t imply independence of errors when models share the same training distribution. In our experiments, even when sampling varies, the plurality answer rarely changes, which is one concrete sign of this. If inference-time methods succeed by injecting stronger objectives, reward signals, or external information, then they move outside the pure self-aggregation setting we study. Our results suggest that without such additional signals diversity alone shouldn’t be expected to yield reliable gains in truthfulness

4. This is a good point - this experiment should not be interpreted in isolation or as evidence about expert reasoning tasks. Its role is narrower: to isolate correlation mechanisms by removing shared factual knowledge. Together with the benchmark results and the forecasting setting (where outcomes lie beyond training cutoffs) it supports the interpretation that correlation is a central limiting factor rather than a byproduct of shared knowledge.

5. We share the intuition that this is a limitation but it is also a favorable setting for aggregation. Binary tasks provide well defined vote shares and avoid discretization artifacts, giving polling style methods their best chance to succeed. The absence of consistent gains in this setting strengthens the conclusion that self aggregation alone is insufficient


We also briefly address 2 additional points:

RE: long form reasoning and chain of thought - our experiments measure agreement at the answer level rather than correlation within reasoning traces, so we don’t make claims about process-level correlation and will clarify this as an open direction.
RE: the forecasting benchmark size - while relatively small it serves as a stringent test case where aggregation should help if it can recover latent expertise without a verifier.  Instead all methods remain near chance which is consistent with our broader findings


Lastly we agree that in many real world settings truth is nuanced and not strictly binary. Our claim is narrower: in verifier absent settings, internal consensus shouldn’t be treated as a reliable proxy for truth. Disagreement signals may still be valuable for identifying uncertainty and triggering retrieval or human oversight which is fully consistent with our results

Overall we view the reviewer’s points as aligned with the paper’s core contribution. The results establish a boundary condition: self-aggregation can amplify consensus, but without verification it doesn’t reliably produce truth. We’ll (1) revise the paper to sharpen this scope, (2) clarify the role of advanced inference-time methods, and (3) make the distinction between selection and control more explicit.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
# Rebuttal to Reviewer Y3sF

Thanks for reviewing our paper and for the links to prior work. Many people claim that different LLMs are essentially "the same," and we're glad that you appreciated the concrete verification of this fact. We address the weaknesses you raised below.

## Saturation and related work (Weakness 1)

> The finding that polling saturates has been shown in a number of previous papers, including https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05120 (TMLR), https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12147 (EMNLP 2025). I don't see how this paper's findings fundamentally differ from these papers, which should have been discussed as related work.

We apologize for missing these in our literature review and have added discussion of all three in the revised draft. That said, we believe our work differs substantively. These papers focus on majority voting and sample-level aggregation within a single model. By contrast, we (1) evaluate five aggregation methods drawn from the social-science polling literature (including the Surprisingly Popular Algorithm and confidence-weighted schemes), (2) study *cross-model* polling rather than within-model sampling, and (3) systematically probe the depth of inter-model correlation (see our response to Weakness 2). We view our paper as a meaningful extension of this line of work rather than a replication.

## The depth of correlation (Weakness 2)

> Explanation of why aggregation methods reflect consensus: this seems like an accepted notion in recent work, it's not clear how this explanation is novel.

It is widely acknowledged that LLMs are correlated, but *how deep* that correlation runs has not been carefully studied. Our key contribution here is showing that correlation is not merely a byproduct of shared factual knowledge. Even when conditioned on strings of random characters with no factual content, LLMs exhibit high agreement in their arbitrary A–D selections. This suggests the correlation is rooted in shared training pipelines and data rather than shared inductive reasoning, which we believe is a novel and informative finding that goes beyond folk wisdom.

## Chain-of-Thought evaluation

> Another fundamental issue with the paper is that the authors only test direct answer settings; sample-and-aggregation methods like SC generally work better with CoT, where it's been argued that sampling marginalizes over CoT paths. Not evaluating CoT at all is a major oversight.

We apologize for the confusion — CoT reasoning was enabled for all supporting models throughout our experiments. We have clarified this in the revised text. Our results therefore already capture marginalization over CoT paths, which strengthens rather than undermines our conclusions about polling saturation.

## SC and external verification (L194)

> The claim that SC only works in math because of external verification (L194, right side) strikes me as odd. What exactly do the authors mean by external verification?

We agree this was unclear in our writing. The sentence at L194 was referring to pass@k scaling with verifiers, not self-consistency proper. Papers studying pass@k [1, 2] find that scaling compute yields correct answers more easily *when a verifier is available* to select among candidates. We have revised L194 to make this distinction explicit.

We are aware that SC without verifiers has produced meaningful gains (5–10%) on benchmarks like GSM8K and SVAMP in the GPT-3 era. However, for more capable models (GPT-4 and above), SC gains have narrowed to 1–4%. Part of our motivation was understanding whether aggregation methods beyond majority voting could recover larger gains, and rigorously characterizing where group polling succeeds and fails.

- [1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787
- [2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17578

## Presentation

> The last parts of the paper look a bit rushed in terms of presentation.

Thank you for flagging this. We have revised the later sections for clarity; the original issues were due to space constraints rather than lack of care.

We appreciate the engagement with our work. We believe the concerns raised are addressable — the missing related work has been added, the CoT misunderstanding has been clarified, and the L194 language has been corrected. We hope the reviewer will consider whether these revisions, together with the novel contributions on cross-model correlation depth and multi-method polling, merit a revised assessment.

comments.author: Authors
comments.comment:
Dear Reviewer Y3sF,

We thank the reviewer for the follow-up and want to address the two remaining concerns directly.
On the substantiality of the extension. The reviewer acknowledges this is an extension of prior work on self-consistency and aggregation but considers it insufficient. We respectfully disagree with this assessment. Prior work (the three papers the reviewer cited, plus the confidence-weighted SC papers in the follow-up) studies within-model sampling: drawing multiple samples from one model and aggregating via majority vote or confidence weighting. Our work differs in three concrete ways that we believe are individually meaningful and collectively substantial:
(a) We study cross-model polling (five models, three families, 125 votes per question), which is the setting where crowd-wisdom theory most strongly predicts gains, since architectural and data diversity should reduce correlation. We show it does not.
(b) We evaluate the Surprisingly Popular algorithm and prediction-weighted voting, which are not variants of self-consistency but distinct aggregation paradigms from the social-science literature designed specifically to recover truth when the majority is wrong. Showing that these methods also fail for LLMs is a new result.
(c) We introduce a controlled experiment (random strings) that isolates the source of correlation, distinguishing shared knowledge from shared inductive biases. This is not tested in any of the cited prior works.

The confidence-weighted SC papers the reviewer cites in the follow-up (ACL 2024 short paper and the 2025 preprint) study a single model's confidence to reweight its own samples. We study whether confidence, predicted popularity, and surprise signals can function as proxy verifiers across model ensembles. These are different questions with different implications.

On the random-string experiment. The reviewer states that the conclusion ("LLMs behave similarly because they have similar training data and architectures") is folk wisdom. We agree that this is widely suspected, but suspecting something and demonstrating it empirically are different contributions. Before our experiment, the alternative hypothesis that inter-model correlation is primarily driven by shared factual knowledge (rather than architectural or training-pipeline similarity) was equally plausible. Our experiment rules out the knowledge-only explanation. We view this as analogous to how confirming a long-suspected physical constant is still a contribution even when the value is unsurprising.

The reviewer suggests we should instead explain what specifically about architecture and training causes consensus. We agree this is a valuable direction, but it is a mechanistic interpretability question that would require a fundamentally different methodology (e.g., ablations on pre-training data composition, architecture modifications, probing internal representations). We do not believe that a paper establishing a boundary condition for inference-time scaling should be required to also solve the mechanistic interpretability problem that the boundary raises.

We hope the reviewer will consider whether the standard for acceptance should be "does this paper answer every follow-up question it raises?" or "does this paper make a clear, well-supported claim that advances the field's understanding?" We believe our work meets the latter criterion.

comments.author: Authors
comments.comment:
Dear Reviewer 2bjV,

We appreciate the reviewer's continued engagement. We want to address the characterization of our findings as "primarily observational," since we believe this understates the contribution.

First, the random-string experiment (Section 4.3) is not observational but interventional: we construct a controlled setting that removes all factual content to isolate the source of inter-model correlation. This is a designed experiment with a clear null hypothesis (independent responses under zero signal), not passive observation of benchmark performance.

Second, we want to clarify the relationship between our work and the advanced inference-time methods the reviewer mentions (contrastive decoding, diverse beam search, reward models). These methods succeed precisely because they introduce external objectives, supervision signals, or structural constraints that break error correlation. Our paper's contribution is showing why such interventions are necessary: naive self-aggregation, even with methods drawn from the social-science polling literature that are known to recover truth from biased human crowds, cannot substitute for verification. Without this baseline result, one might reasonably expect that polling five diverse models with 125 votes should suffice. We show it does not, and we show why (correlated errors from shared priors, not just shared knowledge).

The reviewer suggests that engaging with advanced techniques would strengthen the paper. We agree these are important directions, but testing whether reward-model-guided search or contrastive decoding improves truthfulness is a different research question. Our claim is a boundary result: self-aggregation without external verification does not scale truthfulness. Methods that succeed by adding verification or breaking shared priors fall outside this regime and are fully consistent with our conclusion (Section 5.4). We believe establishing this boundary clearly is a meaningful contribution that the community can build on.

We would be grateful if the reviewer could reconsider whether the combination of (1) the controlled random-string experiment, (2) the cross-model polling analysis with five social-science aggregation methods, and (3) the social-prediction vs. truth-verification separation constitutes a sufficient contribution, given that the boundary we identify is both practically relevant and, as the reviewer noted, clearly presented.

rebuttal_acks.reasons:
Thank you for these clarifications. I had missed the bootstraped CIs which indeed make the correlation analyses more convincing. It is also reassuring to see that correlations are similar for both "truth amplification" and "false signal amplification". As I stated before, when LLM predictions correlate on right answers it's not a problem, the real issue is false positive/false negative cross-LLM correlations. 

I still don't like the 0-100 scale for LLM probing, but all in all, considering all of the paper, I do believe authors make a worthwhile contribution that opens the door for larger-scale future research in this direction. Too many applications exist which use LLM-as-a-judge type of solutions (eg for automated annotation) with too little caution, the AI community urgently needs to put out rigorous standards for what one can expect out of such off-the-shelf LLM-based ensemble methods, and this work is a first step in this direction. 

I have updated my score to an Accept. Should this paper be accepted, I do count on authors to make the changes they said they would, and additionally the following changes:
- regarding the 0-100 LLM scale: I advice authors to clearly state that such scales are not necessarily reliable and to suggest that future work investigates smaller scales (eg Likert scales) or evaluate against human labels.  
- separate the presentation of correlation results between truth/false labels, or at least mention that correlations are consistent across both labels.

I thank the authors for their thoughtful rebuttal, particularly their defense of binary formats (L1) and the forecasting benchmark (L2); however, I am maintaining my score of 3 because the core findings remain primarily observational. By strictly focusing on "naive" aggregation, the work unfortunately precludes advanced inference-time interventions (L3) and limits discussion on modern alignment algorithms (Q4). Furthermore, the absence of Chain-of-Thought evaluation (Q3) leaves a gap in understanding step-by-step error convergence, while deeper mechanistic questions regarding specific training methods (Q2) and pre/post-training origins (Q5) remain unanswered. Ultimately, while we agree that consensus serves better as a control signal than a strict truth measure (Q1 & L4), leaving this empirically untested makes the paper read as a study of basic polling that would be significantly strengthened by engaging with the advanced techniques currently used in the field.

Thank you for the response to my comments.

In response to these points:
1. While I see the social science connections, I would also point out that at least a subset of these have been studied, e.g. confidence-weighted SC is well-established (https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-short.28.pdf, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06233). I agree that the work is an extension of this prior work on self-consistency and aggregation -- my concern is not that the work is replicated prior work exactly, but that the particular extension proposed here on top of prior work is not substantial enough.

2. I see the value of this random experiment -- however, I think the conclusion (LLMs behave similarly because they have similar training data and architectures) is not particularly novel, and in fact is part of the "folk wisdom" about LLMs. I would have liked to see a more precise claim here on exactly what about their architecture/training data leads to this kind of consensus (even if this has to be done on smaller open-source or proxy models), understanding this phenomenon properly feels worthwhile. My concern here is that the current work documents this phenomenon but falls short of providing a strong explanation.

3. I appreciate the clarification on CoT, this addresses my concern. 

Overall, I feel that this paper could benefit from resubmission with more attention to related work, presentation, and perhaps depth of explanation for observed model qualities.
