our_title: Do Diffusion Models Dream of Electric Planes? Discrete and Continuous Simulation-Based Inference for Aircraft Design

match.matched_title: “Do Diffusion Models Dream of Electric Planes?” Discrete and Continuous Simulation-Based Inference for Aircraft Design

submission.title: “Do Diffusion Models Dream of Electric Planes?” Discrete and Continuous Simulation-Based Inference for Aircraft Design
submission.abstract: In this paper, we generate conceptual engineering designs of electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. We follow the paradigm of simulation-based inference (SBI), whereby we look to learn a posterior distribution over the full eVTOL design space. To learn this distribution, we sample over discrete aircraft configurations (topologies) and their corresponding set of continuous parameters. Therefore, we introduce a hierarchical probabilistic model consisting of two diffusion models. The first model leverages recent work on Riemannian Diffusion Language Modeling (RDLM) and Unified World Models (UWMs) to enable us to sample topologies from a discrete and continuous space. For the second model we introduce a masked diffusion approach to sample the corresponding parameters conditioned on the topology. Our approach rediscovers known trends and governing physical laws in aircraft design, while significantly accelerating design generation.
submission.tldr: Hierarchical sampling of aircraft designs via simulation-based inference in discrete and continuous spaces using diffusion models.
submission.lay_summary: This paper shows how AI can help design new electric aircraft. We build a system that learns from thousands of computer‑simulated aircraft and can then propose entirely new designs that still obey physics. The key challenge is that aircraft differ not only in their shapes and sizes, but also in their basic layout, for example how many wings or rotors they have. To handle this, the system uses two diffusion models: one chooses the overall aircraft layout starting from desired goals, and the other fills in the continuous dimensions associated with the layout and those goals. The models are trained on more than 30,000 valid aircraft generated with an aerospace simulator. When asked for designs that meet certain goals, like carrying more weight, the system produces sensible configurations, such as adding extra wings. Overall, the work shows that modern generative models can explore large, complex engineering problems and recover meaningful aircraft design trends.

reviews.summary:
**paper summary**

This paper applies simulation-based inference (sbi) to the design of electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. The core challenge is that eVTOL designs have mixed discrete-continuous structure: 144 possible topologies (number of wings, rotor configs, etc) each with variable-dimensional continuous parameter vectors (up to 136 parameters). The authors address this with a hierarchical two-stage model.

Stage 1 (MixeDiT) samples the topology conditioned on performance objectives, using RDLM (Riemannian diffusion on the probability simplex) for the discrete topology and a standard continuous denoising diffusion model for continuous observations, coupled via a shared loss (Eq. 4).

Stage 2 (MaskeDiT) extends the Simformer architecture with a topology-conditioned binary mask M_tau to handle variable-dimensional parameter vectors, training a score-based diffusion model over the joint (theta, x) conditioned on topology. The dataset consists of ~30k eVTOL designs generated by a probabilistic program and evaluated via the SUAVE simulator.

**review summary**
this is an applied paper with real/interesting problem + reasonable methods. This is refreshing relative to more common datasets/benchmarks. The strongest parts are the case studies showing recovery of physical design laws and the dataset contribution. The less-full parts are the methods contribution + quantitative comparison to baselines (NLE dominates MaskeDiT on MMD), and lack of clarity on what is genuinely novel vs what is direct application of RDLM and Simformer. I would appreciate a more thorough discussion on the attention masking + potential token masking (whether zeros are passed in or tokens omitted). I'm open to revising my assessment after some answers/clarifications to my questions.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
strengths:

- application is real/well-motivated. eVTOL design with 144 topologies x up to approx 130 continuous parameters genuinely exceeds what prior SBI methods handle
- the claim that this pushes D approx 130 against typical benchmarks at D approx 10 is well-supported
- the broader point about variable-dimensional posteriors is a meaningful challenge.
- the hierarchical factorization p(theta|x) = p(theta|tau, x) p(tau|x) is a natural decomposition that allows the per-topology parameter space to have fixed dimension
- the key technical contribution of MaskeDiT (using the topology mask as an attention mask and in the loss normalization) is novel / concretely described
- the mechanism for variable-dimensional diffusion models via masking is clean.
- case studies A-D are informative: physical laws recovered / inferred
- MixeDiT achieves KL(p_D(tau) || p_phi(tau)) = 0.0505 vs. KL vs. uniform = 1.4607, which is strong performance on the marginal topology distribution. The log-scale comparison in Fig. 3 shows that it captures low-prob. topologies.
- acknowledgment of SUAVE's limitations (lift prediction errors ~10% under normal conditions, likely larger outside them) in app. F is honest/appropriate.
- Dataset of ~30k designs with code/data in supplementary is a useful contribution independent of the models.

Weaknesses: See questions.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
(1) comparison with NLE (tables 1 + 3)

- the main baseline is NLE trained per topology. in Table 3, NLE achieves lower MMD. The paper's framing, that MaskeDiT achieves comparable performance while generalizing across topologies, is partially justified, but the MMD gap is not addressed head-on in the main text.

- the paper says NLE requires a separate model per topology. how many NLE models were trained for the 10 topologies in the comparison? what is the total number of parameters of NLE across all 10 models vs a single MaskeDiT model? the multi-topology generalization argument is stronger if the comparison is made explicit in terms of compute

- for topologies not in the top-10 by test sample count, NLE cannot be trained at all (too few samples). Does MaskeDiT generalize to these rare topologies in a way that NLE cannot? This seems important but is only mentioned in passing

- the C2ST numbers are above .5 for both methods. A C2ST of .777 means a binary classifier can distinguish generated vs real with 77.7% accuracy on the joint distribution. Is there a sense of what C2ST level is acceptable/achievable? For comparison, what does the Simformer achieve on its standard benchmarks?

- max marginal C2ST for MaskeDiT is .77 +- .076 vs NLE's .818 +- .043. NLE's higher max marginal C2ST means its worst marginal is worse than MaskeDiT's worst marginal. This is one metric where MaskeDiT is clearly better. Shouldn't this be emphasized more? it suggests MaskeDiT has more uniform quality across variables

(2) posterior predictive checks: the posterior predictive MSE of 9% (mean) is stated, but spread of 1.746 in normalized space (appendix G) is large and not discussed in the main text. looking at fig 19, several variables (cruise lift, state of charge) show wide distributions of x_true relative to the conditioning value x_obs, and a few show systematic biases where the posterior mean is visibly offset from x_obs.

- which variables have the largest posterior pred. error? is the 9% dominated by a few well-behaved variables (total mass)? This is still OK if quantified/stated.

- 9% MSE is computed as average over 10 x variables. are all 10 equally important for the design application? might be worth emphasizing calibration on "design critical" variables

(3) novelty relative to RDLM + Simformer

- MixeDiT is described as combining RDLM and UWM where the novel element is coupling the discrete RDLM with a continuous diffusion with shared loss L-MixeDiT. what would break if you trained two separate models (one RDLM for topology, one DDPM for observations) and composed them at inference? Would the joint transformer embedding provide any advantage?

- for MaskeDiT: the main change from Simformer is the binary mask in the attention and loss. is the mask applied to both rows and columns of attention? this would zero out both the attention from absent components to present ones and vice versa. The text mentions "zeroing out their corresponding token embeddings", which would handle the feedforward case, but the attention masking details deserve confirmation. 

- Also: when M_tau,i = 0 (absent component) is the corresponding token embedding still passed through the transformer with zero values, or is it completely excluded from the sequence? the former could waste compute at inference for rare topologies with few components; the latter is more efficient but harder to batch.

(4) data distribution and simulator: the dataset contains 30k valid designs from 300k initial samples (about 10%). the majority of rejected designs presumably fail structural/stability checks. this implies the valid design space is sparse in the prior.

- the probabilistic program uses a uniform categorical prior over topology. does this mean all 144 topologies are represented roughly equally in the prior, but the pass rate varies significantly across topologies? some topology families (multi-wing, high-rotor-count) might be systematically filtered, which would make p_data(tau) reflect both prior and simulator feasibility. Is the dataset topology distribution dominated by a few feasible configs?

(5) MixeDiT discrete sampling: argmax vs. sampling

- the paper uses argmax over p_tau to get one-hot topology. this is the MAP estimate, not a sample from the posterior. for multi-modal topology posteriors (when both monoplane and biplane are plausible, for example) argmax could underestimate topology diversity. what happens if you instead sample from the final simplex p_tau via Gumbel sampling or softmax temperature? is there a reason argmax is preferred over sampling here?

(6) loss weighting gamma
- gamma .9 strongly emphasizes the discrete head. this makes sense if topology accuracy is the main bottleneck, but it could also mean the continuous model is under-trained. how was gamma chosen? was there an ablation over gamma? the topology KL suggests good topology coverage, but there is no separate eval of the continuous head — the full pipeline eval in 5.3 mixes both, making it hard to isolate whether gamma=.9 is appropriate.

(7) time sampling

- MixeDiT samples t_tau ~ q(t_tau) and t_x ~ U(0,1) independently. this means the discrete and continuous diffusion processes are at different noise levels at each training step. is there any analysis/ablation of whether correlated/synchronized time steps t_tau ~ t_x would be helpful? 

- generation also uses decoupled step sizes. in principle, the topology could be more certain (lower t_tau) before the parameters are sampled. is there a curriculum/annealing of t_tau vs t_x timing during sampling that could help?

(8) dataset split + topology coverage.

the train/test split is 20k/10k. Since there are 144 topologies and only 10 are used for MaskeDiT eval (those with >200 test samples), many topologies have fewer than 200 test samples. 

- how many of the 144 topologies have sufficient data for per-topology eval? 
- Does the model perform well on topologies that are under-represented in training?

(9) minor comments

- broken ref in appendix D.2 "When considering the 3D samples in Fig. ??" (maybe 7 or 13)
- main text should cite/reference the complete table in Appendix I with additional metrics

reviews.summary: The paper presents an SBI-based framework for aircraft design. The authors present a pipeline for learning a diffusion-based generative model on data of aircraft design topology, continuous design parameters, and the corresponding simulated aircraft performance and characteristics. The framework uses a diffusion-based generative model specifically designed for the mixed, variable-length parameter space. Empirical results on the eVTOL design are presented.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
This is a neat work with well-motivated, carefully designed techniques for simulation-based inference of aircraft design. The technical challenges are clearly presented and are indeed meaningful, and the empirical results are convincing enough to support the utility of the method.

While the presentation is mostly nice, I feel some technical choices are not fully explained, as questioned in the next form.

Below are minor points to which I don't need particular responses unless there is any misunderstanding.
- Could you provide any hints on the computational resources needed for running the SUAVE simulation? How long did it take to run the 300,000 runs? Such information would be helpful for readers.
- About the preprocessing phase, the authors state: "We move the generation of internal fuselage and wing cross-sections to the run-time simulation ... ." What is the motivation behind this choice? Are these two variables nuisance and do not need to be inferred?
- Do you think the final data size, 30,276, was sufficient? Any possibility of further improvement with larger data?
- How does the simulator, SUAVE, robustly perform on the support of the prior distribution? Are there failure cases that SUAVE does not give plausible outputs (other than the structural interference)?
- Although the title of Section 5.2 mentions "Posterior over ...", its contents are on the analysis of the likelihood estimation.
- No (expected) coverage analysis is presented in the empirical results. It will be helpful to assess the quality of the posterior.
- In Figure 4, the posterior variance looks way larger than I expected. For example the range of 1000-3000kg of total mass of such a light aircraft sounds a big deal. Do you have any comments on the posterior variance as well?
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
(1) If I understood correctly, the model is learned so that the observation, $x$, can either be sampled or conditioned upon. I first thought sampling of $x$ is not of interest here and that $x$ should only be in the conditioning part because the goal is the design optimization using (samples from) posterior $p(\tau,\theta \mid x)$. Why do you want to enable sampling of $x$ as well?

(2) The MaskeDiT part of the model uses the Simformer architecture. Is the arbitrary conditioning capability of Simformer essential for the proposed method? I could not fully follow the motivation to use Simfomer here. Could you elaborate more?
reviews.final_justification: The information provided in the authors' response would further strengthen the paper. I keep my originally positive score (5).

reviews.summary: This paper presents a novel diffusion-based framework for generating conceptual designs of VTOL aircraft. The authors follow a simulation-based inference (SBI) framework utilizing hierarchical diffusion models; the first model generates the topology from a set of 144 options, while the second samples the specific parameters. The full pipeline allows for the generation of conceptual designs from physics parameters such as lift, drag, and mass. They use SUAVE as a data generator and validator to assess whether the generated designs are physically plausible.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

- The paper presents a highly novel method for simulation-based inference based on generative modeling, which would allow for faster design cycles compared to other tools such as SUAVE.

- The paper is technically sound. The authors extensively explain their framework, method, and results, which appears to make the work reproducible. Also they include the code as supplementary material.

- This paper could serve as a basis for future work to improve design cycles in engineering.


## Weaknesses

- The paper could benefit from additional visual explanations. While Figure 1 and Figure 2 are included, they are not explicitly explained in the text.

- Furthermore, extra visualizations of the framework's inference process (e.g., showing the transition from noise to a final design) would be very helpful for clarity.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Right now, your framework is limited to 144 aircraft topologies. Would it be possible to extend it to previously unexplored aircraft designs? For example, could it be used to discover more efficient designs that are currently outside the conventional design space?

2. What is the difference between your framework and, for example, the use of surrogate modeling of CFD flows for the continuous optimization of aerodynamic surface designs? What are the specific use cases for each, and how do you differentiate your framework from these established approaches?

3. You compare your model to NLE (another machine learning-based method). Do other classical methods exist, aside from SUAVE, for this task?
reviews.final_justification:
I recommend accepting this paper. I believe it proposes an original framework to address a problem that is currently understudied.

The authors’ rebuttal has clearly addressed my previous concerns, and they will improve figures for more clarity for final version, so I am increasing my score to support acceptance. I believe this study will be valuable to both the engineering and applied ML communities.

reviews.summary: The main idea of the paper is about generative design for electric vertical take off and landing aircraft through simulation-based inference. The core idea is a hierarchical two stage diffusion pipeline. The first stage samples aircraft topology conditioned on desired performance observations. The second stage samples continuous design parameters conditioned on the sampled topology and the same observations. The result is evaluated on a large dataset generated with a conceptual aircraft simulator and additional feasibility filters.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

1) The problem settings are significant. The paper addresses a genuinely important and difficult problem. Moving simulation based inference beyond small benchmarks toward a realistic engineering design pipeline is valuable, and the application domain is compelling.

2) The idea is innovative. The combination of a topology model with a topology conditioned parameter model is a nontrivial way to handle mixed discrete and continuous design spaces. The masking mechanism for variable dimensional inference is also practically meaningful.

### Weakness:

1) The practical claim is weakened by the fidelity limits of the simulator and the dataset construction. The paper itself acknowledges that many generated aircraft are unrealistic and that the simulator may be inaccurate for unusual configurations. This does not invalidate the machine learning contribution, but it does reduce confidence in the downstream design significance.

2) The quantitative evaluation is not strong enough to fully support the paper’s claims. The main baseline comparison is limited to neural likelihood estimation on only ten topologies with sufficient test frequency. Moreover, the baseline is actually better on average maximum mean discrepancy, which makes the superiority of the proposed method less clear.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How sensitive are the results to the large rejection rate in dataset generation? If the learned model is robust to this source of mismatch, my confidence in the practical usefulness of the method would increase.

2) The comparison with neural likelihood estimation is limited to ten common topologies, and neural likelihood estimation achieves lower average maximum mean discrepancy. Can you clarify whether the main advantage of your method is scalability across topologies, conditional flexibility, or better sample quality?
reviews.final_justification: Thanks for the reply, I will raise my score

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful assessment. We address each concern below and will revise the manuscript accordingly.

> 1. The practical claim is weakened by the fidelity limits…

 We appreciate the point raised by the reviewer. As noted in the paper, our work occurs at the conceptual design stage, where these cheap to run, low fidelity tools are standard, and where designers are used to working with large inaccuracies and high uncertainties (see Appendix E, in “Limitations of dataset approach”). High‑fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) or multidisciplinary analysis (MDA) for these unconventional configurations is prohibitively expensive: accurately simulating just a single aircraft at this level can require months of expert effort only to explore a restricted set of disciplines, e.g. solely aerodynamics in the case of CFD. The goal of the conceptual design stage is therefore not to accurately evaluate the performance of an aircraft within a single discipline e.g. structural, aerodynamic etc., but rather to explore a trade space dominated by trends and interactions between performance and design variables. Within this context, our goal is not high‑fidelity design accuracy (reserved for the detailed design stage), but rather to robustly learn the typical trends seen in aircraft performance as correlated with design. As for design realism, our framework can generate both realistic and unrealistic designs, which is somewhat necessary for being able to generate novel though realistic designs. As demonstrated by case study A, realistic aircraft can be obtained quite easily through rigorous conditioning, which can also be further explored in future work. We appreciate the reviewer’s observation that this does not invalidate the ML contribution. As better, cheaper simulators become increasingly available, such as surrogate models of high fidelity CFD, future work can apply the same methods to these higher fidelity simulators.

> 2. …limited to neural likelihood estimation on only ten topologies…

Please see the additional quantitative evaluation in response to the reviewer’s second key question below.

## Key Questions

>1. How sensitive are the results to the large rejection rate…


We highlight the practical usefulness of the method via the successful inclusion of the posterior predictive checks. In these checks we feed generated designs back through SUAVE and compare the resulting performance distributions to the conditioning specifications. The close agreement we observe indicates that the learned model is robust to the mismatch between the dataset generation prior and the feasible design space, and correctly recreates feasible designs.


>2. …comparison with neural likelihood estimation is limited …main advantage of your method is scalability across topologies, conditional flexibility, or better sample quality…


We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful question. The comparison of MaskeDiT with neural likelihood estimation (NLE) is quite restrictive - NLE requires training a completely different model for each topology, which becomes impractical in the settings considered here without prohibitive quantities of data. Our goal is to enable flexible conditioning and scalability across many topologies with a single unified model. We ran additional experiments to demonstrate that this goal is met.
| Training set size | **NLE** |        | **MaskeDiT** |        |
|-------------------|---------|--------|--------------|--------|
|                   | MMD     | Joint C2ST | MMD     | Joint C2ST |
| 2890 | 0.00151 | 0.693 | 0.00428 | 0.807 |
| 2741 | 0.00287 | 0.699 | 0.00391 | 0.882 |
| 1371 | 0.00068 | 0.735 | 0.00450 | 0.764 |
| 1341 | 0.00108 | 0.722 | 0.00338 | 0.729 |
| 1174 | 0.00285 | 0.792 | 0.00495 | 0.865 |
| 1091 | 0.00307 | 0.833 | 0.00324 | 0.736 |
| 392  | 0.00300 | 0.764 | 0.00351 | 0.767 |
| 31   | NaN     | 1.000 | 0.00396 | 0.678 |
| 18   | NaN     | 1.000 | 0.00460 | 0.804 |

The table above shows the C2ST and MMD versus the number of data points for 9 cases. Firstly, note that for the two lowest-data topologies presented, NLE is trained on so little data that NaN values are predicted, leading to C2STs of one and NaN MMD values. Secondly, note that across topologies, C2ST and MMD remain relatively stable when using MaskeDiT, whereas C2ST improves with greater data for NLE but is poor in the low data cases. NLE and MixeDiT are roughly equivalent in terms of C2ST in between ~400 to ~1500 training data points. In terms of MMD, which (as a kernel based metric) is more sensitive to overfitting than C2ST, certain topologies perform much better than others, and though the MMD is worse on average for the MaskeDiT architecture, it is also more stable.

Overall, these new results further demonstrate the ability of our approach to flexibly scale across topologies unlike the inflexible NLE approach.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and address each point below. We will incorporate these clarifications in the revision.

> … Figure 1 and Figure 2 are included, they are not explicitly explained…

Additional explanations of figures 1 and 2 will be included in the text for the final version, similar to the descriptions below.

Figure 1: The left shows the tree of components for an aircraft with 1 main wing, two forward propellers and four lifting rotors. The middle shows the outputs from SUAVE, which is the design performance $x$, for this aircraft. The right plot shows the CAD rendering of the same design as depicted in the tree.

Figure 2: MixeDiT-MaskeDiT architecture. Models are summarized on the left, with the full design pipeline highlighted on the right. Specifically, the leftmost figure after the key provides an overview of the MixeDiT model. MixeDiT uses a discrete model acting on topology $\tau$ coupled to a continuous model acting on performance $x$, we show the flexibility in using two independent diffusion processes. The middle figure depicts MaskeDiT, which uses the design $x$ and topology $\tau$, expressed as a mask $m_i$ in order to determine the appropriate design parameter values $x$. The rightmost figure illustrates a full design pipeline, where MixeDiT is used to determine $\tau$ from $x$, and MaskeDiT is used to determine $\theta$ from $\tau$ and $x$.

> … extra visualizations…

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion, and we will include further visualizations in the appendix. 

## Key Questions

> 1. ...framework is limited to 144 aircraft topologies… possible to extend it to previously unexplored aircraft designs?

The 144 topologies used in this work cover a broad range of unconventional aircraft architectures and were chosen to test mixed continuous–discrete SBI at scale. In practice, we find that this set is sufficient to cover novel aircraft well beyond what is considered conventional by aircraft designers. However, extending the architecture to a broader set of topologies is possible and will be considered in future work.

>2. …difference between your framework… use of surrogate modeling of CFD flows

Surrogate modeling of aerodynamics flows (using CFD or otherwise, or other surrogate models for thermal, structural etc.) is typically used as a cheap way to evaluate the performance of a fixed aerodynamic surface, where the goal is to improve a known baseline design, and hence return a single-point optimized design. In fact, SUAVE itself uses a Gaussian Process surrogate of a Vortex Lattice Method in order to predict aerodynamic performance.

Our approach addresses a fundamentally different problem: inverse design over a multi-topology, multi-physics space, focusing on **inverse-design**. Consistent with our SBI setting, we learn a full conditional distribution over aircraft designs that meet specified performance targets. This SBI formulation enables sampling and comparison across vastly different topologies, which is not possible with typical surrogate modelling based optimization methods that focus on purely the forward process.

>3. …Do other classical methods exist, aside from SUAVE, for this task?

We thank the reviewer for raising this question and for prompting clarification regarding SUAVE. SUAVE is a simulator and, as such, cannot be used for design generation or sampling: it operates strictly in the forward direction and evaluates performance $x$ only once one already has a fully specified design $\theta$.  

Classical approaches to design generation in aerospace engineering generally fall into two categories. Optimization‑based methods are powerful but typically applied at later design stages [Martins21] due to:

1. the size and complexity of the conceptual design space

2. point solutions being less useful at earlier stages, where various concepts (or in our case a distribution of concepts) is preferred

Knowledge-based engineering (KBE) consists of procedural, rule‑based methods that emulate an engineer’s step-by-step reasoning. These approaches, largely explored in the 1990s, tend to rely on extensive conditional logic, are widely regarded as inflexible, and have seen limited development in recent decades [Kroo88].

For the full paper, we will add descriptions of these approaches in the “Additional Literature” section of the Appendix.

[Kroo88] Kroo, Ilan. "A quasi-procedural, knowledge-based system for aircraft design." Aircraft Design, Systems and Operations Conference. 1988.

[Martins21] Martins, Joaquim RRA, and Graeme J. Kennedy. "Enabling large-scale multidisciplinary design optimization through adjoint sensitivity analysis." Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization 64.5 (2021): 2959-2974.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the encouraging and insightful feedback. We address each point below and will integrate the requested clarifications and additional context into the revised manuscript.

### Response to minor points

> Could you provide any hints on the computational resources …

Appendix H highlights the ~25s per simulation on a 14 core CPU. Thus, 300,000 designs takes about 125,000 minutes, which is about 2090 hours, or about 86 days – almost three months if you were to do this in serial. We did our best to parallelise this runtime with the resources we had available. It took us approximately 2-3 weeks.

> …internal fuselage and wing cross-sections to the run-time simulation… motivation behind this …

The motivation is mainly tractability: including the internal fuselage and wing cross-sections would increase the design space substantially (from 136 to 331 continuous variables) while contributing limited value for the conceptual-level trends we study. We therefore treat them as simulator-side design uncertainty rather than primary inference targets.
> Do you think the final data size, 30,276, was sufficient? …

We appreciate the question and we would expect performance to improve further with larger datasets, particularly by capturing rarer configurations. However, the current dataset has shown to be sufficient for the model to recover meaningful physical trends across a wide range of topologies, suggesting good coverage at the conceptual‑design level.
> How does the simulator … robustly perform on the support of the prior…

SUAVE has known failure modes on parts of the prior’s support. We explicitly detect these cases and reject the corresponding samples. The most common failure modes are:

* Structural infeasibility, such as extremely slender wings or component intersections
* Non‑convergent simulations, where the mission solver fails to find a feasible trajectory
* Vorex Lattice Method (aerodynamic computation) mesh failures, which can occasionally produce artifacts such as negative drag, or very large drag

> … title of Section 5.2…

Thank you for pointing this out: Section 5.2 analyzes the learned likelihood, not the posterior. We will update the section heading accordingly to avoid confusion.

> In Figure 4, the posterior variance looks way larger than I expected…

The reviewer raises an excellent point regarding the posterior predictive check. Since submission of the paper, we found that we were plotting the posterior predictive check incorrectly. After corrections, we have much narrower variance.

| Variable | L2 Error | Variance |
|---------|----------|----------|
| Avg. Drag | 0.03664 | 0.92336 |
| Avg. Lift | 0.06586 | 0.24366 |
| Fuselage Mass [kg] | 0.01894 | 1.31054 |
| Lift Rotor Mass [kg] | 0.15431 | 0.73251 |
| Total Mass [kg] | 0.07108 | 0.07895 |
| Total Wing Mass [kg] | 0.04837 | 0.48306 |
| Cruise AoA | 0.03357 | 1.53491 |
| Figure of Merit | 0.01235 | 0.63502 |
| Cruise Lift | 0.06586 | 0.24366 |
| State of Charge | 0.02358 | 0.47555 |

Average L2 error is 5.3%, and the square root of the average variance is 0.82. Variance is dominated by cruise angle of attack and fuselage mass - we expect a large variety of cruise angles of attack even if the designs do not vary much. The MSE is dominated by the error in the lift rotor mass, with all other errors under 7.1%. We will correct this in the final version.

## Key Questions

> (1) If I understood correctly, the model is learned so that the observation, x, can either be sampled or conditioned upon …

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. While the primary focus of this work is indeed conditioning on specified performance targets x, enabling the model to sample x as well is useful in realistic design settings where not all performance variables are known or fixed in advance. In practice, aircraft requirements rarely specify the full vector of performance metrics, and our framework allows designers to condition on a subset (e.g. lift and drag) while leaving others (e.g. state of charge) unconstrained. This is done in case studies A and B.

> (2) … Is the arbitrary conditioning capability of Simformer essential …

First, Simformer’s arbitrary‑conditioning capability provides the flexibility required for many inverse‑design tasks. Once the topology is fixed, MaskeDiT can condition on any subset of design or performance variables, as illustrated in case studies A and B. This is an essential property for conceptual‑stage design, where only partial specifications are typically available. Second, Gloeckler et al. demonstrate that Simformer outperforms traditional NPE‑style approaches for posterior inference.

Once again thank you for your encouraging review and feedback.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback and address each point below. We will incorporate these clarifications in the revision.

## (1) comparison with NLE (tables 1 + 3)

Thanks to the reviewer’s comments, we have included an **additional experiment at the end of the response to reviewer qwbu**.

> … NLE trained per topology… generalizing across topologies …

NLE trains a separate model per topology, allowing specialization and thus lower MMD. MaskeDiT must generalize across many topologies with a single model, therefore we wish to maintain comparable sample quality while learning over a much larger mixed discrete-continuous space. This enables flexible conditioning and trend learning across topologies. We provide further evidence at the end of the response to reviewer qwbu.

> … NLE requires a separate model per topology… explicit in terms of compute

Ten NLE models (50k parameters each) were trained. Scaling to 144 topologies requires 7.2M parameters vs. 5.1M for MaskeDiT (41% more).

> for topologies not in the top-10… Does MaskeDiT generalize …

As can be seen in the additional experiments at the end of the response to reviewer qwbu, and from the physical trends recovered in the case studies, MixeDiT generalizes to rarer topologies.

> the C2ST numbers are above .5 for both methods …

Simformer’s largest standard benchmark, the 20 dimensional Hidden Markov Model, reaches 0.57 with 10,000 samples and 0.53 with 100,000. As no standard benchmarks exist for mixed discrete-continuous design, we rely on posterior predictive checks and case studies.

> max marginal C2ST for MaskeDiT …

We will emphasise the maximum marginal C2ST metric more in the text. 

## (2) Posterior predictive checks


See response to reviewer LP15 for discussion of posterior predictive checks. Lift rotor mass dominates the PPC error; lift and drag coefficients are the most critical variables, while component masses are less important.
## (3) novelty relative to RDLM + Simformer

The reviewer highlighted the sparsity of details regarding the novelty relative to RDLM and Simformer.

> … what would break if you trained two separate models…

The joint discrete-continuous formulation enables conditioning in either direction, unlike methods with fixed sampling order.

> …is the mask applied to both rows and columns of attention?...

For MaskeDiT, the attention mask zeros out both the relevant rows and columns, preventing attention in either direction.

> …M_tau,i = 0 (absent component)... token embedding… with zero values…

We pass the corresponding token embedding through with zero values, we will note the reviewer’s suggestion about excluding zeroed tokens.

## (4) data distribution and simulator

>...pass rate varies significantly across topologies…

The prior is intentionally broad and many samples fail structural or stability checks. The topology prior is governed by the distributions in Appendix E, and it encodes only coarse domain knowledge, such as rough parameter scales, rather than a joint feasible set (which for this problem is unknown a priori). In our test dataset, topologies have a median of 182 samples, with the top‑10 topologies counting for 22.4% of feasible designs.

## (5) MixeDiT discrete sampling: argmax vs. sampling

We appreciate the insightful question. In MixeDiT, we follow the RDLM decoding rule and use argmax over the final simplex as a deterministic readout, as the RDLM process approaches a one-hot endpoint during training, making argmax stable. However, argmax might underestimate topology diversity when multiple topologies remain plausible, and we will note this limitation and discuss sampling-based alternatives in the final version.

## (6) loss weighting gamma

We selected $ \gamma $ through a grid search, evaluating topology cross-entropy over the validation set. The choice of $ \gamma = 0.9 $ emerged as the best trade‑off in this sweep.

## (7) time sampling

> MixeDiT samples t_tau ~ q(t_tau) and t_x ~ U(0,1) independently…

Thank you for this thoughtful suggestion. In training, we sample $ t_{\tau} $ and $t_x$​ independently so that the model is exposed to mixed discrete/continuous noise levels. As in Zhu et al., this was intended to preserve flexibility between the topology and observation channels, but we did not run an ablation against synchronised timesteps. For sampling, our current Algorithm 2 uses a synchronised schedule. We did not explore curricula where topology converges earlier than the observations, though this is a promising extension.

## (8) dataset split + topology coverage

There are 10 topologies with more than 200 test samples. For the discussion on performance for under-represented datasets, see the additional experiment and the response to (4).

## (9) minor comments

We thank the reviewer for the minor comments, which will be amended.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
**Summary**

In this paper, the authors propose a hierarchical diffusion-based approach for Simulation Based Inference (SBI) in the specific context of aircraft design. More precisely, they consider MixeDiT for discrete topologies and simulator observation in a first stage (multimodal diffusion model). Then they consider MaskeDiT to infer the continuous parameters given the topology and the current observation. After the training of this model, the authors were able to recover true aerospace design trend. 

**Reviewer Concerns**

All reviewers agree that this is a real engineering problem, truly benefiting from recent generative modelling approaches. As highlighted by Reviewer qZeg "application is real/well-motivated. eVTOL design with 144 topologies x up to approx 130 continuous parameters genuinely exceeds what prior SBI methods handle". Reviewers appreciated the abilities of the model to recover physical laws. Most of the reviewer concerns (in particular regarding the limited size of the data) were successfully addressed during the rebuttal period.

our_title: HyperMLP: An Integrated Perspective for Sequence Modeling

match.matched_title: HyperMLP: An Integrated Perspective for Sequence Modeling

submission.title: HyperMLP: An Integrated Perspective for Sequence Modeling
submission.abstract: Self-attention is often viewed as probabilistic query-key lookup, motivating designs that preserve normalized attention scores and fixed positional semantics. We advocate a simpler and more unified perspective: an autoregressive attention head can be viewed as a dynamic two-layer MLP whose weights are instantiated from the context history. From this view, attention scores form an ever-growing hidden representation, and standard MLP activations such as ReLU or GLU naturally implement input-conditioned selection over a context-dependent memory pool rather than a probability distribution. Based on this formulation, we introduce \textbf{HyperMLP} and \textbf{HyperGLU}, which learn dynamic mixing in both feature space and sequence space, using a reverse-offset (lag) layout to align temporal mixing with autoregressive semantics. We provide theoretical characterizations of the expressivity and implications of this structure, and empirically show that HyperMLP/HyperGLU consistently outperform strong softmax-attention baselines under matched parameter budgets.
submission.lay_summary: Modern AI models for language, vision, and many other domains rely on a component called attention, which lets the model decide which parts of its input to focus on at each step. Today this is almost always implemented in one specific way, by turning scores into probabilities and taking a weighted average, and most efforts to improve attention still try to preserve that exact shape. We step back and show that attention is more naturally described as a small neural network whose internal connections are built on the fly from the surrounding context, which means the "probability" interpretation is not essential. Building on this view, we introduce two new components, HyperMLP and HyperGLU, that learn richer ways of mixing information across both features and time while respecting the causal structure that language models depend on. Under matched compute and parameter budgets, they consistently outperform standard attention across language modeling, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

reviews.summary: This paper reframes autoregressive attention as a dynamic two-layer MLP whose hidden pre-activation is the length-t score vector and whose weights are instantiated from the context prefix. Building on this perspective, the authors propose HyperMLP and HyperGLU, which augment the standard attention mechanism with learned input-conditioned sequence-space mixing operators R(1)(x) and R(2)(x) parameterized in diagonal-plus-low-rank form with rank r_s=16, alongside feature-space gating via diagonal cores M(1), M(2). A reverse-offset layout is introduced to align the canonical prefix extension of these temporal operators with autoregressive truncation semantics. The paper provides extensive theoretical analysis: expressivity characterizations showing HyperMLP is a strict superset of token-wise ReLU attention, a three-stage memory view, and a budget asymmetry argument justifying QK compression over VO compression to pay for temporal mixing. Experiments are conducted on the MAD synthetic benchmark suite and NanoGPT/OpenWebText2 at small scale, plus FineWeb-Edu language modeling at 340M/15B tokens and 1.3B/100B tokens, compared against softmax attention, ReLU attention, and several sub-quadratic alternatives.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The paper is well written and easy to follow
2. The controlled design study in Table 1 is well-structured.

Cons:
1. The introduction explicitly motivates HyperMLP by arguing that "marginal returns of continued scaling are increasingly difficult to sustain," positioning the work as an expressivity-per-resource improvement relevant to large-scale practice. Yet the largest experiment is 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, roughly three orders of magnitude smaller than models where scaling saturation is actually observed. At the 1.3B scale, benchmark scores are generally low across all models, e.g., MMLU-Pro ranges from 0.109–0.120, MATH from 0.001–0.013, making it difficult to determine whether HyperGLU's aggregate ranking advantage reflects a durable architectural improvement or noise amplified by near-random-baseline performance. Without experiments at 7B+ or evidence that the gap widens (or at least persists) with scale, the central expressivity-per-resource claim remains untested in the regime where it matters.

2. The language modeling evaluation relies heavily on aggregate ranking over many low-sensitivity benchmarks, obscuring whether gains are meaningful. At the 1.3B/100B scale (Table 2), HyperGLU achieves Avg Rank 1.88 with 9 top-1 finishes, but inspecting individual benchmarks reveals that many "wins" are within noise margins. With no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests reported across any evaluation, it is impossible to tell whether the aggregate ranking advantage is statistically robust or an artifact of many near-tied comparisons where small fluctuations cascade into rank differences. The one benchmark where HyperGLU shows a large absolute gain ARC-Challenge is not discussed or explained, making it unclear whether this reflects a genuine capability difference or an evaluation artifact.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: At sequence length 1024, HyperGLU already shows 32–35% wall-clock overhead relative to FlashAttention (Table 5), what is the measured wall-clock overhead at sequence lengths 4096 and 8192?

reviews.summary:
This paper argues that self-attention can be viewed as a dynamic, two-layer MLP where the weights are initialized from the context. 
Build on this perspective, the authors propose HyperMLP and HyperGLU, which incorporate sequence level mixing to overcome the modeling limitations of traditional attention.
The paper provides thorough theoretical analysis for the characterizations of this formulation and really detailed explanation in Appendix.
Empirically, the authors conduct detailed controlled design study and report gains over softmax and ReLU attention baselines on language modeling tasks.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Although the perspective of treating MLPs as attentions has been widely accepted, taking the opposite approach—viewing attention as a form of MLP—represents a relatively new alternative. This proposal introduces an insightful and unified framework that allows us to view a wide variety of different model architectures through this single perspective.
2. This paper presents several theoretical claims (e.g. how input-dependent mixing can generalizes polyhedral routing), providing insights that help explain architectural design choices and experimental results.
I have reviewed the mathematical analysis and found it to be correct. Overall, these are quite helpful for developing a deeper understanding of the work.
3. The authors are very honest about the limitation of their work, specifically efficiency and scalability problems.

Weaknesses:
1. The idea of treating attention as an MLP is quite similar to previous approaches that view attention as a hypernetwork. [1][2]
In fact, the latter one maybe more accurate since the weights of the MLP in this context are dynamically initialized based on the input. 
A detailed comparison with these related work will be beneficial to better understand the contribution of this work.
2. The overall logic and reading experience of the paper (for myself) are not particularly smooth, especially in section 2.4 and 2.5. 
The introduction from existing problems to new modelsing methods in section 2.4 is not very smooth (why $W_{MLP}^{(j)}$ is parameterized like this?) and the mathematical notation in section 2.5 is too dense without a clear logical thread. To better present the work to more general audience, I suggest making the mathematical intuition much clearer before each mathematical claims. The authors could also move more content into the Appendix.
3. The scope of experiments remain limited. Currently, experiments have only been conducted on MAD framework and language modeling task. Broader domains, such as ViT, have not yet been explored. Also, the scale of the experiments remain small.
4. Figure 1 and 3 have too much information and it's hard to get the main idea.

[1] Mai, Florian, et al. "Hypermixer: An mlp-based low cost alternative to transformers." Proceedings of the 61st annual meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (volume 1: long papers). 2023.

[2] Schug, Simon, et al. "Attention as a hypernetwork." arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.05816 (2024).
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Proposition 2.6 (iii) mentions that linear attention will collapse the selective mechanism because the active set is always the full pool. However, in this perspective, softmax attention is actually full-pool selection as well. More specifically, the entire analysis is mainly built on ReLU attention. Would there be any difference when considering softmax attention?
2. The authors mention that they use $n_{head} = 2$ for their method, but it's not clear what is used for other methods. If all the methods use two heads, I'd like to see how the standard setup for attention performs.
3. In a long-context setting, since this method involves modeling along the sequence dimension, would this make the model more difficult to train? I would like to see some results under long context setting.
4. Why are the baselines for two model sizes different in language modeling task? This seems a bit like cherry-picking.
5. I was wondering if it is possible to extend the MoE to attention with this perspective. I would like to hear the author's thoughts regarding this.
reviews.final_justification:
This is one of the few papers I have reviewed that strikes a balance between theoretical depth and practical application.
The authors addressed the vast majority of my questions during the rebuttal phase, which has given me a much deeper understanding of the work. Overall, I believe this is a high-quality paper that deserves to be accepted.

reviews.summary: This paper presents a unified interpretation of autoregressive self-attention, showing that an attention head can be viewed as a dynamic two-layer MLP whose effective weights are instantiated by the context prefix. From this perspective, attention scores need not be constrained to form a probability distribution via softmax; instead, standard MLP nonlinearities such as ReLU or GLU can be understood as performing input-dependent selection over a context-conditioned memory. Motivated by this reformulation, the authors introduce HyperMLP and HyperGLU, which perform dynamic mixing in both feature and sequence dimensions using a reverse-offset (lag) parameterization designed to respect autoregressive structure. The paper complements this architectural proposal with theoretical analysis of its expressivity and structural implications, and reports consistent gains over strong softmax-attention baselines under matched parameter budgets in language modeling experiments.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
S1. The central reinterpretation of autoregressive attention as a dynamic two-layer MLP is technically credible and conceptually unifying. It provides a coherent foundation for the proposed architecture, and the paper supports this perspective with nontrivial theoretical characterization rather than relying solely on intuition.

S2. The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad and, importantly, uses matched parameter budgets across comparisons. This makes the reported gains more convincing, as they are less likely to be explained by differences in model scale and more likely to reflect the benefits of the proposed operator itself.

S3. The architecture is carefully designed to respect autoregressive structure, particularly through the reverse-offset (lag) layout for temporal mixing. This is a meaningful technical choice, since sequence-mixing methods often overlook prefix-consistency and causal alignment in autoregressive settings.

W1. The practical efficiency of the method remains unclear relative to highly optimized attention implementations such as FlashAttention. Even if the asymptotic complexity is competitive or favorable, wall-clock speed and systems-level efficiency will strongly affect real-world adoption.

W2. The proposed design introduces additional architectural complexity, including the lag-based layout, low-rank parameterization, and nonlinear activation/gating choices. These components may require substantial tuning and specialized kernel engineering to achieve stable training and competitive throughput.

W3. The evidence at frontier scale is still limited. In particular, it remains uncertain how well the approach will perform for substantially larger models, longer context windows, and more mature large-scale training regimes without further scaling studies.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can the authors report end-to-end training and decoding throughput, peak memory, and KV/cache-related costs relative to strong FlashAttention-based baselines on the same hardware and precision, at context lengths such as 2k/8k/32k? Since practical adoption depends heavily on systems efficiency, it would also help to clarify what kernel/operator optimizations are still missing for HyperMLP/HyperGLU.

2. Can the authors clarify the assumptions and scope of the theoretical characterization? In particular, which conclusions are structural and which depend on simplifying assumptions? Do the theory results imply any specific inductive biases, expressivity tradeoffs, or limitations relative to standard softmax attention?

3. How sensitive are the results to the main design choices, especially the lag layout, low-rank parameterization, and activation/gating form? Which components appear essential versus mainly efficiency-oriented? A compact sensitivity study and a recommended default configuration would make the method easier to assess and reproduce.

4. Are there regimes where standard softmax attention remains clearly preferable, or where the gains of HyperMLP/HyperGLU diminish? For example, do tasks requiring very sharp token-level selection or exact retrieval expose limitations of the proposed operator? If so, would the authors expect hybrid architectures to be a more promising direction than full replacement?

5. Since the method introduces lag-based sequence mixing, can the authors comment on behavior as context length increases beyond the training regime? If available, results on train-short/test-long settings would help clarify whether the proposed structure preserves, improves, or degrades long-context behavior relative to softmax attention.
reviews.limitations: A clearer limitations discussion would strengthen the paper. In particular, practical efficiency appears likely to depend substantially on specialized kernel/implementation work, especially when compared against highly optimized attention implementations such as FlashAttention. In addition, the current experiments do not yet establish performance at frontier model scales or in substantially longer-context regimes.

reviews.summary: This paper reconstructs the attention mechanism into a dynamic two-layer MLP. The authors proposed HyperMLP/HyperGLU, which incorporates the mixing of input conditional feature space and sequence space through low-rank/DPLR parameterization, and adopts a lag layout to maintain autoregressive consistency. HyperMLP/HyperGLU breaking through the bottleneck in the expressive capability of traditional attention.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: As mentioned above.
reviews.final_justification: My concerns have been addressed. I decide to keep the rating.

We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and the thoughtful feedback.

## On the systems side / wall-clock results.

Thank you for the valuable question about computational costs. Our paper is positioned primarily as an **algorithmic / perspective contribution** rather than an **engineering contribution**. The main goal is to highlight the expressivity advantages of the proposed structure and provide architectural insight for the community. On the systems side, we therefore report our current chunked implementation, while future work will focus on a more efficient **fused CUDA kernel**. 

Below, we evaluate forward wall-clock performance on an **Nvidia H100 GPU**. Even without heavy engineering optimization, **HyperMLP / HyperGLU consistently remain between FlashAttention and naïve softmax**, and overall are much closer to FlashAttention than to the naïve implementation.

| Softmax (Naïve) | 0.0231 | 176,999.65 | 0.0554 | 147,824.38 | 0.1457 | 112,418.30 | 0.4646 | 70,531.88 |
| Softmax (Flash) | 0.0204 | 201,202.64 | 0.0431 | 190,169.77 | 0.1020 | 163,847.10 | 0.2801 | 116,973.66 |
| HyperMLP | 0.0207 | 197,482.07 | 0.0461 | 177,512.17 | 0.1132 | 144,757.25 | 0.3274 | 100,081.07 | 
| HyperGLU | 0.0217 | 188,901.48 | 0.0495 | 165,527.71 | 0.1279 | 128,105.31 | 0.3760 | 87,143.39 |
| Gated Slot Attention | 0.0232 | 176,620.66 | 0.0428 | 191,501.74 | 0.0789 | 207,636.70 | 0.1586 | 206,580.40 |

At **1K**, both Hyper variants are already competitive with, and in some cases faster than, recent linear baselines; at **2K**, **HyperMLP** is essentially tied with **Path Attention**; and only **beyond 4K** do those linear baselines clearly pull ahead. We view this as consistent with the paper’s intended scope: the proposed operator is already practically competitive in a **non-fully-optimized** implementation, while further gains should come from **fused CUDA kernels** and more specialized scheduling.

More broadly, we see this as a normal stage in the development of a new structure. The original **Transformer** was introduced in 2017, while highly optimized implementations such as **FlashAttention** arrived **years later**. A structure paper may not contain its final engineering form; rather, the key first step is to show clear algorithmic value, after which systems optimization can follow. We hope HyperMLP / HyperGLU can follow the same pattern, and perhaps reach a strong engineering realization even faster by building on the lessons from the Transformer / FlashAttention line of work.

## On additional empirical breadth. 
Thank you for this valuable question. First of all, we believe the paper's strongest empirical evidence is the **controlled ablation structure** itself. By isolating each design choice rather than reporting only one final model, the paper provides a cleaner scientific picture of which components are necessary and why. See our response to Reviewer kte5 "On statistical significance" for more details. 

Given the limited time and compute available during the rebuttal period, we do not have enough time to launch larger LM training within the rebuttal window. Instead, we used that budget to broaden the empirical picture with additional **vision and time series forecasting** experiments. The outcome is again consistent: HyperMLP / HyperGLU stably outperform softmax attention in these additional settings as well.

We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and for the detailed, thoughtful comments.

## On practical efficiency vs. FlashAttention.
Due to space limitations, please see our response to `Reviewer NVxN` under "On the systems side / wall-clock results."

## On theory scope: what is structural vs. what depends on assumptions.  
The following aspects are **structural**:
- autoregressive attention as a dynamic two-layer MLP over the prefix,
- the three-stage memory view,
- the role of sequence-space mixing in enlarging the matched-budget function class,
- the necessity of the lag-layout / reverse-offset construction for aligning canonical prefix extension with autoregressive truncation,
- the QK-vs-VO asymmetry.

By contrast, some finer points depend on simplifying assumptions or restricted subclasses:
- the geometric “active-set” discussion is most direct for the gated ReLU / GLU family studied here,
- comparisons involving L2-normalized or linearized variants are meant as limiting cases, not equivalences to softmax,
- some propositions fix the context / routing region to isolate the structural point more cleanly.

We will also clarify the implied tradeoff: the HyperMLP family adds a stronger sequence-space inductive bias, which is especially useful when the bottleneck lies in context-conditioned mixing rather than token-wise exact selection alone.

## On sensitivity to the main design choices.
We agree that a compact sensitivity summary is useful, and the **controlled design study** already supports one. Using the full NanoGPT loss-curve table (`./nanogpt_results_labeled.csv` in our code repository), our main takeaways are:

| Factor | Result |
|---|---|
| Temporal mixing | R-cg-q -> R-cg-q-12o: loss 3.0828 -> 2.9956, 80/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 0.1219 (95% CI [0.1117, 0.1319]); G-cg-q -> G-cg-q-12o: loss 3.0530 -> 2.9865, 80/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 0.0903 (95% CI [0.0776, 0.1015]) |
| Lag layout | G-12o! vs. G-12!: loss 3.0386 vs. 4.3662, MAD avg 78.52 vs. 46.18, 79/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 1.3488 (95% CI [1.3149, 1.4068]); R-12o! vs. R-12!: loss 3.0497 vs. 4.3567, MAD avg 81.82 vs. 46.28, 79/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 1.2544 (95% CI [1.2314, 1.2949]) |
| GLU over ReLU | 6/6 wins on final NanoGPT loss, 6/6 wins on NanoGPT AUC; exact matched-pair sign test p = 0.0156 for both; median improvement 0.0127 (loss), 0.0121 (AUC) |
| Two-sided mixing | 4/4 wins on final NanoGPT loss; exact sign test p = 0.0625; median improvement 0.0108 |

*Statistical note.* Temporal mixing and Lag layout are evaluated on the full NanoGPT checkpoint trajectory; 95% CIs use a moving-block bootstrap (block size 5). GLU over ReLU uses 6 strictly matched ablation pairs, and Two-sided mixing uses 4 matched comparisons.

So if we had to recommend one default configuration based on the current evidence, it would be: **GLU + QK compression + temporal mixing on both stages + lag layout**, with **RoPE / KV-conv** as secondary improvements rather than the main driver.

## On regimes where softmax may remain preferable
Yes, we do think there are regimes where standard softmax attention remains attractive: (i) the pure systems-efficiency regime, where a mature FlashAttention-style implementation may outweigh the structural gain of a less optimized operator, and (ii) settings where the normalized probability-selection bias of softmax is already a good inductive match, so the added sequence-space mixing of HyperMLP / HyperGLU brings smaller gains. So we see hybrid architectures as promising.

## On behavior beyond the training regime
Our current experiments already go up to 4096 training context length, and the paper gives the linear overhead of DPLR mixing. As with the rest of the paper, our focus here is mainly algorithmic / perspective rather than a final engineering solution for very long context.

The key point is that the HyperMLP perspective is flexible: longer context does not force us to use global DPLR dense mixing over all positions. The lag-layout analysis already suggests prioritizing **recent lags**, which motivates a natural extension for very long context: apply HyperMLP mixing only on a recent window (e.g. the last 1K tokens), while keeping older positions as vanilla attention / identity mixing. This caps the extra DPLR cost by the window size rather than the full context length.

Under the *forward* layout, this gives a simple expressivity ladder for the sequence-mixing matrix:
1. Sliding-window local attention: lower-right block = identity, elsewhere = 0.  
2. Vanilla attention: full identity.  
3. Sliding-window local HyperMLP: upper-left = identity, lower-right = DPLR dense.  
4. Full HyperMLP: global DPLR dense.

Thus, beyond the current training regime, we do not view the choice as all-or-nothing between vanilla attention and full HyperMLP: windowed local HyperMLP is a natural intermediate extension.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and for the detailed, thoughtful comments.

## On hypernetwork-style related work and HyperMixer. 
This is a very good point, and we will expand the related-work discussion in the revision. We already mention this distinction briefly in the page-2 footnote, and we will make it clearer in the appendix. The key difference is the setting. Our paper works in the causal autoregressive regime relevant for decoder-only LLMs and next-token prediction, where sequence-space mixing is much more constrained because each output position requires a different causal mixing pattern and the operator must still support efficient parallel training. By contrast, MLP-Mixer / HyperMixer-style token mixing is typically studied in encoder-only settings, where the same sequence mixing can be reused across positions and does not need to satisfy autoregressive semantics. Likewise, Attention as a Hypernetwork is related mainly at the viewpoint level, whereas our work uses autoregressive prefix attention to derive a new causal sequence-mixing operator, the lag-layout / reverse-offset construction, and the matched-budget expressivity analysis. So although the ideas are related at a high level, we do not think they are solving the same structural problem.

## On writing and structure.
Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that **Sections 2.4-2.5** can be made easier to follow, and we will revise them for clarity in the final version.

## On broader domain evaluation.
Due to the character limitation, please see our response to **Reviewer NVxN** under `On additional empirical breadth.` for additional experiment results.

## On Proposition 2.6 and softmax vs. linear attention. 
Thank you for the valuable question. Proposition 2.6 (iii) is stated within the Appendix C.1 linear subnetwork interpretation, following prior works like the Saxe et al. (2022) view of ReLU networks as gated deep linear networks. In that regime, ReLU attention yields an input-conditioned mask over hidden slots, i.e. a dynamic linear subnetwork / activated subpool. The ungated linearized variant removes exactly this mechanism: the gate becomes trivial, the activated set is always the full pool, and the ReLU-style routing collapses. Softmax attention, however, does not satisfy this structural assumption. Its output cannot be written as a linear or piecewise-linear map of $x_t$ due to the coupled nonlinear transformation $h_t \mapsto \mathrm{softmax}(h_t)$. Therefore, it lies outside the gated-linear / subnetwork regime considered in Proposition 2.6(iii), and the "full-pool vs. activated-subpool" distinction is not directly applicable in this case.

## On the number of heads used by different methods. 
In Table 2 (language modeling), all baselines use their own **default settings**, including `n_head`. In the **controlled design study**, we set `n_head = 2` in order to keep the controlled elements consistent across comparisons. We will state this more clearly in the revision.

## On long-context setting and trainability.
Our experiments already go up to a **training context length of 4096**. The DPLR mixing contributes an overhead that grows linearly with sequence length in the form analyzed in the paper, and we agree that this makes very-long-context engineering especially important. At the same time, the HyperMLP perspective does **not** mean one must use global dense DPLR mixing over the entire context forever. One natural extension is to use **local windowed HyperMLP**, i.e. apply DPLR sequence mixing only on a recent window (for example, the latest 1K tokens) while keeping older positions as vanilla attention / identity mixing. 

## On different baselines at different model sizes.
We will clarify this in the revision. This is not intended as cherry-picking. Our primary baseline throughout is **standard Softmax Attention**, which we include consistently at all scales. The additional efficient-attention baselines are included mainly as reference points to recent research. Since not every alternative had equally stable or reproducible training recipes at both scales under our compute budget, we used the strongest reproducible recent baselines available at each scale. Our priority in this research was **clean controlled comparisons** like Table 1, not sweeping a larger set of partially tuned variants.

## On MoE-style extensions. 
Yes, we believe this is a promising direction. As discussed in the paper, multi-head attention can already be viewed as parameterizing a low-rank MLP in each head (see Figure 3(b)). From this perspective, an MoE-style extension is quite natural: one could imagine mixing experts on top of these per-head low-rank MLPs.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for highlighting our strengths and for the valuable questions.

## On scaling-law motivation vs. claim. 
Thank you for this valuable question. We want to clarify that our discussion of scaling laws is intended as a **motivation rather than a claim**. It reflects the broader call for architectural changes that improve capability per unit resource as brute-force scaling becomes increasingly costly; it is **not** a claim that this paper verifies any particular scaling-law form, nor that it performs frontier / production-scale LLM training. The contribution of this paper is instead at the **operator / theory** level: we identify a richer matched-budget class via dynamic sequence-space mixing, characterize it theoretically, and validate it in the moderate-scale regime that is feasible in an academic setting. We will revise the introduction to make our scope more precise.

## On the need for broader experiments.  
Given the limited time and compute available during the rebuttal period, we do not have enough time to launch larger LM training within the rebuttal window. Instead, we used that budget to broaden the empirical picture with additional **image classification and time series forecasting** experiments. The outcome is again consistent: HyperMLP / HyperGLU stably outperform softmax attention in these additional settings as well.

Due to the character limitation, please see our response to **Reviewer NVxN** under `On additional empirical breadth.` for the full image classification and forecasting tables.

## On statistical significance  
We agree that the Open LLM Leaderboard table should be read as broad reference coverage, not as the paper's sole evidential basis, especially because its core tasks are extremely difficult in the 340M-1.3B regime. We are aware that some models at similar scale on the public leaderboard achieve stronger numbers, but such systems typically involve many additional choices in data, training, and engineering that are aimed at maximizing benchmark performance. Our goal in this paper is different: rather than optimizing a large collection of details to push leaderboard numbers, we design the main experiments as a controlled scientific study, changing as few separable elements as possible so that their effects can be observed cleanly. Concretely, the most important and clean evidence in the paper is the **controlled design study**, whose variety is already substantial; to make this point more concrete, as below, we analyze the full NanoGPT loss-curve table (`./nanogpt_results_labeled.csv` in our code repository) rather than only the endpoint numbers shown in the paper:

| Factor | Result |
|---|---|
| Temporal mixing | R-cg-q -> R-cg-q-12o: loss 3.0828 -> 2.9956, 80/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 0.1219 (95% CI [0.1117, 0.1319]); G-cg-q -> G-cg-q-12o: loss 3.0530 -> 2.9865, 80/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 0.0903 (95% CI [0.0776, 0.1015]) |
| Lag layout | G-12o! vs. G-12!: loss 3.0386 vs. 4.3662, MAD avg 78.52 vs. 46.18, 79/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 1.3488 (95% CI [1.3149, 1.4068]); R-12o! vs. R-12!: loss 3.0497 vs. 4.3567, MAD avg 81.82 vs. 46.28, 79/80 checkpoints better, mean improvement 1.2544 (95% CI [1.2314, 1.2949]) |
| GLU over ReLU | 6/6 wins on final NanoGPT loss, 6/6 wins on NanoGPT AUC; exact matched-pair sign test p = 0.0156 for both; median improvement 0.0127 (loss), 0.0121 (AUC) |
| Two-sided mixing | 4/4 wins on final NanoGPT loss; exact sign test p = 0.0625; median improvement 0.0108 |

*Statistical note.* Temporal mixing and Lag layout are evaluated on the full NanoGPT checkpoint trajectory; 95% CIs use a moving-block bootstrap (block size 5). GLU over ReLU uses 6 strictly matched ablation pairs, and Two-sided mixing uses 4 matched comparisons.

These controlled comparisons directly show that the main architectural effects are real, separable, and not an artifact of rank aggregation.

## On wall-clock overhead. 
We evaluate the wall-clock performance on an Nvidia H100 GPU for sequence lengths up to 8K tokens; due to the character limitation, we place the full table in **our response to Reviewer NVxN** under "On the systems side / wall-clock results." The short version is that, even with our current chunked and not heavily fused implementation, HyperMLP / HyperGLU consistently stay between FlashAttention and naïve softmax across all tested lengths, and are overall much closer to FlashAttention than to the naïve implementation. At 1K, both Hyper variants are already competitive with, and in some cases faster than, recent linear baselines such as Gated Slot Attention and Path Attention. At 2K, HyperMLP is essentially tied with Path Attention. Only beyond 4K do those linear baselines clearly pull ahead. We therefore view the current measurements as fully consistent with the **paper's intended positioning** as an **algorithmic / perspective contribution** rather than a finished **engineering artifact**.
