submission.title: Heterogeneity-Aware Knowledge Sharing for Graph Federated Learning
submission.abstract: Graph Federated Learning (GFL) enables distributed graph representation learning while preserving graph data privacy. However, it suffers from heterogeneity in node features and graph structures across clients. To address this challenge, we propose a novel graph Federated learning method via Semantic and Structural Alignment (FedSSA). For node feature heterogeneity, FedSSA infers class-wise node distributions through a variational model, clusters clients according to the inferred distributions, and aligns local distributions with cluster-level representatives. For structural heterogeneity, FedSSA employs spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and introduces a spectral energy measure to characterize graph topology, enabling structural alignment between local and cluster-level spectral GNNs. Experiments on eleven homophilic and heterophilic graph datasets under non-overlapping and overlapping partitioning settings demonstrate that FedSSA consistently outperforms eleven state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/blgpb/FedSSA.
submission.tldr: FedSSA improves graph federated learning by aligning both node-level semantic knowledge and graph structural knowledge across clients.
submission.lay_summary:
Many real-world data can be represented as networks, such as social networks, citation networks, and recommendation systems. In practice, these networks are often stored by different clients and cannot be directly shared due to privacy concerns. Graph Federated Learning allows these clients to train models collaboratively without sharing raw data, but it faces a key challenge: Different clients may have very different node information and connection patterns.

We propose FedSSA, a method that helps clients learn from others with similar semantic and structural patterns. Instead of forcing all clients to share the same knowledge, FedSSA groups clients according to their data characteristics and aligns useful knowledge within each group. Experiments on various network datasets show that FedSSA achieves better performance than existing methods.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes a novel method called FedSSA (Graph Federated Learning Based on Semantic and Structural Alignment) to address the heterogeneity problem caused by non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data in Graph Federated Learning (GFL). The authors point out that existing GFL methods often conflate node feature heterogeneity with structural topological heterogeneity. To address this, FedSSA proposes a framework for separate processing: at the semantic level, it extracts class-conditional semantic distributions for cluster alignment using a Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE); at the structural level, it utilizes a spectral graph neural network to extract a "spectral energy measure" and performs structural clustering and alignment based on the Grassmann manifold. Furthermore, this paper provides a convergence proof and validates the effectiveness of the method on 11 graph datasets.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengthness：First, the motivation is clear, and the proposed method is novel. The design of constructing spectral energy features using the learning coefficients of the spectral filter and mapping them to a Grassmann manifold for clustering using chordal distance demonstrates strong mathematical intuition and innovation.

Second, this paper not only proposes a systematic algorithmic framework but also provides detailed convergence analysis (Theorem 4.2). It proves that the method still has the theoretical guarantee of linear convergence to the neighborhood of the optimal solution when facing both semantic and structural alignment errors.

Third, the experimental design is very comprehensive, comparing as many as 11 baseline models on 11 benchmark datasets (covering both homologous and heterologous graphs). FedSSA shows a consistent performance advantage in both overlapping and non-overlapping graph partitioning settings; for example, in the heterologous graph scenario, the average accuracy surpasses the suboptimal method by 2.82%.

Weakness: First, although FedSSA avoids the transmission of raw graph data, it requires clients to upload the latent distribution parameters (mean and covariance matrices) and spectral coefficients for each category. Such high-dimensional, high-order statistical information is still vulnerable to inference attacks or membership inference attacks. The paper lacks a clear discussion of these potential privacy leakage risks.

Second, the model introduces additional key hyperparameters, namely the number of semantic clusters $K_{node}$ and the number of structural clusters $K_{struct}$. Although the authors provide a sensitivity analysis in Section 5.4, in real-world cross-silo federated scenarios, it is very difficult to pre-set or determine these optimal cluster numbers through grid search because the server cannot see the complete distribution picture of the global data.
Third, if some clients face extreme Non-IID situations (such as the complete absence of certain categories locally, or only a very small number of samples), the local VGAE will be unable to effectively infer a reliable distribution, which may severely undermine the effectiveness of the subsequent GMM-based global semantic alignment mechanism.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1.It is strongly recommended to add a discussion of the potential privacy risks when sharing Gaussian distribution statistics and spectral coefficients in the final version (or the Impact Statement in the appendix). Explore the feasibility of adding noise to uploaded parameters using differential privacy and its impact on the convergence error term $\mathcal{E}$.
2.Please explain what heuristics or unsupervised metrics across clients should be used to initialize $K_{node}$ and $K_{struct}$ in practical deployments. 
3.It is recommended to add experiments on "pathological non-IID" client distributions in the appendix. For example, forcibly restricting certain clients to access data from only 1-2 categories and observing the critical point of collapse of the semantic clustering module in FedSSA. 
4.Although Appendix E analyzes time complexity, frequent uploading of multi-class covariance matrices may cause communication bottlenecks. It is recommended to add a comparison chart of the actual data volume (in megabytes) transmitted in one round of communication for each baseline model.
reviews.final_justification: FedSSA handles graph Non-IID data by treating feature heterogeneity and structural heterogeneity separately. It aligns semantics via VGAE and aligns topology via spectral features on Grassmann manifolds. Works on 11 datasets, comes with convergence guarantees.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes FedSSA, a novel graph federated learning method that addresses both the node feature heterogeneity and structural heterogeneity. The key idea of FedSSA is to enforce semantic and structural alignment, sharing the knowledge of both node features and structural topologies. On one side, VGAE is used to infer the latent distribution of features for each type of node. These distributions are then clustered on the server side to construct a cluster-level representative distribution, which guides the semantic alignment of the local model. On the other hand, the spectral energy metric is proposed to characterize local structures, thereby achieving alignment and knowledge sharing among cluster-level spectral GNNs. Experimental results and theoretical analysis both validate the effectiveness of FedSSA.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
This paper addresses an important problem, focusing on heterogeneity in graph federated learning, which is technically difficult due to privacy concerns. The proposed method obtains significant improvements over lots of baseline methods across eleven datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. Furthermore, theoretical proofs are mathematically correct.

Weaknesses:
The server approximates Gaussian mixture models as a single Gaussian distribution to reduce computational complexity. However, this approximation may introduce biases in cases of extremely diverse or multimodal data distributions.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. When using a single Gaussian distribution to approximate the cluster-level representative distribution, has the quantitative impact of this simplification on the final classification accuracy been verified through ablation studies?
2. Will eigenvalue decomposition become a bottleneck in spectral energy calculation?
3. Due to the large number of datasets and comparison methods, Table 1 and Table 2 appear to be dense. It is suggested to make them clearer.
reviews.final_justification: The authors’ response has addressed my concerns, and I will maintain my score.

reviews.summary:
This paper proposes a novel graph federated learning method (i.e., FedSSA) via semantic and structural alignment. FedSSA successfully addresses the fundamental and challenging problem (i.e., heterogeneity) in graph federated learning.

To address node feature heterogeneity, FedSSA proposes a novel variational model to infer class-wise node distributions and then minimizes the divergence between local and cluster-level distributions to facilitate semantic knowledge sharing. To address structural heterogeneity, FedSSA proposes a spectral energy measure and then aligns the spectral characteristics of local spectral GNNs with those of cluster-level spectral GNNs to enable structural knowledge sharing.

This paper theoretically proves that FedSSA has a linear convergence rate. Moreover, experiments on 11 homophilic and heterophilic graph datasets show that FedSSA outperforms 11 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, with an average improvement in classification accuracy of approximately 2.82%.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
1. Unlike previous methods that only focus on structural heterogeneity or do not distinguish between the two types of heterogeneity, FedSSA explicitly and separately handles feature heterogeneity and structural heterogeneity. This "divide and conquer" strategy has strong logical rationality.

2. This paper provides a detailed linear convergence analysis (Theorem 4.2), and gives a complete mathematical proof in Appendix. I carefully checked all the mathematical proofs, and they are theoretically rigorous and complete.

3. Experiments covered 11 datasets, including highly challenging heterophilic graphs, and considered both non-overlapping and overlapping partitioning settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of FedSSA.

4. The reported results are reproducible based on the provided codes. The code implementation is well-organized and consistent with the methodological description.

# Weaknesses
1. The proposed method appears to be sensitive to computational resources. This overhead may limit its application on mobile or low-power clients.

2. The proposed method involves four hyperparameters, but lacks guidance on how to adjust these parameters in real-world scenarios.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. In the methodology, since the proposed method employs semantic clustering and structural clustering, the proposed method appears to be sensitive to computational resources. Could the authors provide a discussion on the computational complexity of the proposed method?
2. Although the results are promising, some experimental settings are not clear. Please provide the details of graph partition setting across clients. 
3. What is the total communication cost per round, and how does it compare with the standard baseline method (i.e., FedAvg)?

If these issues are incorporated into the revised version, my concerns will be addressed, and I will accordingly raise my overall recommendation rating.
reviews.final_justification: My concerns have been largely addressed during the rebuttal phase, and I therefore recommend acceptance.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thanks for your positive comments!

---

**1. Re: “application on mobile or low-power clients”:** Thanks! We would like to clarify that FedSSA is primarily designed for **cross-silo** graph federated learning scenarios, which involve a moderate number of clients, each equipped with sufficient computational resources. Considering computational, memory, and communication overhead, FedSSA is not well-suited for **cross-device** graph federated learning settings, where clients are typically resource-constrained (*e.g.*, mobile or low-power clients). Extending FedSSA to cross-device graph federated learning is an important direction for future work.

---

**2. Re: “adjustment of hyperparameters”:** Thanks! First, the adjustment of $K_\mathrm{node}$ and $K_\mathrm{struct}$ depends on the degree of heterogeneity. If the heterogeneity is strong, larger values of $K_\mathrm{node}$ and $K_\mathrm{struct}$ are recommended to facilitate cluster-level knowledge sharing. Otherwise, smaller values of $K_\mathrm{node}$ and $K_\mathrm{struct}$ are sufficient to address heterogeneity with low computational complexity.

Second, the adjustment of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ depends on the properties of the graph. If the graph tends to be homophilic, smaller values of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are recommended, which allow the spectral GNN to capture low-frequency signals. Otherwise, larger values of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are recommended, as they impose stronger sparsity on the spectral GNN.

---

**3. Re: “computational complexity”:** Thanks! On the client side, the computational complexity of VGAE is $\mathcal{O}(K e_m d+n_md^2)$, where $n_m$, $e_m$, $d$, and $K$ denote the number of nodes, edges on the $m$-th client, feature dimensionality, and the order of bases, respectively. Furthermore, the computational complexities of semantic knowledge alignment and spectral knowledge alignment are $\mathcal{O}(Cd)$ and $\mathcal{O}(K)$, respectively, where $C$ denotes the number of classes. Therefore, the total computational complexity of FedSSA on the client side is $\mathcal{O}\big(d (Ke_m + n_md+ C)+K\big)$.

On the server side, the computational complexity of semantic clustering is $\mathcal{O}(MC K_\mathrm{node}d)$, where $M$ and $K_\mathrm{node}$ denote the number of clients and node-level clusters, respectively. In addition, the computational complexity of structural clustering is $\mathcal{O}(M^2dK +M K_\mathrm{struct})$, where $K_\mathrm{struct}$ denotes the number of structural clusters. Therefore, the total computational complexity of FedSSA on the server side is $\mathcal{O}\big(M(C K_\mathrm{node}d+MdK+K_\mathrm{struct})\big)$.

In summary, the computational complexity of FedSSA is modest and our FedSSA can be efficiently implemented.

---

**4. Re: “details of graph partition”:** Thanks! Following prior work [R1], we conduct experiments under both non-overlapping and overlapping partitioning settings.

**1) Non-overlapping partitioning:** Given $M$ clients, the METIS algorithm is used to partition the original graph into $M$ subgraphs.

**2) Overlapping partitioning:** Given $M$ clients, we first employ the METIS algorithm to partition the original graph into $\lfloor\frac{M}{5}\rfloor$ subgraphs, where $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ denotes the floor function. Then, for each partitioned subgraph, half of the nodes and their corresponding edges are randomly sampled. This procedure is repeated five times for each partitioned subgraph to obtain five distinct yet overlapping subgraphs.

---

**5. Re: “communication cost and comparison”:** Thanks! First, we report the total communication cost per round on two datasets. 

|Methods|*Cora* Non-overlap. 5 Clients|*Cora* Non-overlap. 10 Clients|*Cora* Non-overlap. 20 Clients|*Cora* Overlap. 10 Clients|*Cora* Overlap. 30 Clients|*Cora* Overlap. 50 Clients|
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|FedAvg|5.51s|2.19s|5.63s|5.40s|7.27s|12.08s|
|FedSSA (Ours)|2.87s|3.46s|4.94s|6.48s|11.17s|16.47s|

|Methods|*Roman-empire* Non-overlap. 5 Clients|*Roman-empire* Non-overlap. 10 Clients|*Roman-empire* Non-overlap. 20 Clients|*Roman-empire* Overlap. 10 Clients|*Roman-empire* Overlap. 30 Clients|*Roman-empire* Overlap. 50 Clients|
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|FedAvg|8.20s|5.76s|8.46s|10.25s|18.47s|19.12s|
|FedSSA (Ours)|5.78s|6.01s|11.93s|9.04s|16.59s|24.78s|

Second, FedSSA introduces only a modest additional communication cost when compared with FedAvg. Specifically, the average communication cost per round of FedSSA on *Cora* is 7.57s, whereas FedAvg requires 6.35s. Meanwhile, the average communication cost per round of FedSSA on *Roman-empire* is 12.36s, whereas FedAvg requires 11.71s. However, FedSSA achieves significantly better performance than FedAvg. Specifically, the average performance of FedSSA is 81.27% on *Cora* and 65.47% on *Roman-empire*, which is much higher than FedAvg with 66.27% on *Cora* and 37.10% on *Roman-empire*.

match.matched_title: Evolution of Benchmark: Black-Box Optimization Benchmark Design through Large Language Model

submission.title: Evolution of Benchmark: Black-Box Optimization Benchmark Design through Large Language Model
submission.abstract: Benchmark Design in Black-Box Optimization (BBO) is a fundamental yet open-ended topic. Early BBO benchmarks are predominantly human-crafted, introducing expert bias and constraining diversity. Automating this design process can relieve the human-in-the-loop burden while enhancing diversity and objectivity. We propose Evolution of Benchmark (EoB), an automated BBO benchmark designer empowered by the large language model (LLM) and its program evolution capability. Specifically, we formulate benchmark design as a bi-objective optimization problem towards maximizing (i) landscape similarity to target tasks and (ii) algorithm-differentiation ability across a portfolio of BBO solvers. Under this paradigm, EoB iteratively prompts LLM to evolve a population of benchmark programs and employs  a reflection-based scheme to co-evolve the landscape and its corresponding program. Comprehensive experiments validate our EoB is a competitive candidate in multi-dimensional usages: 1) Benchmarking BBO algorithms; 2) Training and testing learning-assisted BBO algorithms; 3) Extending proxy for expensive real-world problems.
submission.tldr: An early exploration of automated black-box optimization benchmark design with LLM-driven program evolution.
submission.lay_summary: Optimization methods are widely used in science and engineering, and researchers need good test problems to compare them fairly. However, many of these benchmarks are still designed by hand, which is slow, labor-intensive, and can limit diversity. In this paper, we study whether large language models can help automate this process. We introduce Evolution of Benchmark (EoB), a system that uses a language model to repeatedly generate and improve small programs that define optimization tasks. The goal is to create benchmark problems that both resemble real-world tasks and highlight the differences between optimization methods. Our experiments show that this approach can produce useful benchmarks for several purposes: evaluating optimization algorithms, supporting the training of learning-based optimizers, and providing lower-cost stand-ins for expensive real-world problems.

reviews.summary: This work positions itself as an automated generation of benchmark for general black-box optimization, which is guided by LLM and evolutionary dynamics (called evolution of benchmark of EoB). The various design choices of the evolution of the benchmark are described including comparison between candidate programs and selection driven by multiple objectives: landscape similarity to target indicator (LSI) and algorithm distinguishing capability (ADC).
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths 

1) With recent efforts in generation of heuristics for optimization using evolutionary dynamics, the dual problem of automatizing the benchmark itself, which is given as this works focus, is interesting and important.

2) The multiple-objective approach taken in this work seems the most adapted choice given the task of benchmark generation.

3) The paper presents a somewhat broad encompassing framework.

Weaknesses

1) The main issue is that the scope of the paper seems overstated. The introduction section suggests the benchmarks created relate to general black-box optimization, but the implementation given in the paper seems much narrower: the problems composing the benchmarks seem to be continuous, single-objective, bound-constrained functions.

2) The second serious issue is that the paper reads as a sequence of components rather than an end-to-end explanation of the design choices. Within this style of presentation, it is not clear at all why certain choices were made (see questions).

3) The manuscript seems to only deal with generation of functions to constitute benchmarks. But a benchmark is also defined by its instance dimensions, evaluation budgets, etc., which does not appear to be considered.

4) The paper identifies benchmark diversity to the distribution of algorithm-performance standard deviations (see Fig. 3), but this is not the same as landscape diversity. It is entirely possible to obtain large deviations within a very narrow class of landscape types.

5) For claiming high generality of the measures for benchmark diversity, one would expect either strong analytical justifications or extensive experimental comparison. However, neither are really included.

6) As currently designed, it seems the method presented would depend heavily on the manual prompt engineering used in the evolution of benchmarks (e.g. Fig. 8, 9 and 10), limiting the claims of a fully automatized benchmark generation.

7) Table captions should be more details to allow for unambiguous understanding of the results presented.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Why do LSI and ADC as implemented in this work constitute a general setting for good indicators of benchmark quality?

2) What is the computational budget of EoB in terms of the number of LLM class, wall clock time, and monetary cost?

3) Could the authors justify the choice of exploratory landscape analysis (ELA) for LSI ? What are other alternatives and why was ELA the most appropriate one ? 

4) Why are the atoms of the co-evolution of benchmark composed of the atoms “break symmetry”, “Adding Valley”, “Smoothing Valley” (see Fig. 2) ? Why are these sufficient to create general benchmark ? Any analytical justification ?

5) Why is CoCo-BBOB (year 2010) used as the main baseline comparison ?
reviews.limitations:
The authors claim that "By automating the benchmark design process, the substantial labor resources and specialized expertise costs could be significantly reduced."

The discussion around benchmarking cost would be more complete if in addition to Evaluation efficiency shown in Table 1, more details of the cost (see question 2 here-above) of benchmark evolution would be detailed.
reviews.final_justification:
I appreciate the responses to my questions and concerns. However, I still believe the work suffers from a strong limitation in its definition of benchmark diversity. In particular, the distinction between performance variance and landscape diversity is not properly addressed.

My concern regarding end-to-end automation is not about the existence of a workflow, as clearly demonstrated by the authors, but rather that the diversification mechanism is heavily hand-designed, relying on prompt engineering and predefined heuristics. This introduces a strong bias in the types of benchmarks that can be generated.

Overall, I find that the approach is not sufficiently clear or general to justify acceptance in its current form.

reviews.summary: The paper presents an LLM-based evolutionary method for generating synthetic functions to benchmark black-box optimizers. In many real-world applications, designing human-crafted benchmarks can be expensive, whereas these LLM-generated functions can be obtained at much lower cost. Specifically, the authors formulate the generation of such related functions as a bi-objective optimization problem, maximizing both the landscape similarity to target hard-to-model BBO tasks and the ability of the benchmark to effectively differentiate among various BBO algorithms. The resulting generated functions can then be treated as unknown oracle functions for benchmarking black-box optimizers.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:  
1. LLM-generated benchmark design for BBO is genuinely underexplored compared with optimizer design. This paper explores a meaningful direction that could reduce much of the cost required to evaluate existing optimizer designs.  
2. The paper is well presented and explains the method clearly. The authors also include detailed prompt-generation guidelines, which are valuable for reproducing the method.  
3. The method is reasonable and straightforward, and it shows some promising results, especially in reducing computation time compared to real-task settings.

**Weaknesses**:  
1. A crucial concern of the paper is whether these LLM-generated functions truly resemble the actual real-world tasks they are intended to proxy (see the Question section).  
2. Modeling real-world black-box tasks from a limited budget of paired examples is already a common idea in black-box optimization. In this paper, the method appears to characterize the target tasks by deriving features from limited optimization interest using NeurELA and then searching for synthetic functions that minimize the distance in this feature space. Conceptually, this is related to classical surrogate or probabilistic modeling approaches in BBO, such as Gaussian processes, which also build approximations of unknown tasks from limited evaluations. The paper currently does not clearly position itself against these existing approaches, nor does it explain why the proposed feature-matching evolutionary framework is preferable.
3. The paper is missing some important ablation studies on key hyperparameters and design choices, such as the $\sigma$ in the Landscape Similarity Indicator objective, the population size $N$, and the choice of optimizer for solving the bi-objective optimization problem (as they adopt an evolution strategy in this method).
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
**Questions**:  

1. The paper does not sufficiently measure how well the generated functions resemble the actual real-world target tasks. A key question is how existing BBO optimizers perform on these generated functions compared with their performance on the real-world target tasks. Does optimizer performance on the synthetic benchmark consistently align with its behavior on the corresponding real-world tasks? The authors should provide experimental results that clearly show this consistency, for example by comparing the ranking or standings of BBO optimizers on the generated functions against their rankings on the real-world target tasks. A quantitative metric measuring this gap is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark. Without such quantification, it is difficult to assess whether strong performance on the synthetic benchmark really translates to strong performance on the closely related real-world tasks.  

2. The paper also lacks extensive experiments on standard black-box optimization methods, such as Bayesian optimization and other classical model-based approaches, on the proposed LLM-generated benchmarks. How do these standard methods perform on the generated functions? Since these are widely used BBO approaches, such experiments would help clarify whether the proposed benchmark is broadly useful beyond the selected solver pool in the paper.  

3. Are the generated functions mainly stochastic and non-differentiable, or are they mostly deterministic and differentiable? In many real-world applications, the unknown oracle objective is complex, stochastic, noisy, and often gradient-free. However, the synthetic functions in the paper are generated using components such as asymmetric masking, nonlinearity composition, and polynomial periodicity, which appear to produce mostly deterministic and differentiable functions. This may make the generated benchmarks less realistic and could narrow their applicability to real-world BBO scenarios.  

4. The choice of using standard deviation in the second objective appears heuristic. Since many black-box optimization methods are stochastic and can produce different outcomes under different random seeds, the standard deviation alone may not be sufficient to measure how well a benchmark distinguishes among algorithms. The authors could leverage the objective matrix in a more principled way. For example, uncertainty quantification could be used to measure the confidence in algorithm rankings, where higher confidence would indicate that the benchmark more clearly distinguishes among algorithms.  

5. The paper introduces prompt-based techniques to enhance population diversity. However, can the authors provide experiments that clearly show these techniques indeed improve diversity? Numerical results measuring the diversity of the generated synthetic functions would be valuable for supporting this design choice.  

6. Can the authors provide a numerical measure of feature-level closeness between the generated synthetic functions and the target tasks? Similarly, a numerical measure of how distinguishable the algorithms are on these synthetic functions should also be reported. Such quantitative evidence would make the evaluation more convincing.  

7. How does the method perform when varying important factors such as the population size $N$ and the number of target tasks of interest $H$? Are the results consistent under these changes? In addition, how sensitive is the method to key hyperparameters such as $\sigma$? These analyses are important for understanding the robustness of the method.  

8. What is the motivation for choosing the proposed evolutionary strategy with $N$ trade-off variables as preference vectors? Since this is itself a bi-objective black-box optimization problem, one could also apply existing BBO methods to solve it. A comparison between the proposed evolutionary strategy and at least one standard BBO method for solving the outer optimization problem would be valuable.  

9. Are the crossover, mutation, and selection operators in the evolutionary strategy entirely carried out by the LLM through hand-crafted prompts? If so, these operators are themselves treated as black-box mechanisms driven by the LLM, which makes it difficult to analyze their behavior clearly. It would be valuable to provide experiments or case studies showing how the LLM performs crossover or mutation between functions to generate new candidates. Such analysis would improve understanding and trust in the method. In addition, the behavior of these operators may vary significantly across LLMs, so a careful comparison between different LLM backbones would also be important.
reviews.limitations: The paper still has several important limitations, many of which are reflected in the Weaknesses and Questions sections.  These limitations reduce confidence in whether the proposed benchmark can be reliably applied to real-world black-box optimization scenarios.
reviews.final_justification: The authors fully addressed my concerns by providing additional extensive empirical results during the rebuttal. I am therefore satisfied with the response and raised my score to an acceptance level.

reviews.summary: The paper proposes Evolution of Benchmark (EoB), an automated framework that leverages LLMs to design Black-Box Optimization (BBO) benchmarks. The authors formulate benchmark design as a bi-objective optimization problem, aiming to maximize both landscape diversity and algorithm-differentiation ability. The system uses an iterative "evolutionary" prompting strategy, including a "Reflector" module to analyze previous iterations and a "Crossover" module to synthesize new benchmark functions from successful parent programs. The framework is evaluated on its ability to benchmark BBO algorithms, train learning-assisted BBO models, and act as a proxy for expensive real-world problems.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The paper addresses a significant bottleneck in the BBO community, the reliance on labor-intensive, human-crafted benchmarks.

Framing the design as an optimization of diversity and differentiation is a principled approach that goes beyond simple random generation of functions. The inclusion of a "Reflector Strategy" allows the LLM to act as a meta-optimizer, dictating specific "Evolution Recipes".

Demonstrating the framework’s application in generating training data for learning-assisted BBO algorithms is particularly timely, as these models require large, diverse datasets that traditional benchmarks cannot provide.

Weaknesses: 

The "Innovation" strategy mentioned in the Reflector module is ambitious, but the manuscript could more clearly define how the LLM ensures these new landscapes are mathematically sound and not just "noisy" versions of existing functions. While BBO benchmarks are often multi-dimensional, the snippets suggest a focus on functional synthesis. It remains unclear how well the LLM-generated benchmarks scale to very high-dimensional search spaces where human intuition often fails.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
It seems that some of the designed functions have a similar landscape to existing BBOB benchmark instances. How does it ensure these new landscapes are mathematically sound and not just "noisy" versions of existing functions?

As the functions are usually simple, can you discuss the unique advantages of using EoB when compared to the traditional symbolic regression or expression-tree-based generators? While the authors have mentioned that the traditional method can be time-consuming, those instances are reusable once generated.

Since LLMs can be non-deterministic, are the benchmarks produced in different runs consistent in their "algorithm-differentiation ability"?

Can you provide more details on the API costs and computational time required for the LLM to evolve a high-quality population of benchmarks?
reviews.final_justification: The paper presents one of the first attempts at automated benchmark instance generation for BBO, and the results are promising.

reviews.summary: The paper proposes an LLM-supported method for the automated design of single-objective continuous optimization problems to generate higher-quality benchmarking data that can support the development of LLM-based optimization heuristics. The main idea is to create synthetic functions that approximate expensive real-world optimization problems, enabling large-scale experimentation and learning without the high computational cost of evaluating real-world instances. This synthetic benchmark data can then be used to train or guide the design of more effective optimizers for real-world optimization tasks.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow. Please find below my comments regarding soundness, presentation, significance, and originality, presented as strengths and weaknesses.

Strengths:

- The paper addresses a relevant and crucial problem for the optimization and benchmarking community.

- A good sensitivity analysis is presented with respect to different components of the proposed approach.

- The proposed framework can be particularly beneficial when only a small number of expensive real-world optimization instances are available, as it allows the generation of similar synthetic instances that can later be used to learn improved heuristics for solving those real-world problems.

Weaknesses:

- In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors should also mention that there are other automatic approaches for extending benchmark suites, for example, MA-BBOB, affine function recombination, and recent LLM-based approaches for benchmark generation.

Relevant references include:

Vermetten, D., Ye, F., Bäck, T., & Doerr, C. (2023). MA-BBOB: Many-affine combinations of BBOB functions for evaluating AutoML approaches in noiseless numerical black-box optimization contexts. In International Conference on Automated Machine Learning (PMLR).

Dietrich, K., & Mersmann, O. (2022). Increasing the diversity of benchmark function sets through affine recombination. In PPSN (pp. 590-602). Springer.

Ono, Y., Harada, T., & Miura, Y. (2025). Large language model-driven evolutionary optimization benchmark generation algorithm. In GECCO Companion (pp. 151-154).

Skvorc, U., van Stein, N., Seiler, M., Grimme, B., Bäck, T., & Trautmann, H. (2026). LLM Driven Design of Continuous Optimization Problems with Controllable High-level Properties. arXiv:2601.18846 (EvoStar 2026).

- The main idea of treating the task as a bi-objective problem that balances landscape diversity and algorithm performance differences resembles the Instance Space Analysis (ISA) framework, where similar objectives are combined and optimized to analyze algorithm performance across instance spaces.

Muñoz, M. A., & Smith-Miles, K. A. (2017). Performance analysis of continuous black-box optimization algorithms via footprints in instance space. Evolutionary Computation, 25(4), 529-554.

- The idea of evolving high-level properties of optimization problems is also presented in the work by Skvorc et al. (2026, published at EvoStar 2026), which should be acknowledged as related work.

- The first listed contribution in the introduction is not entirely correct, since there are already at least two published works proposing LLM-driven approaches for generating optimization benchmarks:

Ono et al. (2025) and Skvorc et al. (2026).

- The mention of IOHProfiler in Section 2.1 is misleading. IOHProfiler is not a benchmark suite, but rather a framework for benchmarking optimization algorithms, which supports multiple suites such as COCO/BBOB and CEC.

- The authors should better justify the selection of NeurELA as the landscape feature representation. Previous studies (including Cenikj et al., 2026, cited in the paper) show that different landscape feature sets can produce substantially different similarity relationships between optimization problems. Repeating the experiments with multiple landscape feature sets as a sensitivity analysis would strengthen the contribution.

- Please explain why a type of Euclidean distance metric is used to measure similarity between instances (Equation 3). What would happen if a cosine similarity measure were used instead? A short justification or sensitivity analysis would improve clarity.

- The generalization section is not sufficiently clear. For a true zero-shot generalization evaluation, one would expect the model to be trained only on COCO-BBOB and EoB-BBOB, and then evaluated on UAV and HPO tasks. Including EoB-UAV and EoB-HPO in the training data may introduce data leakage. It would be useful to evaluate additional scenarios where these datasets are excluded from training.

- The paper would benefit from analysing the coverage of the newly generated benchmark instances relative to existing benchmarks (e.g., COCO, UAV, HPO). This could be performed in both the feature space (landscape features) and the performance space, to investigate whether the generated instances truly extend the diversity of existing benchmarks or only the number of instances.

Minor comments:

- There is an extra point in line 268.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
[**W1 & W3 & W4, related works on benchmark generation**]

We agree with the reviewer that the related works you provided should be discussed and included into our paper. To address this, we provide following discussion and will revise it into our paper.

Recently, a line of works focus on using affine combination across instances in CoCo-BBOB to automatically create new test instances, which enhanced benchmark diversity by filling the space gap in the instance space (**Dietrich, K., & Mersmann, O. (2022),  Vermetten, D., Ye, F., Bäck, T., & Doerr, C. (2023)**). Despite these efforts that require certain expert-level experiences, a new line of works explore the possibility of using LLMs as end-to-end benchmark designer. LLM-EBG (**Ono, Y., Harada, T., & Miura, Y. (2025)**) constructs an evolutionary metric that measures a function instance’s performance as the performance gap between two optimizers, then LLM is used to evolve high-performance function code. Skvorc et al. (2026) leverage an up-to-date evolution of heuristic  framework (LLaMEA) and pre-trained feature predictor to customize function instances that fit certain high-level landscape property. Our work follows the core idea in this line, while making several novel designs: 1) we propose multi-objective evolution of benchmarks to address practical benchmark design needs. 2) we propose two key measure LSI and ADC as key aspects for benchmark generation and we validate their effectiveness through comprehensive experiments. 3) we are the first work that uses LLM to generate training distribution for learning-assisted optimizers.

[**W2, a related work on bi-objective modeling**]

We acknowledge that ISA (Muñoz, M. A., & Smith-Miles, K. A. (2017)) proposed a concept similar to what we proposed in EoB: the bi-objective measure for benchmarking functions. The key difference is that EoB makes a step forward by using such bi-objective measure to generate benchmark, while ISA focuses on problem-algorithm performance analysis. We will include ISA as a related work.

[**W5, IOHProfiler**]

We agree with the reviewer and will revise our description on IOHProfiler as you suggested.

[**W6, NeurELA**]

We would like to clarify that we select NeurELA as feature extractor for two major reasons: 1) NeurELA is more computationally efficient than traditional ELA. 2) NeurELA is pre-trained under learning-based context, as claimed in its appendix, such pre-training leads to useful features that show correlation with traditional ELA, more importantly, it automatically filters out irrelevant features. We have conducted preliminary experiments on this issue, and the results suggest using NeurELA rather than the feature sets of ELA. We provide the performance comparison in the table below, where we use different ELA sets to generate EoB-UAV/HPO, and then train different MetaBBO with the generated benchmarks and test the performance following the protocol in Sec. 4.3.1.

|  | LDE | GLEET | SYMBOL | RLDEAFL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neur-ELA | **0.8036** | **0.8242** | **0.8054** | **0.8312** |
| ELA: Meta-Model | 0.8012 | 0.8061 | 0.7724 | 0.8168 |
| ELA: Distribution of the Objective Function Values | 0.7998 | 0.8150 | 0.7812 | 0.8255 |
| ELA: Convexity | 0.8025 | 0.8180 | 0.7950 | 0.8120 |
| ELA: Local search | 0.8005 | 0.8012 | 0.7680 | 0.8290 |
| ELA: Levelset | 0.8030 | 0.8210 | 0.7920 | 0.8180 |
| ELA: Curvature | 0.7985 | 0.8090 | 0.7740 | 0.8210 |

The results above reveal that NeurELA is a good choice in practical. The benchmark generated by using NeurELA features could achieves maximum training effectiveness.

[**W7, distance measure**]

Let us explain the reason behind. We use L2-distance since we focus on the distance in the feature space, in particular, each dimension of the feature vector. Cosine distance is not a proper choice since it focuses more on the directional alignment of two feature vectors. We provide evolution results by using these two distances at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/uav_gen0_pareto_comparison.png .

[**W8, zero-shot generalization**]

We first apologize for the writing mistake: in Sec. 4.3.1, lines 371-373, we test the trained model on “UAV-test” and “HPO-test”, not “UAV-train” and “HPO-train”. Under this setting, the protocol for zero-shot generalization is proper. We will revise this mistake.

[**W9, truly extend the diversity**]

We provide feature space visualization of our EoB in the UAV problem setting as an example (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/visualization_uav_eob.png). In this figure, we plot UAV problems and the synthetic instances generated by our EoB (i.e., EoB-UAV), the results clearly show that EoB truly delivers feature diversity for complex tasks. For the performance diversity, we believe the results provided in Fig. 3 are direct proof of such diversity.

[**Minor**]

We will remove the extra point :)

We will appreciate the reviewer if the score could be reconsidered.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We appreciate the reviewer for the professional and valuable comments. We are pleased that the reviewer recognizes our work as a timely work for current learning-assisted optimization research. We provide following point-to-point responses to address your remaining concerns.

[**W1 & Q1, noisy issue**]

We would like to explain why EoB could avoid the noisy issue. Since we use a bi-objective optimization framework to search for problem instances, the tradeoff between the LSI (landscape similarity) and ADC (algorithm distinguishing capability) would mathematically help reduce the risk of too similar noise functions around the CoCo-BBOB instances. Our experiments results (both Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 4.3) also demonstrate that functions generated by EoB hold differences with CoCo-BBOB. The similar mathematical structure between EoB and CoCo-BBOB may reveal that: 1) changing a small part in a function’s mathematical definition may lead to certain high-level landscape variation. 2) designing benchmark by human is difficult since we may not realize such small differences.

[**W2, high-dimensional case**]

We provide an additional experiment where we use EoB to evolve a 100D benchmark. The pareto dynamics are provided at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/pareto_100Devolution.png . From results, we could observe that functional synthesis learned by LLM still works, where manual human design may fail.

[**Q2, differences with GP**]

We highlight that EoB fundamentally differs from traditional Genetic Programming (GP) or expression-tree-based generators by replacing blind symbolic search with heuristic reasoning. Traditional GP is time-consuming and heavily dependent on expert knowledge, requiring expertise in defining the symbolic set, balancing exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and implementing specialized acceleration techniques. In contrast, EoB leverages the LLM’s profound understanding of mathematical structures and optimization domain knowledge, enabling a more efficient Evolution of Heuristics (EoH) inspired process. EoB can synthesize structurally sound and diverse benchmarks significantly faster than GP, requiring only high-level knowledge to outperform results from traditional methods.

While LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, EoB employs a population-based evolutionary strategy that ensures high-quality and consistent outcomes. To evaluate this stability, we conducted 5 independent EoB-UAV searching runs with different random seeds. As shown in the table below, the peak ADC achieved in each run remains highly consistent, with all runs significantly outperforming the standard BBOB baseline. This demonstrates that the selection pressure within our evolutionary loop effectively mitigates LLM-induced randomness, leading to a reliable convergence on high-quality benchmark suites.

| **Run Index** | **Run 1** | **Run 2** | **Run 3** | **Run 4** | **Run 5** | **CoCo-BBOB (Baseline)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Max ADC** | 0.8256 | 0.8398 | 0.8713 | 0.8380 | 0.8516 | 0.3918 |

[**Q4, computational cost**]

Using DeepSeek-v3.2, a complete evolutionary run takes approximately 20 minutes with a total API cost of $0.37 (avg. $0.01 per function). Compared to traditional GP, which often requires hours of intensive symbolic search and expert tuning, EoB is significantly faster while generating benchmarks of higher structural quality and diversity. These functions are fully reusable once generated, offering a highly cost-effective and superior alternative to both manual expert design and traditional symbolic generators.

At last, we thank again for your insightful discussion with us. Should the above responses address your concerns, could you consider raising the score to reflect that.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the detailed comments. We provide following responses to address your concerns.

[**W1 & Q1, proxy consistency**] We have addressed this precisely by defining a performance consistency metric $C(B_{source}, B_{target})$ in Section 4.3.3 and Table 3. The results there clearly show that compared to representative benchmark CoCo-BBOB, EoB generates synthetic proxy functions that better align with the algorithm performance behavior on target realistic tasks.

[**W2, surrogate model**]

We would like to argue that our EoB should not be positioned within the scope of surrogate modeling. The reasons behind are: 1) EoB’s task is benchmark generation,  which requires generation of multiple similar and distinguishable function instances for one or more given problem of interests. Surrogate models such as GP construct a model for a target problem.  2) EoB uses feature-based search to reduce the difficulty of GP on high-dimensional problems. 3) EoB is an end-to-end automated benchmark generation framework, while surrogate modeling requires more expert-level knowledge on selecting and tuning approximation models.

[**W3 & Q7, design choices**]

**$sigma$**. We would like to clarify that  $sigma$ is a self-adaptive parameter computed from the target task's distribution in the NeurELA feature space. This data-driven mechanism ensures the LSI objective is **scale-invariant** and robust across diverse target optimization tasks. We will add this detail into the revised paper.

**evolutionary strategy**. We kindly remind the reviewer that in EoB, we did not use any evolutionary strategy for solving the bi-objective benchmark generation problem.

**population size N**. We ablated this parameter by N=8 and N=64 and provide the results at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/pareto_front_popsize.png. From the results, we selected N=32.

**generation size H**. We would like to first explain that we use H=24 because CoCo-BBOB contains 24 functions. Setting H=24 facilitates a fair comparison with this representative benchmark baseline. We also provide evolution results of H=240 at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/pareto_front_H240.png, where the results show that H is not a sensitive parameter.

[**Q2, bayesian optimization**]

Following your suggestion, we extended our experiments to include $q$-LogEI, TuRBO and IWBO. We tested them on the EoB-BBOB suite. The results show that EoB-BBOB  suite achieves max ADC score of 0.698 (compared to 0.323 on COCO-BBOB), which is consistent with our conclusion.

[**Q3, deterministic and differentiable function**]

We would like to clarify that the functions generated by EoB are deterministic and differentiable. However, EoB provides flexibility for users: one can either regard these functions as black-box functions or white-box ones. This flexibility exactly leads to several advantages and broad usages of EoB as we claimed in Sec. 5. We hope the reviewer could reconsider this point.

[**Q4, ADC measure**] 

We understand your concern, however, the standard deviation measure we used in ADC is also a quantitative measure that could reflect the algorithm performance differences across different optimizers. To clear your concern, we apply non-parametric statistic test (Friedman) on the objective matrix to analyse the significance of optimizers’ performance differences, and plot its positive correlation with our standard deviation measure at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/adc_confidence.png. We believe this result clearly show that our ADC measure is sufficient.

[**Q5, initialization prompt**]

We provide visualization results at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/uav_gen0_pareto_comparison.png to show the advantage when we inject the engineered prompt to EoB for initialization. It clearly demonstrates that: without such design, the initial population generated by EoB is less diverse.

[**Q6, numerical measure**] Following your suggestion, we provide LSI (feature level closeness, larger is better) score (Ours: 0.3073 v.s. CoCo: 0.0094). We also provide ADC scores (EoB: 0.8349 v.s. CoCo-BBOB: 0.3918).

[**Q8, evolutionary strategy**]

Since the core task in this paper is benchmark generation through code evolution, we use LLM as an evolutionary optimizer. The other BBO optimizers, can not be used for such code evolution tasks. The motivation of the N reference vectors follows standard setting of multi-objective optimizers to ensure the diversity on the initialization population.

[**Q9,  crossover, mutation, and selection**]

Yes, these operators are carried out by LLM, and we have provided clear elaboration of their black-box behaviors in Sec. 4.2.1 and Fig. 2, where we visualize how these operation impact the function’s code and then facilitates the co-evolution of landscapes.

We hope the above responses could address your concerns. We will also appreciate the reviewer if the score could be raised accordingly.

rebuttals.rebuttal:
We appreciate the reviewer for your thoughtful comments, which we address by following point-to-point responses.

[**W1, scope overstatement**] We agree with the reviewer that a more conservative scope statement should be made, hence, we will revise the scope in intro as continuous single-objective black-box optimization, and use this accurate scope as a case study to show the effectiveness of our EoB as a general benchmark design framework. We hope the reviewer would not consider this issue as a weakness of EoB, since single-objective continuous black-box optimization is already a quite broad domain, a meaningful testbed for EoB.

[**W2 & Q1 & Q3 & Q4 & Q5, design choices**] We would like to clarify that the design choices of EoB are non-trivial. They naturally arise from the multi-objective LLM-driven evolution framework, and for sure, carefully designed by us with clear motivation.

LSI & ADC (your Q1). Given a group of unknown realistic BBO problems, how could we extend or proxy them by easy-to-analyse synthetic functions? In EoB, we address this by using LSI to ensure the similarity of the generated functions with the target tasks, and ADC to ensure these functions are challenging enough. As the reviewer stated at “Strength”, this is  the most adapted choice given the task of benchmark generation.

ELA (your Q3). ELA has a long-standing reputation in analysing landscape properties of diverse optimization problems. In many earlier automated algorithm selection works and recent learning-based works, ELA is a predominant choice to identify problems, which is a good choice for EoB to compute LSI. To the best of our knowledge, there are no particular better alternatives.

Atoms (your Q4). We would like to first clarify that the atom operations are not limited to the three you have mentioned, actually the atom operations in EoB’s evolution include Smooth Global Modulation, Cross-dimensional Interaction, Frequency Warping, High-frequency Oscillation, Rotational Transformation, Break Symmetry, Smooth Asymmetric Perturbation. Representative benchmark such as CoCo-BBOB is constructed exactly by using these mathematical operations to create diverse landscapes.

Baseline (your Q5). While the CoCo-BBOB set dates back to 2010, it remains our community’s golden standard for validating algorithms’ performances. By directly comparing EoB to it, we show its limitations and hence further underscore the importance of novel exploration such as our EoB.

[**W3, benchmark detail**] We would like to explain to the reviewer that our primary target in this paper is to discover functions with landscape diversity and algorithm differentiation ability. To this end, we set the searching objectives as 2 in EoB, and let the other settings you mentioned as fixed (e.g., 10D, maxFEs=20000 for EoB-BBOB). To extend these settings, one can either use EoB as CoCo-BBOB (the same group of functions but set different dimensions and maxFEs), or add more searching objectives into EoB’s objective space. We will revise the above discussion into our paper.

[**W4 & W5, landscape diversity**] To clarify, we will provide a visualization of the distribution of EoB functions in the feature space in https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/visualization_uav_eob.png, which confirms that our functions possess landscape diversity. More importantly, all of the results in our paper reveal that our LSI and ADC measures are general enough to assist LLM in generating benchmarks for both synthetic and realistic tasks.

[**W6, prompt engineering**] We have to note that the proper prompt templates we constructed is a common practice in existing LLM-based algorithm design works to 1) let the LLM understand the context and necessary knowledge; 2) align LLM’s thinking with a structural framework. With these unified and templated protocols, EoB is fully automated by the LLM’s automatic code evolution.

[**W7, table captions**] Following your valuable suggestions, we have revised those table captions: 1) Table 1: The wall-clock evaluation time using EoB or target realistic tasks for MetaBBO approaches, less is better; 2) Table 2: The final test-performance of GLHF tained by different baseline benchmarks; 3) Table 3: Test-performance consistency between baseline benchmarks and realistic tasks. 

[**Q2, computational budget**] EoB calls LLM 20 times (2 times per generation x 10 generations of evolution) for generating a function. Using DeepSeek-v3.2, a complete evolutionary run takes approximately 20 minutes with a total API cost of $0.37 (avg. $0.01 per generated function). These benchmarks are fully reusable once generated, offering a highly cost-effective alternative to expert design.

We hope the above responses could address your concerns and sincerely hope the reviewer could reconsider the scores to encourage the research on automated benchmark generation, which is truly a valuable and less-discussed aspect in our community.

comments.author: Authors
comments.comment:
[**Q1, justification for the design choices**]

**1. LSI/ADC**. We would like to provide the reviewer an important use case the EoB addresses: suppose a user has a couple of realistic BBO tasks to solve, however these tasks are very expensive to simulate. In such case, we want to construct synthetic functions that: 1) have high LSI to make them as similar as possible with the reslistic problems in the landscape space; 2) have high ADC to make them challenging enough to tell the differences between optimization algorithms. With these two key points, the users could analyse the algorithm-task performance for subsequent algorithm design. We hope this could justify our LSI/ADC designs for you.

**2. ELA**. For LSI, we aim to measuring the landscape similarity, where we need some landscape feature analysis tools to provide us meaningful problem-specific features. To this end, we use NeurELA, a Transformer-based ELA feature extractor to provide such features. We also ackonwledge that there are alternatives such as traditional ELA (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2001576.2001690) and a recent DeepELA (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11297580) framework, however, traditional ELA depends on inefficient statistical computation and DeepELA is limited by its inability on high-dimensional problems (such as UAV in our paper). We will add this justification into our revised paper.

**3. Landscape Construction**. Due to the narrow space provided in the last rebuttal round, we can not provide very clear justification of how EoB’s landscape construction help build a general benchmark. In this response, we first provide examples (”mutation.png” and “crossover.png” at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/uav_gen0_pareto_comparison.png)) of how EoB’s LLM mutate and crossover atom landscape changes into the sourcecodes of the generated functions to improve LSI and ADC scores. Guided by the evolution, specifically, by embedding diverse methematical operations (sign(), sqrt(), sin(), max() etc.) into a function, EoB continuously construct corresponding landscapes to make the function more like a benchmark function. That is, these mathematical operations, would introduce diverse landscape properties, and since this is guided by EoB’s bi-objective search, the generated function would become better monotonically. At last, please recall the analytical results in our paper, where we have validated that EoB could generate more diverse benchmark than CoCo-BBOB and its generated benchamark provide more landscape knowledge to help learning-based optimizer to learn generalizable optimization policy. We promise to revise the discussion above into the paper.

[**Q2, extent of automation**]

We would like to further explain why we claimed EoB as an end-to-end automation framework.  We first respectfully request the reviewer to check the newly updated jupyter-notebook file at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/custom_tutorial.ipynb, where we provide a step-by-step tutorial how a normal user uses EoB to generate benchmark for his/her own problem of interests. It is a fully automated end-to-end workflow: EoB only require the user to provide evaluation data of the target problems, then EoB runs itself automatically and output all generated functions for the user. We believe such extent of automation, is already a breakthrough compared to those traditional human-dependent benchmark construction approaches.

[**Q3, distinction between performance variance and landscape diversity**]

We would like to first clarify that our major aim in this paper (either claimed in the introduction or the methodology section) is not focused on landscape diversity. Instead, we propose a bi-objective evolution paradigm that generate benchmark which 1) improve LSI to ensure the generated benchamrk show landscape similarity with target problem of interests; 2) improve ADC to further enhance the difficulty of the generated functions to better differentiate optimziation algorithms. 

As for the relationship between the performance variance and landscape diversity, there are not direct connections. Instead, we emphasize that the landscape diversity emerges as the pareto-front of the bi-objective evolution moves forward, for which we provide the evolution paths at (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/eob_bbob_pareto_evolution.png , https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/eob_uav_pareto_evolution.png and https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/eob_hpo_pareto_evolution.png). These paths clearly show the tradoff between ADC and LSI gives birth to function instances with different properties, which indirectly enhance the landscape diversity. We will add this valuable discussion into the revised paper, as you suggested.

We hope the above justifications could clear your concerns. If so, we respectfully hope the reviewer could reflect our efforts in the final score.

comments.author: Authors
comments.comment:
[**Q1, stochastic and non-differentiable aspects of EoB**]

Aha! We would like to appreciate the reviewer for your further clarification on this aspect, and we now figure out what is the exact concern. Actually, our EoB have already generated (capable of) many non-differentiable function instances. This is achieved by:

1. Our target problems of interests, such as CoCo-BBOB, UAV and HPO tasks, include sufficient non-differentiable functions (problem instances). For example, in the representative CoCo-BBOB set, 13 of 24 function instances are non-differentiable somewhere in the searching range. In the definitions of these functions, non-differentiable mathematical operations are included such as sign(), abs(), floor(), max() and sqrt() (sqrt is not differentiable at 0). 
2. Our EoB’s operation space is the code space, where LLM iteratively mutate and crossover the sourcecode of a function, by using numpy operations. Since numpy operations include non-differentiable mathematical operations (as mentioned above), the searching of EoB naturally ensure that the generated function could be non-differentiable.
3. We also respectfully request the reviewer to re-check function examples EoB generates for CoCo-BBOB, UAV and HPO (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result, EoB-BBOB.py, EoB-UAV.py, EoB-HPO.py). We believe you can find many non-differentiable operations inthe sourcecodes of these functions.

Given the explaination on non-differentiable aspect of our EoB, we agree with the reviewer that we could push EoB a step forward: to embrace the stochastic problems. To this end, we select a representative stochastic benchmark: CoCo-BBOB-noisy (https://numbbo.github.io/coco/testsuites/bbob-noisy), which originates from CoCo-BBOB’s 24 basic functions but add uninform, gaussian or cauchy noises per evaluation to create time-variant stochastic problems. We use EoB to generate 24 functions by using CoCo-BBOB-noisy as target benchmark. We provide the rank consistency (eq. 5 in our paper) between {CoCo-BBOB or EoB} and {CoCo-BBOB-noisy} in the small table below:

| Scenario | CoCo-BBOB | EoB-BBOB-noisy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CoCo-BBOB-noisy | 0.215 | 0.736 |

The results show that: 1) the algorithm performance indeed varies a lot between CoCo-BBOB and CoCo-BBOB-noisy due to the added stochastic; 2) Thanks to our EoB’s bi-objective searching ability, its generated functions perform more consistently with CoCo-BBOB-noisy. We believe this experiment could clear your concern.

We promise you that we will add this valuable aspect into our EoB, this is absolutely an important revision, thanks for your insights!

[**Q2, effects of the LLM-based operators**]

We fully understand your concerns and agree that a more detailed illustration could enhance your (and future readers) undertanding on these operators. To this end, we provide examples of the crossover (”crossover.png”) stage and the mutation (”mutation.png”) stage at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/uav_gen0_pareto_comparison.png) . In the illustration, we also show how different LLMs perform as you suggested. We do not include selection stage since it is notcontrolled by LLM (see our paper). In the results, we could observe that LLM’s reasoning ability surely improve the solution quality by introducing effective code-level crossover and mutation, with a reasonable thinking on the relationship between landscape change and corresponding code-level changes. Besides, different LLMs may perform differently, our choice, DeepSeek-V3.2, is more aggressive to facilitate exploration-exploitation tradeoff hence leads to further performance improvement. In contrast, Gemini is somewhat conservative. Thanks for your suggestion, we will definitely add the above discussion into our revised paper!

[**Q3, the explaination of $\sigma$**]

Let us explain the details of $\sigma$. First, we emphasize that **$\sigma$ doesn’t need any tuning**. Specifically, $\sigma$ is defined as the mean Euclidean distance to the nearest neighbor among all target task instances:

$\sigma = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \min_{j \neq i} \| \mathbf{a}_i - \mathbf{a}_j \|_2$
where $\mathbf{a}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{16}$ is the feature vector of the $i$-th instance, by feeding the {x, f(x)} data of the problem into NeurELA. Hence, we must emphasize that, **$\sigma$ is not a hyper-parameter**, hence, it is not sensitive. Instead, it is just a scale factor to facilitate universal computation of LSI under different taget problem distribution of interests. For example, if we use EoB to generate benchmark for UAV and HPO tasks respectively, $\sigma$ will ensure the LSI’s value scale consistent. By doing so, EoB could perform stably and generally across different benchmark generation scenarios.

In the end, we really appreciate your careful review on our paper, we are here and welcome any further questions!

comments.comment:
[**Q1, DeepELA**]

We ackonwledge DeepELA is also a feasible feature extractor for EoB. However, we would like to clarify that DeepELA is not a dimenional-free method, that is, if we consider its pre-trained model such as  (large_50d_v1, https://github.com/mvseiler/deep_ela/tree/main/deep_ela/models) , it is only capable of providing features for HPO tasks in our paper, since UAV tasks in our paper features much higher dimensions. Under this context, we add DeepELA into HPO testing experiments and provide the table below for you. 

|  | LDE | GLEET | SYMBOL | RLDEAFL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neur-ELA | **0.7621** | **0.8342** | **0.7428** | **0.8593** |
| Deep-ELA | 0.7509 | 0.7923 | 0.7295 | 0.7967 |
| ELA: Meta-Model | 0.7528 | 0.7685 | 0.7324 | 0.7891 |
| ELA: Distribution of the Objective Function Values | 0.7424 | 0.7858 | 0.7188 | 0.7812 |
| ELA: Convexity | 0.7495 | 0.7612 | 0.7397 | 0.7954 |
| ELA: Local search | 0.7487 | 0.7705 | 0.7242 | 0.7761 |
| ELA: Levelset | 0.7398 | 0.7902 | 0.7315 | 0.7905 |
| ELA: Curvature | 0.7462 | 0.7698 | 0.7332 | 0.7747 |

Indeed, DeepELA show competitive performance against traditional ELA sets, however, NeurELA is more capable in our EoB’s tasks. We think this is possibly because NeurELA is more compatible with learning-assisted approaches, as we elaborated in the last rebuttal round. To summarize, we hope the reviewer could understand us on the choice of NeurELA.

[**Q2, feature space analysis**]

We think the reviewer’s suggestion is constructive and will indeed enhance EoB’s contribution as a benchmark for traditional optimizers. To this end, we use CoCo-BBOB to generate 240 instances (random shift and rotation on the 24 basic functions), MA-BBOB to generate 240 instances (randomly select functions in CoCo-BBOB as those for interpolation), and our EoB to generate 240 instances by running our method repeatedly. We then show PCA-based feature space visualization of these 720 instances at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoB/result/visualization_mabbob_coco_eob.png . This result reveal that, since MA-BBOB depends on the selection of functions to be interpolated  and uses such interpolation to fill the function space, it is indeed an useful tool to augment existing benchmark. Yet, it is also limited by the interpolated functions since the affine combination operation. EoB-generated instances, on the one hand, expands a more uniform instance range, and on the other hand, provides moderate novel-feature instances beyond CoCo-BBOB and MA-BBOB. This is because the bi-objective searching, where an objective is to generate problem with algorithm differentiation capability, which pushes LLM to explore novel problems with novel ela features. 

Again, we appreciate your valuable time for such valuable discussions. If your concerns were indeed addressed, could we respectfully request a score reconsideration. We will be here if any further questions need to be discussed.

rebuttal_acks.reasons: Thank you for your response. All of my concerns have been addressed. I have also reviewed the discussions from the other reviewers and did not find any major issues. Although there are requests for additional results and explanations, I do not believe these will affect the main contribution of the paper. Therefore, I will maintain my positive score.

The rebuttal clarifies some aspects, particularly the computational cost and the scope

However, my main concerns remain insufficiently addressed. In particular, the justification for the design choices (LSI/ADC, ELA, and landscape construction) and the extent to which the method is truly automated remain unclear.

Importantly, the definition of benchmark diversity, which is central to the contribution, remains problematic. The distinction between performance variance and landscape diversity is not addressed in a meaningful way.

These issues are central to the paper’s claims and would require more substantial revisions.

Thank you to the authors for their efforts in addressing my concerns, especially through the extensive additional experiments. I believe these experiments and discussions are important and should be incorporated into the final version of the paper. That said, I still have the following concerns:

1. The authors have convinced me that the synthetic benchmarks generated by the proposed method can resemble the target tasks and yield rankings of black-box optimization methods that are broadly consistent with those observed on real-world tasks. However, I am still not fully convinced at the conceptual level by the focus on deterministic and differentiable functions. In many real-world settings, the oracle is often stochastic and non-differentiable. Optimizing such functions can be fundamentally different from optimizing deterministic, differentiable ones, which may in turn lead to inconsistent method rankings. Could the authors explore whether their framework can also generate stochastic and non-differentiable functions, and then evaluate whether the resulting rankings remain consistent? This remains my main concern regarding the reliability and generality of the proposed benchmarking approach. In my view, the key contribution of this work is the design of a method for generating benchmarks for black-box optimization, rather than enabling white-box optimization through deterministic and differentiable surrogates, although I do appreciate that aspect of the paper.

2. Regarding the questions of mutation, crossover, and selection, Section 4.2.1 and Figure 2 are currently not sufficient to clearly address how the LLM actually performs these operators. I believe several concrete examples would be very helpful, for instance, showing input functions and output functions before and after each operation performed by the LLM. Such evidence would substantially improve the trustworthiness of the method. In addition, different LLMs may induce different behaviors or biases in these operations, so a more detailed study of model-specific effects would be highly appreciated.

3. The data-driven procedure for choosing $\sigma$ is important and deserves a more detailed explanation, as it appears to be one of the sensitive hyperparameters in the method. The current paper lacks sufficient discussion of this point.

I would be willing to raise my score if these remaining concerns are carefully addressed.

Thank you for the rebuttal. I appreciate the authors’ effort in clarifying several of my concerns.
I have a few follow-up questions.

1. Thank you for clarifying the use of NeurELA. Nevertheless, it would strengthen the study if you could perform a sensitivity analysis using DeepELA instead, in order to assess how sensitive the proposed approach is to the particular choice of landscape representation.

2. More generally, consider a future scenario in which I develop a new optimization algorithm and benchmark it on your generated suite. A reviewer may still criticize the study for not including another benchmark suite, such as that of Skvorc et al. (2026) or MA-BBOB. In that case, the key missing aspect is not simply additional benchmarking, but an analysis of whether these different benchmark suites occupy the same landscape space. For example, representing them all with NeurELA and comparing their coverage of the feature space would provide a much stronger basis for judging complementarity, overlap, and representativeness.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
The paper presents an LLM-assisted framework for Black-Box Optimization Benchmark Design which features an LLM-based evolutionary method for generating synthetic functions to benchmark black-box optimizers. This is an important research challenge because in many real-world applications, designing human-crafted benchmarks can be expensive, whereas these LLM-generated functions can be obtained at much lower cost. In particular, the authors formulate the generation of such related functions as a bi-objective optimization problem, maximizing both the landscape similarity to target hard-to-model BBO tasks and the ability of the benchmark to effectively differentiate among various BBO algorithms. The resulting generated functions can then be treated as unknown oracle functions for benchmarking black-box optimizers.

Overall, the reviewers are mostly positive of this paper. The rebuttal has been quite effective in addressing most concerns. A few concerns still remain and while I agree with the reviewer on those points, I view them as potential future work. Specifically, a key concern is that this work suffers from a strong limitation in its definition of benchmark diversity. The distinction between performance variance and landscape diversity is not properly addressed. The diversification mechanism is heavily hand-designed, relying on prompt engineering and predefined heuristics. This introduces a strong bias in the types of benchmarks that can be generated.

Having said that, this paper presents a very new idea to address a key bottleneck in the existing development cycle of black-box optimizers. Despite the clearly substantial limitations, I still see that this idea will be of great interest for researchers in this field & can help foster more impactful ideas. As such, I recommend acceptance for this work.

I hope the authors will take into account the feedback on writing clarity from the reviewers to put forward a camera-ready version with best clarity.
