comments.comment:
Thank you for increasing your confidence! We truly appreciate it as well as your valuable suggestion. Your feedback has helped strengthen and shape the paper. In the revision, we will clarify that the reduction in computational complexity primarily stems from the imposed spatial locality, and explicitly distinguish this practical design choice from the classical Krause model.

--- 

**Updated on 04/07**

After reading the reviewer's final justification, we would like to further clarify that while the local neighborhood is defined spatially for efficiency, **the interaction itself is governed by representation-space similarity via Top-$k$ selection**. 

Thus, spatial locality serves as a practical constraint, whereas **the bounded-confidence mechanism is implemented through similarity-based selection**, remaining consistent with the core principle of Krause dynamics. We will clarify this distinction in the revision to avoid confusion.

---

rebuttal_acks.reasons:
Thanks to the authors for their detailed response to my concerns. I am satisfied with the scaling‑law results and now have a clearer understanding of the mechanism behind the proposed transformer architecture. I still have several questions.

1. What is the key mathematical intuition behind the Kruse Synchronization Transformer in reducing attention sinks?

2. Could you provide more details on the local masking strategy used in this paper? Is the method sensitive to the choice of local masking strategy?

I would like to thank the authors for their reply and adding results. However, I want to clarify a bit more regarding my questions.

1. Regarding long context performance:
    1.1 PG-19's average sequence length is much longer than 4K, and training / eval up to 4K in my opinion is not convincing enough to justify strong long context capability. Besides, even at the 1K to 4K regime, we could observe the relative advantage of Krause-Attention diminishing quickly compared with standard attention. A more convincing setting would be fine-tuning / evaluating on long context dataset (e.g., PG-19 / Books3) with 8-32K context length.
    
    1.2 For long-context (e.g., at least 8-16K), sliding window attention (with sink) usually has a window size of at least 512-1K. It is unclear when window size is large, if there's still notable improvement of Krause-Attention over sliding window attention with sink (and if there's still notable practical speedup since $K$ could also need to be significantly larger to be competitive) as the eval in the paper restricts to a very small window size of 32.
    
    1.3 As a plus, it would be more convincing if long-context downstream eval results could be shown, such as on LongBench.

2. Regarding sliding window attention with attention sink
    2.1 For the experiment in Q2, is attention sink baseline is just learning a single sink token at each layer, which is much less parameters than adding a Krause branch? If this is true, in my opinion the proper comparison should be a parameter-matched sliding window attention branch with attention sink.

In general, I genuinely appreciate the authors reply, but my major questions on performance on realistic long context data and how Krause Attention compares (performance, runtime) with sliding window attention with sink using a realistic window size has not been fully addressed.

Thank the authors for their responses and efforts to run additional experiments/ablations. 

Regarding appropriately strong baselines from the prior work [1-5], that's the closest in spirit to Krause Attention would be the Routing Transformer [3], which clusters the queries Q and keys K, maintaining a top-k set of cluster centroids for each, and when computing attention scores routes keys to cluster centroids of Q. It's plausible that Routing Transformer's Attention has a bias for multi-cluster dynamics and dynamic sparsity. And I think that makes it a particularly strong and highly relevant baseline to compare against to judge the merits of Krause Attention against. 

The results of the Krause Attention-based Transformer with 20M params on CIFAR compared to RoPE and sparse attention is definitely promising and a good start, but a single experiment at the CIFAR and 20M scale is not sufficient evidence for the generality of the proposed approach. It would be nice to have run image classification results on a few standard suite of classification benchmarks (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet) to see if the results hold at standard ViT-B/L model scales and dataset complexity. 

For the language modelling results on WikiText-103, the performance gains on PPL of Krause Attention compared to Window Attention baseline are very small and reasonable to assume to be within the margin of error. The authors can run the standard  zero-shot downstream benchmark evals (LAMBADA, Blimp, CBT, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-e) using their trained from scratch model checkpoints. Since most if not all Transformer and Attention improvements benchmark the base model quality using this it's easy to compare these quantitative results. 

Overall, I do think there is a very interesting idea in this paper, but the experimental validation (strong and appropriate baselines, dataset size/complexity, model size) are not of sufficient rigor. While the authors have made efforts in the rebuttal to address some of these concerns. I'm still not entirely convinced for the reasons above.  

I think these additions are beyond the scope of 1 week rebuttal but they will greatly improve the evidence to support the main claims and their generality. I will maintain my current score.

Thank you for your response and clarification. I would suggest clarifying that the reduction in computational complexity mainly comes from this design choice, rather than from Krause attention itself.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
The paper received mixed reviews, with two reviewers recommending weak acceptance and two reviewers voting for weak rejection despite the extensive author rebuttal. The AC has examined the reviews, the author rebuttal, and all post-rebuttal discussions carefully. The AC acknowledges that the authors made unusually substantial efforts during the rebuttal period: including scaling experiments on models trained from scratch (200M/500M parameters), LongBench evaluations at 8K context, parameter-matched comparisons against sliding-window + sink token, a Routing Transformer baseline, and ViT-B results on CIFAR-10/100 -- which goes beyond what is typically expected in a short rebuttal cycle.

The AC agrees with the positive reviewers, and with the authors' framing, that the bounded-confidence formulation of Krause Attention offers an interesting and principled inductive bias for mitigating attention sinks, with broad empirical coverage across vision (ViT/Swin), autoregressive generation, and language modeling. The AC also notes the authors' clarification that LLM experiments were positioned as a compatibility study rather than a full replacement of self-attention. However, the concerns from the negative reviewers were not fully resolved even after this clarification. 3mNZ (the most confident reviewer at confidence 5) noted that several rebuttal additions felt preliminary, quoting: "the zero-shot performance scores on downstream tasks for 200M/500M Krause Attention LMs seem on average quite low for Transformer models of that size," and that the CIFAR-scale gains and the absence of ImageNet + ViT-B/L results limit confidence in the generality claims at standard scales. gJSx, while upgrading to weak accept, also flagged that "the questions on its scalability and long-context capability still remain," noting that the Krause branch ultimately serves a complementary role alongside global attention rather than replacing it, and that very long-context evaluation (16K–32K) is acknowledged by the authors to be out of scope of this submission.

Overall, while the work has clear merits and the rebuttal materially strengthened the empirical case, the AC's read of the post-rebuttal state is that the two positive reviewers settled at weak accept (rather than moving to a stronger endorsement) and the two negative reviewers did not raise their scores after the rebuttal. When calibrating mixed-rating papers among the broader ICML submission pool, this lack of a clear advocate makes the paper difficult to prioritize. Therefore, the AC reluctantly decides to not accept the work in this cycle, with the hope that the authors will incorporate the additional experimental results, the clarification on the complementary role of the Krause branch, and the suggested broader baselines and scales (Routing Transformer comparisons, ViT-B/L on ImageNet, longer-context LM evaluations done at the proper scale) into an improved version for the next venue. The AC believes the core idea is promising and that a stronger empirical package would make this a competitive submission.

our_title: DARC: Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding

match.matched_title: DARC: Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding

submission.title: DARC: Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding
submission.abstract: Preference-based alignment methods (e.g., RLHF, DPO) typically optimize a single scalar objective, implicitly averaging over heterogeneous human preferences. In practice, systematic annotator and user-group disagreement makes mean-reward maximization brittle and susceptible to proxy over-optimization. We propose **Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding (DARC)**, a retraining-free inference-time method that frames response selection as distributionally robust, risk-sensitive decision making. Given multiple preference samples or scalable disagreement proxies, DARC reranks candidates by maximizing a *KL-robust (entropic)* satisfaction objective, and provides simple deployment controls that cap or penalize the corresponding entropic risk premium relative to the mean, enabling explicit risk budgets without retraining. We provide theoretical characterization linking this decoding rule to principled pessimism and KL-based distributionally robust optimization. Experiments on alignment benchmarks show that DARC reduces disagreement and tail risk while maintaining competitive average quality under noisy, heterogeneous feedback.
submission.lay_summary: Large language models are often aligned using human preference feedback, but people do not always agree on what makes an answer good. Existing alignment methods usually average these preferences into a single score, which can cause models to choose responses that look good on average but are risky, polarizing, or unsatisfactory for some users. This paper proposes DARC, an inference-time method that selects model responses while explicitly accounting for disagreement and risk. Instead of retraining the model, DARC reranks a set of candidate responses using a robust objective that favors answers with high expected satisfaction and lower uncertainty across users or evaluators. The method also provides practical controls for limiting risk during deployment. Experiments show that DARC reduces disagreement and improves worst-case outcomes while maintaining competitive average response quality, especially on prompts where user preferences are highly divided.

reviews.summary: The work claims to explore a central concept in preference-based optimization, the problem of learning from heterogeneous human preferences rather than assuming a single latent scalar utility. This works pertains to inference time selection under uncertainty. The authors propose Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding (DARC), that penalizes candidate responses with high disagreement. To remove the need for multi-annotator data at inference time, it estimates disagreement by applying style-preserving perturbations to candidates and measuring the variance of a reward model’s scores across these perturbations. The paper connects this empirical variance penalty to a lower confidence bound (LCB) on expected satisfaction and to distributionally robust optimization (DRO) via a KL-robust entropic objective.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
* The work provides a theoretical justification for mean-dispersion decoding rules. By linking finite-sample LCB bounds (Prop 3.3) with $\chi^2$-DRO (Prop 3.6) and KL-robust entropic objectives (Theorem 3.5), it gives foundation for a practice that is often treated as an ad-hoc heuristic.
* Comparison with recent inference-time baselines (DeAL, HedgeTune) makes the empirical results relevant. DARC demonstrates consistent improvements across these methods in Table1 and Table 2.
* Using style-preserving perturbations to estimate variance at inference time is a good solution to the lack of multi-annotator data. It requires no changes to the underlying model or reward model.

**Weakness**
* Over-reliance on "style-preserving" perturbations for proxy estimation, In (Appendix H.13 and and Section 5.1), the rewrite prompt strictly enforces "style-preserving perturbations". Reward models are notoriously easily hacked via specific spurious correlations (like verbosity, sycophancy, or formatting). If a candidate response is highly rewarded solely because it is sycophantic, a style-preserving perturbation will keep the sycophancy. The RM will output uniformly high scores across all variants, yielding a low variance proxy ($\hat{\sigma} \approx 0$). Consequently, DARC will fail to penalize this hacked response. It lacks ablations on alternative perturbation strategies that explicitly probe these spurious features
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: * Why restrict the proxy estimation strictly to "style-preserving" perturbations (Appendix H.13 and Section 5.1)? If the reward model relies on a spurious correlation (e.g., length or a specific sycophantic phrase), and your rewrite prompt preserves that feature, the variance will be artificially low and DARC will fail to penalize the hacked response. Did you experiment with perturbations that explicitly target known RM hacks, and how would DARC perform in that setting?

reviews.summary: In this paper, the authors proposed DARC, a retraining-free inference-time method that reranks LLM candidate responses by maximizing a KL-robust value instead of mean reward, targeting robustness under heterogeneous human preferences. The authors derive uniform lower confidence bounds on expected satisfaction, connect them to KL-DRO and $\chi^2$-DRO characterizations, and offer three practical decoding variants (entropic, τ-constrained, ε-tie-breaking) and a multi-scorer extension. Experimental results on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 with both proxy and human evaluation show that DARC reduces disagreement risk and improves tail robustness.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
> **Strengths:**

1. The authors formulate a well-defined problem connecting preference heterogeneity to inference-time robustness, which has been clearly articulated.

2. The proposed method is modular, inference-time only, and stacks on top of training-time robust policies (cDPO/rDPO) with minimal overhead.

3. The authors provide evaluations on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 across two LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) with scaling validation on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, where DARC variants consistently outperform baselines. The authors also include human evaluation with 5 annotators, proxy validity diagnostics, mismatch analysis, robustness checks, and ablations. Further, the case studies also illustrate the method's behavior.

> **Minor Weaknesses:**

1. The LCB and DRO guarantees (Proposition 3.3, Theorem 3.5) assume i.i.d. scalar satisfaction samples, but the practical instantiation uses perturbation-based RM score variance as a proxy.

2. The Tradeoff metric μ̂ − λσ̂ directly rewards what DARC optimizes (high mean, low σ̂), so improvements on this metric are partly by construction. Rather, CVaR and human scores are more informative.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
Please refer to the weaknesses.

> **Questions:**

1. Figure 3 Q1 bucket shows ∆Tradeoff ≈ 0 or slightly negative for low-disagreement prompts. Does it suggest that DARC's conservatism may cost mean reward when disagreement is low?
reviews.final_justification: The rebuttal clarified my primary concerns.

reviews.summary: Human preferences are noisy and pairs that may seem to have the highest mean reward can actually have considerable disagreement. The authors propose instead a disagreement-aware formulation that penalizes candidates with large disagreement tails relative to the mean score. Therefore, they rerank candidates at inference time that are less likely to overrule preferences and have more consensus. This method decreases reward risk and is more robust to disagreement.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

*The paper is well presented, particularly at the beginning. Figure 1 in particular is a strong visual and makes the paper easy to understand.

*The idea of the paper is intuitive and relevant. Disagreement-aware methods are important in alignment.

*The math is, to the best of my ability, correct. I followed the equations and did not notice any obvious mistakes.

*The paper's results suggest meaningful improvements and match the claims made at the beginning and throughout. I also appreciated that the evaluation lines up with the paper's motivation, since they explicitly look at high-disagreement / high-variance prompts instead of only reporting overall averages. I was pleased to see ablations and a large set of baselines, and that the method seemed to compare favorably to them, especially on the disagreement-related metrics:


Weaknesses:

*The primary weakness with this paper is one the authors acknowledge. As they say, the proxies are “scalable screening signals, not calibrated human-disagreement estimates.” They elaborate on this concern in the appendix, but it makes their contributions less compelling. The main guarantees and proofs are for i.i.d. scalar satisfaction samples. I am not confident in how much of the theory survives once the i.i.d. scalar-sample setup is replaced by the perturbation pipeline. This isn't the same as human disagreement.

*Another weakness the paper has is that it does not consistently improve reward. I acknowledge that this is not the point of the paper, but it is worth noting that reward can stay flat or even get slightly worse. As Figure 3 shows, gains increase as disagreement does. This is fine and in some ways the point of the paper, but the use of this method may be limited to more selective domains.

*The final major weakness I saw is that some of the experimental and metric bookkeeping is harder to follow than it could be. The relationship between human disagreement, proxy disagreement, and the reported Risk / Tradeoff columns is not fully clear on first read. Algorithm 1 lists a an (LCB) variant but does not include a branch for it.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
My questions to the authors largely have to do with the weaknesses I listed, and I have context there for my questions.

1. Do you have any concrete for how realistic your setup is, relative to real human disagreement?
2. The primary situation where this method would outperform others is in disagreement-heavy situations. What is the tradeoff in low-disagreement situations? Is the method still useful there?
3. Can you elaborate on the LCB method mentioned?
reviews.final_justification: My original score was a weak accept, but I was more uncertain. The author's rebuttals were solid and addressed my points of clarification. While I am choosing not to increase the score, I am now more confident in this being the correct score as opposed to weak reject. My thoughts on each dimension are summarized in the original review.

reviews.summary:
This paper tackles the challenge of inference-time alignment for Large Language Models (LLMs) under systematic preference heterogeneity. Moving away from the standard practice of collapsing diverse human feedback into a single scalar reward, the authors elegantly reframe response selection as a risk-sensitive decision problem over satisfaction distributions.
To address this, the authors introduce DARC (Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding), a retraining-free reranking framework. DARC relies on multiple preference samples (or disagreement proxies) to estimate the satisfaction distribution for candidate responses, selecting outputs by maximizing a KL-robust entropic value. A practical strength of the method is its deployment-time risk controls, which explicitly regulate the trade-off between mean satisfaction and robustness via an entropic risk premium. This is complemented by an $\epsilon$-tie-breaking mechanism designed to favor less controversial candidates among near-optimal options.
The theoretical grounding is solid: the authors derive uniform lower confidence bounds for expected satisfaction, successfully connecting their pessimistic selection rules to Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) and providing a clear justification for the KL-DRO entropic objective. They further generalize DARC for multi-scorer settings using a soft worst-case operator. Empirically, both automated and multi-annotator human evaluations confirm that DARC effectively improves tail robustness and mitigates disagreement-related risks without sacrificing average quality, with the most pronounced gains observed on high-disagreement prompts.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

* **Practical Significance:** The paper targets a critical failure mode in standard RLHF pipelines—the brittleness of mean-reward reranking under diverse human preferences. Offering a retraining-free, drop-in decoding rule is highly appealing for practical deployment.
* **Solid Theoretical Grounding:** The connection drawn between the KL-robust entropic objective and pessimistic LCB/DRO frameworks is neat. While the individual components (risk-sensitive objectives, soft worst-case aggregation) are established, synthesizing them into an explicit, risk-budgeted decoding rule for alignment is a solid and original contribution.
* **Rigorous Empirical Setup:** The authors carefully control for generation confounds by using fixed candidate pools. Reporting both mean and tail-oriented metrics provides a comprehensive view of the method's effectiveness.
* **Clear Narrative:** The overall structure of the paper is logical and easy to follow, transitioning smoothly from problem formulation to theory, algorithms, and finally evaluation.

## Weaknesses
* **Hyperparameter Clutter:** The method introduces a heavy load of hyperparameters ($\beta$, $\tau$, $\epsilon$) and closely related variants (constrained vs. penalized, multi-scorer). The paper currently lacks a sharp, practical "when-to-use-which" guide, making the framework feel overly complex to tune for practitioners.
* **Presentation and Formatting.** While the overall narrative is clear, there is a noticeable error in the figure sequencing. Figure 3 is introduced and placed on page 7 , whereas Figure 2 appears and is referenced later on page 8. The authors should swap the numbering of these figures so they appear in sequential order as they are introduced in the text.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. **Memory overhead of perturbations:** Table 7 clearly demonstrates that the time latency overhead for generating perturbations is well under 3.2%. However, the paper does not address the potential VRAM bottleneck associated with decoding $N_{aug}$ sequences in parallel. Could you clarify the exact memory footprint required for these parallel rollouts, especially when scaling this approach to the 14B model evaluated in Appendix H.12? 

2. **Mitigating proxy False Positives:** Appendix H.11 provides an excellent and honest taxonomy of proxy mismatch cases. Given that False Positives are heavily driven by the reward model's sensitivity to superficial surface-form changes, are there straightforward heuristics or calibration steps that could be applied during the perturbation phase to filter out these formatting artifacts? 

3. **Hyperparameter transferability:** The ablation studies in Figure 2 effectively map out the performance impact of $\beta$, $\epsilon$, and $K$ on a fixed candidate pool. Have you tested how stable these optimal values are when transferring the method across fundamentally different domains (e.g., from open-ended conversational formats like MT-Bench to strictly objective coding or math benchmarks)?
reviews.final_justification:
I have considered both the paper and the authors’ rebuttal, and I find that my main concerns have been sufficiently addressed. I therefore raise my score to Weak Accept.

The rebuttal improved my assessment of the paper’s soundness. In particular, my concern about the memory overhead of perturbation-based decoding was addressed with concrete VRAM measurements, which clarified the practical cost of the method. The response on proxy false positives was also useful, as it provided both mitigation heuristics and additional empirical results, making this aspect of the method clearer.In terms of originality, I still find the paper to contain a meaningful idea: framing decoding-time alignment as risk-constrained decision making under heterogeneous preferences is conceptually interesting, and the connection to robust entropic decoding gives the method a more principled basis.For significance, the rebuttal increased my confidence that the method may generalize beyond the main benchmark setting. In particular, the added evidence on hyperparameter transferability across math and code tasks addressed an important concern about robustness across domains.The rebuttal also improved clarity. The planned revisions, especially a clearer explanation of when to use different DARC variants, should make the paper easier to follow.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the rigorous and insightful assessment, which helped significantly strengthen the paper’s empirical grounding.
## W1: Hyperparameter Organization & The "When-to-use-which" Guide
We agree the paper would benefit from a clearer, more comprehensive practitioner-facing recipe. To address this, we will add a dedicated **“Variant Selection Guide”** in the revision to clarify the mechanics and intended use cases of each formulation:
- **DARC-$\epsilon$ (default drop-in rule).** Our recommended general-purpose variant. Rather than imposing a hard penalty, it acts as a robust tie-breaker: it stays close to mean-based selection when disagreement is low, while falling back to stronger worst-case protection only when preference heterogeneity is substantial.
- **DARC-$\tau$ (strict risk-constrained formulation).** This variant is intended for settings where a hard risk budget is required (e.g., safe deployment or strict compliance constraints). It maximizes robust value under an explicit risk budget, which strengthens worst-case protection but can reduce average performance when the budget is tight.
- **Multi-scorer variants (scorer-shift protection).** Most appropriate when scorer heterogeneity or reward-model shift is itself the main concern, rather than disagreement induced by perturbations under a single proxy.

In practice, adopting DARC-$\epsilon$ is lightweight: a small perturbation budget ($N_{\text{aug}}=4$ to $8$) already captures most of the robustness gains without requiring extensive tuning. We will make these distinctions a focal point of the revised methodology section.
## W2:Presentation and Formatting
We thank the reviewer for catching this presentation issue. We will correct the figure numbering/order in the revision.
## Q1: Memory Overhead of Perturbations (VRAM)
We appreciate the reviewer highlighting that our initial submission focused primarily on latency. To fully address the concern, we therefore added Table R4 to report peak VRAM. The peak VRAM overhead is modest, increasing by only ~11% at $N_{\text{aug}}=8$ across model scales: **Llama-3.1-8B** ($16.2 \rightarrow 18.1$ GB) and **Qwen2.5-14B** ($27.5 \rightarrow 30.5$ GB). Even when pushed to $N_{\text{aug}}=16$, the memory footprints remain practical at 19.8 GB and 33.1 GB, respectively. Together with the low latency overhead reported in Table 7, this supports using a small augmentation budget (e.g., 4–8) as the default operating point.

### Table R4. VRAM Overhead vs. Augmentation Budget

| Model | Base Reranking Peak VRAM | DARC ($N_{\text{aug}}=4$) | DARC ($N_{\text{aug}}=8$) | DARC ($N_{\text{aug}}=16$) | $\Delta$ vs. Base ($N_{\text{aug}}=8$) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Llama-3.1-8B | 16.2 GB | 17.5 GB | 18.1 GB | 19.8 GB | +1.9 GB (11.7%) |
| Qwen2.5-14B | 27.5 GB | 29.2 GB | 30.5 GB | 33.1 GB | +3.0 GB (10.9%) |

## Q2: Mitigating Proxy False Positives
This is an important deployment concern, and the reviewer’s point is well taken. In practice, to reduce artifact-driven or RM-hack-induced proxy errors, we normalize markdown/bullet formatting, bound length changes, and discard rewrites that add only templated politeness/apology wrappers or near-duplicate surface edits. We now test this issue directly in Tables R1–R2 by comparing Style-only, Targeted-only, and Hybrid perturbation sets. These additional controls help reduce proxy false positives for artifact-driven responses. Under the targeted stress test, proxy–human alignment improves from $\rho = 0.4615$ with Style-only to $\rho = 0.5650$ with Hybrid, and downstream CVaR$_{10}$ improves from **6.87** to **7.35**. Our practical recommendation is therefore to introduce a small Hybrid set as an optional enhancement when stronger protection against spurious reward-side artifacts is desired.
## Q3: Hyperparameter Transferability to Math and Code
While Fig. 2 establishes hyperparameter stability within a fixed candidate pool, we agree that cross-domain transfer is also important. To address this directly, we added Table R5, which evaluates the paper-default DARC-$\epsilon$ recipe without retuning on one math and one code benchmark. On **MATH-500**, DARC-$\epsilon$ improves accuracy/EM ($56.4 \rightarrow 66.8$), achieving a favorable win/tie/loss record of 63/426/11. On **EvalPlus**, Pass@1 similarly improves ($71.3 \rightarrow 78.6$) with 14 wins, 148 ties, and only 2 losses. These results provide encouraging evidence of transfer without retuning in the current single-pool, same-K setup.
### Table R5. Default DARC Transfer to Math and Code

| Benchmark | Domain | Metric | Base (Best-of-K) | DARC-$\epsilon$ (paper defaults) | W / T / L |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| MATH-500 | Math | Accuracy / EM | 56.4 | 66.8 | 63 / 426 / 11 |
| EvalPlus | Code | Pass@1 | 71.3 | 78.6 | 14 / 148 / 2 |

We thank the reviewer again for these thoughtful comments. We will revise the paper accordingly to incorporate the above clarifications and presentation improvements.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thank you for the thoughtful review. We appreciate your focus on the paper’s scope.

## Response to W1 & Q1: Realism of the Proxy and the Theory/Practice Interface

The perturbation proxy is best viewed as a scalable approximation to human disagreement, anchored to real multi-annotator behavior (Zhang et al., 2024), rather than as an exact substitute for it.

- **Empirical realism relative to human disagreement:** Our proxy is not arbitrary. As shown in **Fig. 4**, it achieves significant correlation with actual human disagreement (Spearman $\rho=0.6509$; partial $\rho=0.4084$ controlling for length/reward) and reasonably identifies high-disagreement prompts (Precision/Recall@20% = 0.64, Jaccard@20% = 0.47). Furthermore, explicitly probing spurious features improves robustness against RM hacks (**Table R1**). On a stress-test set, a "Hybrid" proxy—perturbing both style and artifact cues—improves alignment with human disagreement ($\rho$: 0.46 $\rightarrow$ 0.56) and boosts tail robustness ($\text{CVaR}_{10}$: 5.83 Base $\rightarrow$ 6.87 Style $\rightarrow$ **7.35 Hybrid**).

- **Formal theorems vs. scalable proxy:** Our strict guarantees (e.g., Prop. 3.3) apply to the human-sample regime. As noted in **Appendix I**, the i.i.d. assumptions can be relaxed to weakly dependent sampling. When multi-rater data is unavailable, the perturbation proxy serves as a practical alternative, though we do **not** claim it literally inherits these theorems.

- **Robustness to proxy error:** What formally survives is bounded slack. As shown in **Appendix A.12**, if proxy estimates are close to empirical sample statistics, the pessimistic objective incurs a matching additive slack relative to the sample-based optimum, aligning with variance-regularized DRO (Namkoong & Duchi, 2019). We will elevate this discussion to define the proxy more clearly as an empirically validated approximation.

## Response to W2 & Q2: Tradeoffs in Low-Disagreement Situations

We agree DARC is designed for high-disagreement regimes; importantly, its conservatism does not broadly penalize quality when disagreement is low.

- **No broad degradation:** As further supported by **Table R3**, which buckets held-out human-score improvements by baseline human disagreement, the lowest-disagreement bucket (Q1) still has a slightly positive mean human-score delta (+0.125), with outcomes dominated by ties (11 W / 80 T / 9 L).

- **Selective utility:** As disagreement increases, the gains rise monotonically, reaching +1.037 in Q5. We therefore view DARC as staying close to mean-based selection when disagreement is low, while becoming increasingly useful as preference heterogeneity grows.

## Response to W3 & Q3: Metric Bookkeeping & LCB Elaboration

We clarify this point along two axes: metric bookkeeping and the role of LCB.

**Metric bookkeeping.** This point is best clarified by separating **selection-time signals** from **evaluation-time metrics**.

- **Selection-time signals.** In scalable settings, DARC uses **proxy disagreement** as the deployment-time signal for risk-aware selection; **human disagreement** is not assumed available at deployment.

- **Evaluation-time metrics.** The paper reports two complementary evaluations. In **automated/proxy evaluation** (Table 1), Reward/Risk/Tradeoff are proxy-side diagnostics on the proxy scale. In **human-loop evaluation** (Table 2 / Fig. 3), the main external validation comes from held-out human ratings and prompt-level CVaR, with **human disagreement** used to quantify inter-rater heterogeneity and stratify prompts by controversy level. Figure 4 connects these two layers by showing that proxy disagreement is positively associated with held-out human disagreement, which is why it is useful as a scalable screening signal.

We will revise the presentation to make these roles explicit and to rename the reported metrics more clearly, so that the relationship among human disagreement, proxy disagreement, Risk, and Tradeoff is unambiguous on first read.

**LCB and its connection to mean-dispersion.** LCB is a simplified second-moment form derived from the finite-sample analysis rather than the primary deployment rule. In the human-sample regime, its leading uncertainty term scales with $\hat{\sigma}(y)$, yielding a mean-minus-dispersion form with a coefficient $\lambda$ that scales as $O\left(\sqrt{\log(K/\delta)/n}\right)$. This is why the mean-dispersion heuristic is not ad hoc in our setting. We will update **Algorithm 1** to state this LCB form explicitly.

We thank the reviewer for these thoughtful comments, which help us sharpen both the scope and presentation of DARC. We will revise the paper accordingly to incorporate the above clarifications and presentation improvements.

### References

[1] Zhang et al. (2024), *Diverging Preferences: When do Annotators Disagree and do Models Know?*  
[2] Namkoong and Duchi (2019), *Variance-based Regularization with Convex Objectives*

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their careful reading of our manuscript and the highly constructive feedback.

**Clarifications and Presentation Improvements.** We fully agree that the boundaries between our theoretical framework and practical approximations could be stated more sharply. To address this, we will refine the discussion in the revision to explicitly clarify the following:

## Response to W1: The Theory/Proxy Interface

We appreciate the reviewer’s request for a sharper presentation of the theory/practice interface. In the revision, we will make the scope of each component more explicit. Our formal results characterize DARC in the i.i.d. human-sample setting, which provides the clean decision-theoretic regime underlying the LCB/KL-DRO connection. In deployment, when direct multi-rater samples are unavailable, we instantiate the same decision rule with a perturbation-based RM proxy as a scalable surrogate for disagreement. Appendix A.12 already shows that when the proxy uniformly tracks the corresponding empirical mean/risk statistics, the induced pessimistic objective differs from the sample-based optimum by only an additive slack, consistent with the variance-regularized DRO view of Namkoong & Duchi (2019). We will move this scope clarification into the main text and revise Sec. 4 to more clearly present the progression from formal sample-based analysis, to scalable proxy instantiation, to empirical validation in deployment.

## Response to W2: Interpretation of the Tradeoff Metric

We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Tradeoff is partly optimization-aligned, so we do not treat it as the primary standalone evidence for DARC’s effectiveness. Rather, our main conclusions rely on held-out human ratings and prompt-level CVaR, while Tradeoff is used as a supporting risk-adjusted diagnostic. We will revise the presentation accordingly by foregrounding the human/CVaR results before discussing Tradeoff, and by reframing Fig. 3 as a supporting analysis rather than the main evidence of effectiveness.


## Response to Q1: Performance in Low-Disagreement Regimes(Fig. 3 Q1 bucket)

The Q1 pattern in Fig. 3 merits clarification, since near-zero or slightly negative $\Delta$Tradeoff could raise the concern that conservatism may hurt quality when disagreement is low. This is a meaningful question, since disagreement in preference data is often substantive rather than mere annotation noise (Zhang et al., 2024). Concretely:

 - **The Q1 bucket does not appear to indicate broad human-quality degradation.** To examine this more directly, we added Table R3, which buckets held-out human-score improvements by baseline human disagreement. In the lowest-disagreement bucket (Q1), the mean human-score delta **remains slightly positive (+0.125)**, and the outcomes are **dominated by ties (11 / 80 / 9)**. As disagreement increases, the gains rise monotonically: +0.236, +0.451, +0.755, and +1.037 from Q2 to Q5. We therefore view the Q1 pattern as suggesting limited upside for additional risk control in low-disagreement prompts, rather than broad human-quality degradation. More broadly, we view this as a desirable property rather than a limitation: DARC is intended to provide **selective robustness** where disagreement is substantive, while remaining close to mean-based selection when disagreement is weak. In that sense, it should be understood not as an all-or-nothing replacement for standard reranking, but as a tunable inference-time control that becomes most useful precisely in the regimes where preference heterogeneity is consequential.

- **This interpretation is also consistent with the $\epsilon$-rule itself.** Let $y_\mu = \arg\max_y \mu(y)$ be the mean-based choice and $y_\epsilon$ the DARC-$\epsilon$ choice. Since DARC-$\epsilon$ first restricts to the near-optimal robust-value set $F_\epsilon = \{ y : V_\beta(y) \ge V_\beta^{\max} - \epsilon \}$, we have $V_\beta(y_\epsilon) \ge V_\beta(y_\mu) - \epsilon$. Using $\mu(y) = V_\beta(y) + RP_\beta(y)$, this gives $$\mu(y_\mu) - \mu(y_\epsilon) \le \epsilon + RP_\beta(y_\mu)$$ Thus, when the mean-best candidate already has a small risk premium—as expected in low-disagreement prompts—the DARC-$\epsilon$ choice remains close to mean-based selection.

We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments, which have collectively helped us clarify the low-disagreement regime and sharpen the presentation of DARC’s theoretical and empirical scope.

### Table R3. Bucketed human evaluation vs. Base by baseline human disagreement

| Bucket | $\Delta$Human Score (Eps - Base) $\uparrow$ | W / T / L |
|---|---:|---:|
| Q1 | 0.125 | 11 / 80 / 9 |
| Q2 | 0.236 | 17 / 71 / 12 |
| Q3 | 0.451 | 34 / 55 / 11 |
| Q4 | 0.755 | 42 / 50 / 8 |
| Q5 | 1.037 | 51 / 45 / 4 |

rebuttals.rebuttal:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the meticulous and constructive assessment. We agree that a purely style-preserving proxy can miss artifact-driven high-RM responses when the rewarded surface-form cue is preserved across rewrites (e.g., verbosity or sycophantic phrasing). 
## Choice for "Style-Preserving" Perturbations
We initially used style-preserving rewrites because they provide a conservative first approximation to the signal we want the proxy to capture: scorer instability under near-equivalent responses. By minimally perturbing semantics, they reduce the risk of conflating disagreement with genuine content drift, answer-quality changes, or task-level ambiguity introduced by the rewrite itself. In that sense, style-preserving perturbations were intended as a conservative and interpretable baseline proxy.

##  Mitigating RM Hack: New Targeted & Hybrid Perturbation Strategies 
To address this concern directly, we added two new proxy variants under the same total augmentation budget:

- **Targeted-only.** Explicitly probes known RM hacks by normalizing length, formatting, and sycophantic/apologetic phrasing.
- **Hybrid.** Combines style-preserving and targeted rewrites.

We then evaluate them in two complementary experiments:

- **Experiment 1 (proxy-level).** We compare Style-only, Targeted-only, and Hybrid by their alignment with human disagreement, reported both overall and on a fixed stress-test slice where style-preserving perturbations are most likely to under-detect verbosity, sycophancy, or formatting artifacts. This stress-test slice is a fixed artifact-focused subset distinct from the paper’s top-20% human-disagreement slice.
- **Experiment 2 (end-to-end).** We plug the same three proxies into DARC-\(\epsilon\) using the same fixed candidate pools and held-out evaluation protocol as in the main paper, and compare downstream robustness both overall and on the same stress-test slice.

Tables R1–R2 show two takeaways. 
- **First, targeted/Hybrid perturbations reduce under-detection of artifact-driven disagreement, improving proxy–human alignment and downstream robustness on the stress test.** 
- **Second, the two perturbation families are complementary: style-preserving rewrites capture instability under near-equivalent responses, while targeted rewrites expose instability tied to surface-form artifacts.**

### Table R1. Proxy–Human Alignment under Different Perturbations

| Proxy variant | Overall $\rho(\text{human}, \text{proxy}) \uparrow$ | Overall partial-$\rho \uparrow$ | Overall Jaccard@20 $\uparrow$ | Stress-test $\rho \uparrow$ | Stress-test Jaccard@20 $\uparrow$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Style-only | 0.6509 | 0.4084 | 0.47 | 0.4615 | 0.34 |
| Targeted-only | 0.6120 | 0.3751 | 0.44 | 0.5417 | 0.42 |
| Hybrid (4+4) | 0.6725 | 0.4210 | 0.49 | 0.5650 | 0.46 |

### Table R2. Downstream Robustness under Different Perturbations

| Method | Overall Mean $\uparrow$ | Overall Risk $\downarrow$ | Overall Tradeoff $\uparrow$ | Overall CVaR10 $\uparrow$ | Stress-test Tradeoff $\uparrow$ | Stress-test CVaR10 $\uparrow$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Base (Best-of-K) | 7.56 | 0.67 | 6.22 | 6.73 | 5.35 | 5.83 |
| DARC-$\epsilon$ + Style-only | 8.08 | 0.55 | 6.98 | 7.62 | 6.36 | 6.87 |
| DARC-$\epsilon$ + Targeted | 7.84 | 0.53 | 6.78 | 7.45 | 6.75 | 7.20 |
| DARC-$\epsilon$ + Hybrid | 7.96 | 0.51 | 6.94 | 7.71 | 6.82 | 7.35 |

Concretely, table R1 shows progressively better alignment with human disagreement on the stress test from Style-only to Targeted to Hybrid, measured by both $\rho$ ($0.4615 \rightarrow 0.5417 \rightarrow 0.5650$) and Jaccard@20 ($0.34 \rightarrow 0.42 \rightarrow 0.46$). This interpretation is consistent with prior evidence that preference models can over-rely on features such as length, structure, and sycophancy, and that targeted debiasing can mitigate these effects (Bharadwaj et al., 2025).

The same pattern appears end-to-end in Table R2. When plugging these proxies back into DARC-$\epsilon$ using the same fixed candidate pools and held-out evaluation protocol, stress-test CVaR$_{10}$ improves progressively across the method sequence (Base $\rightarrow$ Style-only $\rightarrow$ Targeted $\rightarrow$ Hybrid: $5.83 \rightarrow 6.87 \rightarrow 7.20 \rightarrow 7.35$). Overall CVaR remains strong, with Hybrid achieving the best overall value ($6.73 \rightarrow 7.62 \rightarrow 7.45 \rightarrow 7.71$).

As Tables R1–R2 demonstrate, DARC is robust across proxy choices and naturally accommodates tailored perturbations. We will revise the paper to present the Hybrid proxy as an optional enhancement when stronger robustness against surface-form artifacts is desired.

We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion, which led us to add targeted ablations and sharpen the practical scope of the paper.



### References

[1] Bharadwaj et al. (2025), *Flattery, Fluff, and Fog: Diagnosing and Mitigating Idiosyncratic Biases in Preference Models*

our_title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

match.matched_title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

submission.title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences
submission.abstract: Common deep learning approaches for antibody engineering focus on modeling the marginal distribution of sequences. By treating sequences as independent samples, however, these methods overlook affinity maturation as a rich and largely untapped source of information about the evolutionary process by which antibodies explore the underlying fitness landscape. In contrast, classical phylogenetic models explicitly represent evolutionary dynamics but lack the expressivity to capture complex epistatic interactions. We bridge this gap with **CoSiNE**, a continuous-time Markov chain  parameterized by a deep neural network. Mathematically, we prove that CoSiNE provides a first-order approximation to the intractable sequential point mutation process, capturing epistatic effects with an error bound that is quadratic in branch length. Empirically, CoSiNE outperforms state-of-the-art language models in zero-shot variant effect prediction by explicitly disentangling selection from context-dependent somatic hypermutation. Finally, we introduce *Guided Gillespie*, a classifier-guided sampling scheme that steers CoSiNE at inference time, enabling efficient optimization of antibody binding affinity toward specific antigens.
submission.tldr: We combine protein evolution models with protein language models to simulate and steer antibody affinity maturation
submission.lay_summary: When your immune system fights an infection, antibodies inside your body undergo a rapid evolution called affinity maturation: they mutate repeatedly, and the variants that bind the invader best are selected for further refinement. Understanding this process could help us design better therapeutic antibodies, but capturing it has been difficult. Modern AI methods treat antibody sequences as independent snapshots and ignore the evolutionary process that produced them. Classical evolutionary models do represent this process, but assume that each position in the protein mutates independently of every other position. This misses the reality that amino acids in an antibody work together to recognize their target. We developed CoSiNE, a method that uses a neural network to predict how an antibody is likely to evolve next, while accounting for interactions between positions. We prove mathematically that this approximation is accurate, and we provide a sampling procedure that steers the model toward antibodies that bind specific targets such as viruses. CoSiNE achieves state-of-the-art performance at predicting which antibody mutations improve function, providing a new tool for antibody design grounded in the biology of how antibodies actually evolve.

reviews.summary: This paper introduces COSINE, a framework that reconciles deep learning expressivity with classical phylogenetic dynamics by parameterizing a continuous-time Markov chain with a neural backbone to model antibody affinity maturation. By predicting site-specific rate matrices conditioned on the full sequence, the model captures complex epistatic interactions that independent-site models miss. The authors provide a solid theoretical grounding by proving COSINE is a first-order approximation of sequential point mutation processes with a quadratic error bound relative to branch length. For functional design, the study introduces Guided Gillespie sampling accelerated by Taylor-approximated guidance (TAG), achieving up to a 928x speedup over exact methods without sacrificing performance. Empirically, COSINE delivers state-of-the-art zero-shot variant effect prediction by disentangling selection from mutational bias and successfully optimizes antibody binding while maintaining structural plausibility and humanness.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The paper is technically sound, providing rigorous proofs and solid results against strong baselines. The presentation is clear, effectively bridging the gap between evolutionary biology and deep learning. Its primary significance lies in the massive speedup offered by the guidance approach, making it highly practical for real-world lab applications. The originality is reflected in the creative use of neural rate matrices to capture complex site dependencies within a global context.

Weaknesses

The method’s soundness is limited by an approximation error that naturally increases over longer evolutionary distances. In terms of significance, the current framework cannot handle insertions or deletions, restricting it to fixed-length sequences. Additionally, the reliance on predominantly single-chain training data may hinder the model's ability to fully capture paired-chain interactions.

reviews.summary: This paper presents COSINE, a neural continuous-time Markov chain for modeling antibody sequence evolution during affinity maturation. The method combines the temporal structure of phylogenetic substitution models with neural, context-dependent rate parameterization, and derives a first-order approximation to sequential point-mutation dynamics. The model is trained by likelihood maximization on clonal-tree transitions and extended with classifier-guided Gillespie sampling for inference-time steering. Empirically, the paper reports improved zero-shot antibody variant-effect prediction and promising in silico affinity-optimization results.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The CTMC formulation is well motivated, and the first-order approximation gives the method a clear technical foundation.
2. The VEP evaluation is reasonable, with useful supporting analyses on estimation error, runtime, and branch-length effects in the appendix.
3. Modeling evolutionary transitions rather than only sequence marginals is a meaningful and original contribution for antibody modeling.

Weaknesses:
1. The empirical evidence is still narrow, centered on a small number of antibody DMS datasets.
2. Key choices such as branch-length calibration, score construction, and the compute-quality trade-off of Guided Gillespie are not fully clarified in the main text.
3. The optimization results are entirely oracle-guided and in silico, so broader design claims should be stated more cautiously.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How sensitive are the VEP results to branch-length calibration, both globally and per assay? Stable gains under reasonable alternatives would increase confidence in robustness.
2. Can the authors report per-assay results or paired tests against the strongest baselines, rather than only aggregate correlations? This would show whether the gains are consistent or dataset-specific.
3. How much of the gain comes from context-dependent epistasis modeling, versus evolutionary supervision or model capacity more broadly? Clearer attribution would strengthen the central claim.
4. For Guided Gillespie, are compute budgets and oracle-access patterns matched to the optimization baselines? A tightly controlled comparison is needed to assess this contribution.
reviews.limitations:
1. The empirical evidence is limited to antibody substitution settings.
2. Some conclusions depend on branch-length calibration choices.
3. The optimization results are shown only in oracle-guided in silico settings, so claims about practical design utility should be scoped accordingly.

reviews.summary: CoSiNE is a conditionally site-independent neural CTMC model for antibody affinity maturation. The idea is to predict site-specific rate matrices conditioned on the full parent sequence, giving you a factorized transition model that is tractable but still captures context dependence and epistasis through the neural parameterization. The paper shows a first-order approximation linking this to sequential single-point mutation processes, proposes Gillespie sampling to better respect single-mutation dynamics, and adds a guided Gillespie scheme for target-conditioned optimization. Experiments cover clonal-tree transition modeling, zero-shot variant effect prediction, and in silico guided antibody optimization.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. The problem formulation is well-grounded. Current antibody language models treat observed sequences as i.i.d., but affinity maturation is a lineage-structured evolutionary process. Pointing out this mismatch and building a model around it is one of the paper's clearest contributions.
2. The modeling idea — site-wise matrix exponentials with context-conditioned rate matrices (Eq. 2) — is a nice bridge between phylogenetics and deep sequence models. It keeps likelihood computation tractable while relaxing classical site-independence through whole-sequence conditioning.
3. The first-order approximation result is useful: if single-step rates match the sequential point mutation generator, transition probability error is quadratic in branch length. This gives a principled justification for why the approximation should hold on the short branches typical of affinity maturation.
4. Gillespie sampling is a natural fit here and the paper backs it up empirically. Both synthetic experiments and real-antibody proxy analyses show it outperforms naive factorized sampling from matrix exponentiation.
5. VEP results are strong. On FLAb2-derived DMS assays, CoSiNE is competitive or best across nearly all datasets, and the SHM-corrected selection score adds measurable value over raw transition likelihood.

Weaknesses

1. The theory assumes learned rates match true instantaneous rates, but training on the approximate factorized likelihood doesn't guarantee this. The authors acknowledge that long branches introduce bias from marginalizing out intermediates, and their proposed SNR-weighting doesn't help on real data. So the theoretical guarantees apply to an idealized setting, not the model actually used in experiments.
2. VEP results are encouraging but narrow. The benchmark covers only a few DMS assays, some quite small. Not enough to conclusively establish broad superiority.
3. Guided optimization uses weak external oracles and is evaluated purely in silico. The paper notes that stronger guidance can exceed known biological binders, likely from oracle exploitation. This is better read as proof-of-concept than a validated design pipeline.
4. Evidence for paired heavy/light conditioning is mixed. Table S2 shows single-chain conditioning outperforms paired on four of seven datasets. The margins are small, but this complicates the claimed importance of cross-chain context.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How sensitive are the VEP results to the chosen fixed branch length $t=0.2$ for all assays?
2. Can the authors provide a more direct evaluation of whether learned rates approximate instantaneous rates, beyond synthetic codon experiments?
3. How much of the performance gain comes from the pretrained ESM2 backbone versus the CoSiNE transition parameterization itself?
4. Why does paired conditioning underperform single-chain conditioning on more than half of the Table S2 datasets?
5. Do the authors intend CoSiNE mainly as a model of affinity maturation, or as a general model of protein evolution? The current framing mixes both.
reviews.final_justification:
I thank the authors for the constructive rebuttal. The additional analyses were helpful: the new VEP results, the ESM2 ablation, the clarification of paired vs. single-chain conditioning, and the sharper framing of the optimization setting all strengthen the paper and make its scope clearer.

My main reservation remains the same as in the original review: the theoretical justification relies on learned rates approximating true instantaneous rates, but the current training procedure does not directly establish that. I therefore still view the theoretical connection as a useful motivation rather than a full guarantee for the learned model. I also continue to see the optimization results as proof-of-concept and the empirical validation as somewhat limited in breadth.

Overall, the rebuttal partially addressed my concerns and reinforced my view that this is a worthwhile paper with clear limitations. My final recommendation therefore remains weak accept.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes COSiNE, a neural CTMC model for antibody affinity maturation. The model predicts site-specific rate matrices conditioned on the ful sequence and uses their matrix exponentials to define a factorized transition probability over evolved sequences. This construction is proved to give a first-order approximation to the sequential point-mutation process. COSiNE shows strong results on zero-shot variant effect prediction and guided antibody optimization via Guided Gillespie sampling.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
1. The paper tackles an important and well-motivated problem and reports promising empirical results
2. The paper does not merely present COSiNE as a purely heuristic neural model, but provide a first-order approximation proof with bounded error.

# Weakness
1. The approximation error is $O(t^2)$ in branch length so the theoretical guarantee is only compelling in sufficiently short-branch regimes and leaves a substantial gap between theory and realistic practice.
2. The method’s novelty appears somewhat limited, as the main design choice is to use a neural network to parameterize a context-dependent rate matrix. The paper does not sufficiently justify this design choice relative to a discrete flow matching (DFM) framework, which already provides an elegant way to model time-aware single-mutation dynamics, and no direct benchmark against DFM is provided.
3. The antibody optimization results are evaluated primarily through the model’s guided predictor and auxiliary plausibility measures such as humanness and pLDDT, but the paper does not validate improved affinity using stronger external biophysical evidence such as docking or energy-based metrics. This raises the concern that the method may be optimizing predictor score rather than true binding affinity.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Guided Gillespie sampling may be computationally expensive. Could the authors provide a computational cost analysis, such as how does the runtime scale with sequence length or sampling steps?
2. How sensitive are the zero-shot VEP results to the fixed choice of $t=0.2$? How robust is the performance under other branch-length settings?
3. Could the authors provide analysis on how does COSiNE perform when applied to longer branches or noisier clonal tree reconstructions?
reviews.final_justification: The authors did a good work in the rebuttal and the paper has its value. I'm raising my score.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and for providing valuable feedback. We appreciate your questions and have provided detailed answers below.

> Guided antibody optimization results are not validated using stronger external biophysical evidence like energy-based metrics.

We directly address this concern in our response to Reviewer `2JJG`. In brief, we validate CoSiNE-optimized variants using DiffAffinity, a structure-based $\Delta\Delta G$ predictor trained on SKEMPI2 that outperforms established energy-based methods like FoldX and Rosetta — and is fully orthogonal to our sequence-based guidance predictor. We found that CoSiNE with guidance ($\gamma=1$) achieves the best binding affinity (lowest $\Delta\Delta G$) across all methods, while unguided CoSiNE is also competitive, suggesting our learned substitution rates capture meaningful binding constraints independently of the predictor.

> How does the computational cost of *Guided Gillespie* scale by sequence length $L$ and by number of sampling steps $N$?

As a brief reminder, *Guided Gillespie* utilizes our approximate TAG guidance (Equation 9), which leverages a Taylor-Series expansion to require only a single predictor call per sampling step regardless of sequence length. Empirically, it scales linearly in sequence length (due to the predictor forward pass) and linearly with the number of sampling steps. 

Below we fix the number of sampling steps at 50, noting that the guided runtime increases linearly with $L$ while unguided sampling remains constant because there are no calls to the predictor.

| Sequence Length  | Guided Runtime (seconds) | Unguided Runtime (seconds) |
| - | - | - |
| $50$  | $5.16$ | $3.54$ |
| $100$ | $5.94$ | $3.51$ |
| $250$ | $8.53$ | $3.51$ |
| $500$ | $12.2$ | $3.65$ |

Below we fix the sequence length at 100, noting that both runtimes scale linearly with sampling steps.

| Sampling Steps | Guided Runtime (seconds) | Unguided Runtime (seconds) |
| - | - | - |
| $5$   | $0.612$ | $0.356$ |
| $10$  | $1.22$  | $0.734$ |
| $25$  | $3.07$  | $1.76$  |
| $50$  | $6.14$  | $3.50$  |
| $100$ | $12.2$  | $6.96$  |


> Sensitivity of VEP to the choice of branch length

We show that CoSiNE's zero-shot VEP performance is robust to a range of $t$ values, and we've updated the manuscript to discuss this. Please see our response to `2JJG` for details.

> The approximation error is in branch length so the theoretical guarantee is only compelling in sufficiently short-branch regimes and leaves a substantial gap between theory and realistic practice.

We agree that our theoretical guarantees apply primarily to the short-branch regime, but this aligns with our focus on affinity maturation, which is a rapid process yielding short branches. While approximation errors exist over longer branches, our strong performance in zero-shot VEP and guided optimization demonstrate practical utility. Moreover, we note that classical models like WAG and LG remain widely successful in phylogenetic inference despite making stronger approximations (e.g. complete site independence).

> Comparison of CoSiNE to discrete flow matching (DFM).

While both CoSiNE and DFM use continuous-time Markov chains, they solve fundamentally different problems. DFM is a generative model mapping noise to an i.i.d. data distribution over an artificial algorithmic time ($\tau\in[0,1]$). Conversely, CoSiNE models actual phylogenetic evolution, learning a transition kernel between protein sequences over real biological time ($t>0$). Because DFM is not designed to model realistic state-to-state transitions over arbitrary time intervals, evaluating DFM on evolutionary tasks like affinity maturation would require substantial adaptation, which we consider beyond the scope of this paper but plan to discuss in the revised manuscript.

> How does COSiNE perform on longer branches or noisier clonal tree reconstructions?

To evaluate robustness to both longer branches and noisier tree reconstructions, we trained CoSiNE on the TrRosetta [1] dataset (~15k general protein families). These families span far greater evolutionary distances than antibody clonal trees, and their phylogenies are reconstructed from sequence homology rather than direct lineage tracing, making them inherently noisier. We compare against two classical substitution models, using the WAG and LG likelihood forms to fit new exchangeability matrices from scratch on the same TrRosetta training data. CoSiNE achieves lower test NLL than both baselines across all splits, indicating that context-dependent rate modeling reduces misspecification even under these more challenging conditions.

| Model | Val NLL | Test NLL |
|---|---|---|
| WAG | 1.1702 | 1.2004 |
| LG (4 rate categories) | 1.1390 | 1.1682 |
| CoSiNE | **1.0051** | **1.0274** |

[1] Improved protein structure prediction using predicted interresidue orientations. Yang, J. et al. PNAS 2020

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thank you for your detailed review of our paper. We appreciate your thoughtful questions and have addressed them thoroughly below. We hope this response clarifies our approach and that the reviewer might consider further strengthening their support for our work.

> Sensitivity of VEP to the choice of branch length

We show that CoSiNE's VEP performance is robust to a range of $t$ values, and we've updated the manuscript to discuss this. Please see our response to `2JJG` for details.

> Additional VEP results

We have evaluated CoSiNE on 2 new assays, where CoSiNE outperforms all other methods. Please see our response to `8UQx` for details.

> Validation of guided antibody optimization with external oracle.

To address the concern about weak oracles, we validate our optimized variants using DiffAffinity, a structure-based $\Delta\Delta G$ predictor trained on general PDB complexes (details in our response to Reviewer `2JJG`). In brief, CoSiNE ($\gamma=1$) achieves the best binding affinity (lowest $\Delta\Delta G$) across all methods, while methods that overly exploit the guidance predictor do poorly. All in all, we agree that wet-lab validation remains the gold standard and have modified our claims accordingly.

> Source of CoSiNE Performance Gain

To address this question, we ablated the ESM2 backbone by training a version of CoSiNE from scratch (8 million parameters, random weight initialization) using the same training dataset to understand how important the pretrained ESM2-150 component is for VEP.

#### Expression Datasets

| Model | Koenig (H) | Koenig (L) | Adams |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DASM** | *0.596* | 0.474 | 0.270 |
| **ESM2-650M** | 0.326 | 0.429 | 0.124 |
| **ProGen2-Small** | 0.407 | **0.513** | -0.024 |
| **CoSiNE-ESM2** | **0.613** | *0.508* | **0.464** |
| **CoSiNE-8M** | 0.503 | 0.474 | *0.447* |

#### Binding Datasets

| Model | Koenig (H) | Koenig (L) | Shaneh. (119) | Shaneh. (120) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DASM** | *0.415* | 0.327 | 0.450 | **0.536** |
| **ESM2-650M** | 0.063 | 0.265 | 0.227 | 0.360 |
| **ProGen2-Small** | 0.098 | *0.332* | 0.119 | 0.070 |
| **CoSiNE-ESM2** | **0.456** | **0.371** | *0.498* | **0.536** |
| **CoSiNE-8M** | 0.363 | 0.330 | **0.508** | *0.531* |

**Bold** for best, *Italics* for second best

The ESM2 backbone improves the CoSiNE selection score's correlation with fitness on all but 1 dataset. But, the 8M version still performs exceptionally well — the average $\Delta\rho$ between the ESM2 version and 8M version is only 0.041. Therefore, the ablation suggests that the pretrained ESM2 backbone provides a useful initialization, but is not the primary source of predictive power.

Together with the WAG comparison (response to 8UQx), which shows context-dependent rate estimation matters, and the ESM2-150M baseline in Table 1, which shares CoSiNE's architecture but was trained as a standard language model, these results suggest that the context-aware evolutionary training objective is the primary driver of CoSiNE's VEP performance.

> Paired vs Single Chain Conditioning

We agree that the paired versus single conditioning results are mixed on a per-dataset basis. However, as shown in Table S2, the gains from paired conditioning when it helps are substantial (average +0.121 in Spearman correlation), while the losses when single conditioning is better are negligible (average +0.006). This asymmetry suggests that inter-chain interactions are genuinely informative for some fitness landscapes but not others, rather than paired conditioning being uniformly helpful or harmful.

We note that the majority of our training data consists of unpaired single-chain sequences, which likely limits the model's ability to fully leverage paired context. We expect that as more paired heavy-light sequencing data becomes available, the benefits of cross-chain conditioning will become more consistent. We have updated the manuscript to discuss this nuance more carefully.

> Approximation of Instantaneous Rates and Framing of Contribution

Regarding the evaluation of learned rates: directly validating instantaneous rates requires ground-truth knowledge of the generative process, which is only available in simulation — hence our synthetic codon experiment. We refer the reviewer to Appendix C.3, which analyzes test-set sampling error in the real antibody setting, providing additional evidence that our learned rates are well-calibrated. Regarding scope: CoSiNE is intended primarily as a model of antibody affinity maturation; extending to indels could yield a general protein evolution simulator, but this is left as future work. We agree the current framing conflates these goals and have clarified this in the revised manuscript.

Thank you for your feedback. We appreciate the time and effort that you put into reviewing our work. Below, we address your questions and comments in detail.

> Clarification of VEP correlation calculation

Regarding the question on providing per-assay results rather than aggregate correlations, our current VEP results (Table 1) already show per-assay results, making CoSiNE directly comparable to the existing baselines. We also provide a paired evaluation for modeling held-out clonal trees against the most directly comparable baseline (DASM) in Figure 2. Please feel free to clarify if we are misinterpreting your question.

> Additional VEP results

The table shows Spearman correlations for **2 new VEP benchmarks** measuring binding affinity ([1]). We chose these assays because they use distinct antibodies, antigens, and experimental technologies (MAGMA-seq) from those in Table 1.

CoSiNE outperforms all baselines, consistent with previous results. 

[1] Petersen et al. (2024) An integrated technology for quantitative wide mutational scanning of human antibody fab libraries Nat. Commun 15:3974


> Sensitivity of VEP to the choice of branch length

Please see our response to reviewer `2JJG`, where we find that CoSiNE indeed makes stable gains over baseline methods for a wide range of reasonable $t$ values.

> Validation of guided antibody optimization with external oracle.

We have addressed this concern in our response to Reviewer `2JJG`, where we validate CoSiNE-optimized variants using DiffAffinity, a structure-based $\Delta\Delta G$ predictor trained on PPI complexes in SKEMPI2. We found that CoSiNE with guidance ($\gamma=1$) achieves the best binding affinity (lowest $\Delta\Delta G$) across all methods, while unguided CoSiNE is also competitive, suggesting our learned substitution rates capture meaningful selection constraints independently of the predictor. We agree that wet-lab validation remains the gold standard and have moderated our claims accordingly.

> How much of the gain comes from context-dependent epistasis modeling, versus evolutionary supervision or model capacity more broadly?

We investigate the importance of context-dependence by comparing CoSiNE against a classical context-independent substitution model: a single 20×20 exchangeability matrix fit using the WAG likelihood form. We estimate these parameters via MLE on the same training transitions used for CoSiNE, ensuring a fair comparison. We omit further implementation details for brevity, but are happy to elaborate upon request.

On our test set, CoSiNE achieves significantly lower NLL per token than WAG across all branch lengths, with the gap widening for longer branches. This suggests that sequence-context conditioning allows CoSiNE to capture epistatic interactions that accrue over long evolutionary distances.

| Branch Length    | Num. Mutations | WAG NLL | CoSiNE NLL |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| $[0, 0.01)$      | $1.10\pm0.307$ | $0.0717$ | $0.0663$ |
| $[0.01, 0.05)$   | $3.20\pm1.81$ | $0.171$   | $0.147$  |
| $[0.05, 0.15)$   | $10.1\pm4.22$ | $0.454$   | $0.378$  |
| $[0.15, \infty)$ | $20.6\pm5.45$ | $0.836$   | $0.676$  |

Please also refer to our response to reviewer `EU4y` where we ablate the ESM2 backbone by training a smaller CoSiNE model from scratch. We will provide a discussion of all these experiments in the main text.

> Clarification of key choices in the main text (branch length calibration, score construction, compute-quality tradeoff of Guided Gillespie)

We already discuss selection score construction in Section 4.1, but will discuss VEP branch length calibration (see response to `2JJG`) and compute-quality tradeoff (see Appendix C.7) in the main text. 

> Clarification of controlled oracle budget in CDR optimization experiment

In the local CDR optimization experiment (Section 5.5), we restricted all methods to a maximum of 5 oracle calls per optimized sequence and report this metric in the $N_{\text{oracle}}$ column of Table S4. We will state this explicitly in the main text.

Thank you for your encouraging comments about our work. We are pleased that the reviewer recognizes the practical significance of our guided sampling approach and the originality of our neural CTMC parameterization. To strengthen our contribution, we provide some additional results of interest.

> Validation of guided antibody optimization with external oracle.

To address concerns about external validation, we evaluate CoSiNE-optimized antibody variants using DiffAffinity [1], a structure-based $\Delta\Delta G$ predictor. We follow a slightly modified protocol from Section 5.5: we allow up to 3 mutations in the heavy chain variable region and sample 100 variants per method.

**Why DiffAffinity is an appropriate oracle:** DiffAffinity is trained on SKEMPI2 binding affinity data using structural side-chain representations, making it fully orthogonal to our sequence-based guidance predictor trained on neutralizing antibodies in CoVAbDab. The authors validated DiffAffinity specifically on the same SARS-CoV-2 complex (PDB: 7FAE) used in this experiment, where it outperforms FoldX and Rosetta.

**Results:** CoSiNE with guidance ($\gamma=1$) achieves the lowest $\Delta\Delta G$ (strongest improvement in binding affinity) and the most variants with $\Delta\Delta G<0$ (i.e. binding more tightly than wild-type) across all methods. Methods that over-optimize the neutralization predictor (genetic algorithm, stronger guidance) score poorly due to epistemic uncertainty in the guidance model. Notably, unguided CoSiNE is also competitive (34 variants with $\Delta\Delta G<0$, second highest), suggesting that our learned substitution rates capture meaningful selection constraints independently of the predictor.

| -- | -- | -- | -- |

| CoSiNE (unguided)     | $0.0185$  | $-1.53$  | $34$ |

The CoSiNE selection score is most reliable in a relatively large range from $t=0.1$ to $t=0.4$, where the maximum $\Delta\rho$ across settings is only $0.045$.
