We would like to thank you for your constructive insights and detailed suggestions throughout this review process. We sincerely appreciate your support and the increase in our rating. We will incorporate all your suggestions and the additional discussion into the final version of our paper. Should you have any further questions or suggestions, we are more than happy to engage in discussions and make any necessary improvements. :)

rebuttal_acks.reasons:
I thank the authors for their thorough response. I appreciate the additional details regarding computational cost and the performance with respect to wall clock time. I believe adding them to the paper will strengthen the contribution. The additional explanation of W3 as enabling time-injective reward assignment is helpful.

A couple of points:
- It would be beneficial to test in harder tasks if some of the benchmarks being used are essentially saturated.
- I generally buy the notion of turning points as a crude mechanism for more general credit assignment though it feels like this could be tested more thoroughly and alternative designs could be considered. 

I have raised my score accordingly.

1. The paper may require substantial modification. First, the current title and abstract position step-wise rewards as a primary novelty, which are similar to current works. Second, the paper lacks a sufficiently comprehensive discussion of related methods.

2. I fully understand that the authors have limited computational resources and rebuttal time. Therefore, I will further refer to other reviewers’ comments on the overall completeness and novelty of the work before making my final judgment.

Thank you for the authors’ clarification. The concerns regarding Questions 1–3 have been resolved.

Regarding Question 4, I still have some remaining issues. In particular, the way intermediate states are obtained in this work needs a clearer formalization, as the description in Section 4.2 is insufficient. I would like to know how the SDE and ODE sampling trajectories are obtained in this work. For $x_T$, the entire trajectory of $v_t$ ($t=0,\dots,T$) is predicted and stored to obtain the SDE trajectory. 

1. Then, the stored $v_t$ is reused to obtain the ODE trajectory;  
2. Or, for each intermediate state, $v_t$ is re-predicted to obtain the ODE trajectory.  

If it is case 1, then for the last $t'$ steps of the ODE trajectory, $v_t'=Model(x^{\text{SDE}}_{t'+1})$ rather than $v_t' = Model(x^{ODE}_{t'+1})$. How is the accuracy of the ODE trajectory guaranteed in this case? If it is case 2, is the large amount of computation necessary?  

Moreover, considering that the authors are currently unable to share qualitative results regarding the turning point, I suggest that the authors provide some brief quantitative results, e.g., how the reward scores change at the turning point, statistically.

Will the authors release the code?

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
This paper introduces TurningPoint GRPO (TP GRPO) to address reward sparsity and trajectory dependencies in Flow Matching alignment. The core contributions are a subtraction based stepwise reward and a novel turning point mechanism that captures long term credit assignment by identifying pivotal denoising steps.
While reviewers initially questioned the computational overhead and novelty relative to contemporaneous work, the rebuttal successfully demonstrated that TP GRPO achieves superior performance under equal wall clock time. Technical concerns regarding noise level bias were resolved by clarifying the ODE SDE branching strategy. Strong empirical gains on complex human preference tasks confirm the effectiveness of the method. The paper is technically sound and provides a distinct contribution to trajectory level modeling in diffusion based RL.
The paper received final review scores of 5, 4, and 5. The AC agrees with the consensus regarding the technical merit and empirical strength of the work and recommends acceptance.

submission.title: TIC-VLA: A Think-in-Control Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation in Dynamic Environments
submission.abstract: Robots in dynamic, human-centric environments must follow language instructions while maintaining real-time reactive control. Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising framework, but they assume temporally aligned reasoning and control, despite semantic inference being inherently delayed relative to real-time action. We introduce Think-in-Control (TIC)-VLA, a latency-aware framework that explicitly models delayed semantic reasoning during action generation. TIC-VLA defines a delayed semantic-control interface that conditions action generation on delayed vision-language semantic states and explicit latency metadata, in addition to current observations. We further propose a latency-consistent training pipeline that injects reasoning inference delays during imitation learning and online reinforcement learning, aligning training with asynchronous deployment. To support realistic evaluation, we present DynaNav, a physics-accurate, photo-realistic simulation suite for language-guided navigation in dynamic environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real robot show that TIC-VLA consistently outperforms prior VLA models while maintaining robust real-time control under multi-second reasoning latency. Project website: https://ucla-mobility.github.io/TIC-VLA/
submission.lay_summary: Robots that move through busy places, such as hallways, sidewalks, warehouses, and offices, must understand human instructions while reacting immediately to people and obstacles. A major problem is that the "thinking" part of today’s robot AI can take seconds, but the robot must keep moving safely many times per second, so its understanding may already be out of date. TIC-VLA solves this by separating slow vision-language reasoning from fast motion control, while telling the controller exactly how old the reasoning is and how the robot has moved since then. The controller then uses the current camera view, the robot’s state, and this delayed guidance to choose safe short-term movements without stopping to wait for the reasoning model. The system is trained with artificial and realistic reasoning delays, first by learning from demonstrations and then by practicing in simulation. The paper also introduces DynaNav, a realistic benchmark with moving people, physical robot interactions, and indoor and outdoor navigation tasks. In simulation and real-world tests on a legged robot, TIC-VLA follows language instructions more reliably and collides less often than prior robot navigation methods, even when reasoning takes several seconds. This matters because it brings language-guided robots closer to practical use in shared human spaces, where both understanding instructions and reacting quickly are essential.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes TIC-VLA, a latency-aware framework for language-guided robot navigation that addresses the temporal mismatch between slow vision-language reasoning and fast reactive control. The method employs a dual-system architecture and a latency-consistent training pipeline, explicitly feeding delayed semantic states, latency metadata, and ego-motion offsets into the action policy. Evaluated on a newly introduced simulation benchmark (DynaNav) and a real-world Unitree Go2 quadruped, the system tackles a practically important problem with a sensible design.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
1. The paper targets a real and under-discussed systems problem.
The temporal mismatch between intermittent VLM reasoning and continuous control is a genuine issue for mobile robots, especially on edge hardware. The paper states this problem clearly and frames latency as a modeling issue rather than a mere engineering inconvenience. 

2. The method is structured and easy to understand.
The delayed semantic-control interface is clean: the policy consumes current observations together with delayed VLM features, latency, and ego-motion offsets. The training pipeline is also logically aligned with the deployment story. 

3. The paper conducts comprehensive experiments including simulation and real setup.
In addition to simulation, the authors include real-world deployment on a quadruped robot and provide several ablations on semantic interface design, latency awareness, ego-motion offset, action policy type, and backbone choice. 

## Weakness
1. There is a significant train-test mismatch hidden in the imitation-learning setup.
In the supplementary material, the action policy is trained with delayed ground-truth reasoning annotations and guidance waypoints, and Algorithm 1 explicitly forms delayed KV states from those traces. At deployment, however, the model must rely on its own asynchronously generated reasoning. This raises a serious concern that part of the reported gain may come from training under oracle semantic supervision rather than from truly robust online reasoning under latency.

2. The empirical evidence is not strong enough to support the paper’s broad claims.
The proposed benchmark contains only 85 test episodes across four environments, with only 10 outdoor episodes, and all experiments are reported under a fixed random seed. The real-world evaluation is even smaller: four tasks with five trials each. For a paper making strong claims about robust navigation under latency, this is too limited to establish stability or generality convincingly.

3. The comparisons are not as clean as the tables suggest.
The strongest non-language baseline, NavDP, nearly matches TIC-VLA in success rate on DynaNav (54.12 vs. 55.29), which weakens the claim that language-conditioned delayed reasoning is driving a large gain. Meanwhile, the language-guided baselines are comparatively weak and appear mismatched to this continuous, physics-based, dynamic-navigation setting. The synchronous baseline is also not very compelling, since it literally halts the robot during blocking inference and only moves for short bursts, making it closer to a strawman than a competitive control design.

4. The safety story is weaker than the paper’s framing implies.
TIC-VLA improves collision rate relative to several baselines, but the margin over NavDP is small, and the reasoning-at-test-time ablation actually shows that enabling explicit reasoning improves success while worsening collision rate. That result complicates the narrative that richer semantic reasoning leads to safer behavior in dynamic environments.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. Can authors train the action policy with model-generated delayed reasoning instead of ground-truth reasoning traces?
If the gains remain, it would reduce my concern about train-test mismatch.

2. Can authors report multi-seed results or confidence intervals on DynaNav?
If the improvements are stable across runs, my confidence in the empirical claims would increase.

3. Can authors add a stronger asynchronous baseline without explicit latency metadata / ego-motion compensation?
If TIC-VLA still wins clearly, it would make the core contribution much more convincing.

reviews.summary: This paper addresses the important problem of temporal misalignment between semantic reasoning and real-time control in mobile robot navigation. Existing VLA-based navigation systems often assume that semantic inference and control are temporally aligned, whereas in practice VLM reasoning can incur substantial latency while low-level control must operate continuously at high frequency. To address this gap, the authors propose TIC-VLA, a latency-aware framework that explicitly incorporates delayed semantic states, latency metadata, and ego-motion offsets into action generation. The paper further introduces a three-stage training pipeline designed to improve robustness under asynchronous deployment, and presents DynaNav, a benchmark for language-guided navigation in dynamic environments with human participants. Experimental results in simulation and on real robots suggest that the proposed framework improves robustness and navigation performance under reasoning latency.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem in robot navigation: existing VLA methods often assume that semantic reasoning and control are temporally aligned, while in practice semantic inference is inherently delayed relative to real-time action, especially in dynamic, human-centric environments.
2. The paper proposes a clear and well-motivated solution: TIC-VLA explicitly models reasoning latency during action generation through a delayed semantic-control interface, which incorporates delayed vision-language semantic states, explicit latency metadata, and current observations. In addition, the latency-consistent training pipeline further aligns imitation learning and online reinforcement learning with asynchronous deployment conditions.
3. The paper demonstrates strong empirical results in both simulation and the real world: with the newly introduced DynaNav benchmark and real-robot experiments, TIC-VLA consistently outperforms prior VLA baselines while maintaining robust real-time control under multi-second reasoning latency, showing both practical effectiveness and strong robustness.
4. The paper is clearly presented, and the figures and tables are effective in illustrating both the problem setting and the proposed method.

Weaknesses:
1. After RL fine-tuning, TIC-VLA achieves a success rate of 55.29% in simulation. The paper does not provide a detailed Failure Case section to analyze the specific reasons for the failures.
2. The proposed dual-system architecture is highly dependent on the accuracy of the semantic reasoning (CoT) provided by the upper-level VLM. Should the VLM pass down incorrect semantic features after a long delay, it may induce cascading errors and result in critical navigation failures.
3. The model relies heavily on the ego-motion offset $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta \theta)$ to align the delayed VLM semantic features with the current state. However, in real-world deployments on quadruped robots (such as the Unitree Go2), odometry drift is inevitable. How sensitive is the system to cumulative odometry errors? Does the alignment mechanism of the delayed semantic-control interface break down in the presence of significant drift?
4. In the DynaNav simulation, the authors tested highly challenging, dynamic scenarios featuring pedestrian counts as high as 60 to 200. How does the model perform in highly crowded, dynamic environments in the real world?
5. What is the rationale for selecting a 3-second action prediction horizon? Furthermore, have the authors evaluated how different horizon lengths (e.g., 1 second versus 5 seconds) affect the smoothness of dynamic obstacle avoidance and the overall navigation success rate?
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: Please see weaknesses.
reviews.limitations: The authors should revise the paper to address the weaknesses discussed above and improve the overall clarity of the work. In addition, the paper would benefit from a more thorough analysis and discussion of the method’s limitations and failure cases.
reviews.final_justification: The authors have sufficiently addressed my concerns, so I will maintain my positive score.

reviews.summary: This paper proposes a latency-aware VLA framework, TIC-VLA, to solve language-guided robot navigation in dynamic environments under delayed semantic inference. To address the temporal mismatch between slow reasoning and fast control, it introduces a delayed semantic-control interface including delayed semantic states, latency metadata, and ego-motion offsets by explicitly exposing inference delay to the action policy, which can enable robust asynchronous control. It also proposes a latency-consistent training pipeline to align training and deployment, combined with a realistic DynaNav simulation benchmark. Extensive experiments on DynaNav simulation and real-world quadruped navigation demonstrate improved success under latency and better robustness than prior VLA baselines.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is built around a well-motivated problem. Handling the mismatch between slow but informative VLM reasoning and the need for fast reactive control is an important challenge for embodied agents, especially in dynamic environments. I also appreciate that the paper treats latency as part of the problem formulation rather than as a minor systems issue. This perspective makes the work interesting and gives the paper a clear focus.
2. The technical contribution is fairly substantial. The paper not only introduces a method, but also formulates the problem setting, builds a simulator, and proposes a training and inference framework tailored to delayed semantic feedback. As a result, the paper feels complete. The asynchronous interface and the three-stage training pipeline are both easy to follow and reasonably well designed.
3. The experimental section is solid overall. TIC-VLA shows consistent improvements over prior VLA baselines on DynaNav, and the ablation studies are useful in supporting the main design choices. The real-world results are also meaningful, particularly because the paper evaluates the system not only on high-end GPUs but also on edge hardware under a multi-second reasoning delay. This makes the empirical study well aligned with the paper’s central claim.

Weaknesses:
1. The baseline comparison is not fully convincing yet. Some of the baselines were originally developed for different action spaces or deployment assumptions, but the paper uses these results to argue for limitations in dynamic and physically realistic settings. Since the main evaluation is conducted on a benchmark introduced in this work, it is difficult to tell how much of the gain comes from the proposed method itself and how much comes from the benchmark setup favoring the proposed formulation.
2. The benchmark is interesting, but still relatively limited in scale. DynaNav contains four scene types and 85 test cases, which is a reasonable starting point, but it remains somewhat small for supporting broad claims about dynamic human-centered navigation. Stronger evidence on the diversity of scenes, human behaviors, and generalization beyond the designed environments would make the benchmark contribution more convincing.
3. The paper could do a better job of clarifying its novelty with respect to prior dual-system or asynchronous VLA methods. The delayed semantic-control interface and the latency-consistent training scheme seem to be the main technical novelties, and these are meaningful contributions. However, the current presentation sometimes leaves the boundary with prior work a bit unclear. A more careful discussion of what is genuinely new here, and what is an extension or refinement of existing asynchronous formulations, would strengthen the paper.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. How well does the policy generalize to unseen latency distributions beyond the injected training, like varying latencies or sudden interruptions due to network issues?
2. In Figure 5, why does the performance all increase when the latency increases from 1s to 2s?
3. Could the author provide some cases with sudden changes in the environment, like humans suddenly appearing in nearby positions, since the current examples all leave sufficient reaction times for the robot?

reviews.summary: This paper studies language-guided robot navigation in dynamic environments under realistic inference latency. The core motivation is that vision-language reasoning is slow, while low-level control must run continuously, so existing VLA systems can suffer from a temporal mismatch between stale semantic outputs and current robot state. To address this, the paper proposes TIC-VLA, a latency-aware VLA framework that decouples slow semantic reasoning from fast reactive control through a delayed semantic-control interface. The action policy conditions on current observations together with delayed VLM features, explicit latency information, and ego-motion offsets, allowing it to reinterpret stale semantics in the current control context. The paper further introduces a latency-consistent training pipeline that combines VLM supervised fine-tuning, imitation learning with injected reasoning delays, and online reinforcement learning under asynchronous inference. To support evaluation, the authors also build DynaNav, a dynamic language-guided navigation benchmark in physics-based simulation, and they report results both in simulation and on a real quadruped robot. Overall, the paper presents a latency-aware system design for real-time language-conditioned navigation and evaluates it in both simulated and real-world dynamic settings.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
The main strengths and weaknesses of the paper are summarized below.

Soundness:

Strengths.

The paper addresses a concrete systems issue in language-conditioned robot navigation, namely the mismatch between slow semantic reasoning and the fast control loop required for real robotic platforms. The proposed framework models this mismatch explicitly by introducing a delayed semantic-control interface that exposes reasoning latency and ego-motion offsets to the control policy, allowing the policy to reinterpret semantic information that may no longer correspond to the current robot state. The method itself is technically reasonable and the main design components are described with sufficient clarity, including the use of VLM semantic features, the transformer-based action policy, and the asynchronous inference mechanism. The training pipeline is also coherent, combining supervised fine-tuning of the VLM with imitation learning under injected delays and reinforcement learning in closed-loop simulation. The empirical evaluation is relatively comprehensive. The authors conduct experiments in a dynamic simulation benchmark with multiple scene types and crowd densities, analyze robustness under different reasoning latencies, and include ablation studies examining the role of ego-motion compensation and the choice of semantic interface. In addition, the inclusion of experiments on a real quadruped robot platform provides useful evidence that the system design can operate under realistic deployment conditions.

Weakness.

Despite the generally solid experimental setup, the comparison with existing methods is somewhat limited. The evaluation mainly includes several navigation baselines and a few language-guided navigation models, but it does not include some widely discussed vision-language-action or embodied models such as RT-2, PaLM-E style systems, or other recent VLA policies, which makes it harder to judge how the proposed approach compares with stronger embodied baselines. The backbone model used in the system is also relatively small (InternVL3-1B), and the paper does not investigate whether the proposed architecture remains effective when paired with larger or more capable vision-language models. In addition, although the paper includes real-world robot experiments, the number of trials is relatively small, which limits the statistical strength of the conclusions drawn from the real deployment results.

Presentation:

Strengths.

The paper is generally well structured and the main motivation is clearly introduced at the beginning. The problem of reasoning latency in embodied systems is explained in an intuitive way, and the proposed system architecture is illustrated through clear diagrams that help the reader understand how semantic reasoning and low-level control interact within the framework. The description of the training pipeline is also reasonably clear, especially the three-stage process involving VLM fine-tuning, imitation learning with injected latency, and reinforcement learning under asynchronous inference. The appendix is particularly detailed and provides useful implementation details, including model architecture choices, data generation procedures, and additional experimental settings, which helps improve the reproducibility of the work.

Weaknesses.

Some parts of the presentation could nevertheless be improved. Several architectural choices, such as the number of cross-attention layers in the action expert or the particular design of the semantic interface, are introduced without much discussion of alternative designs or sensitivity analysis, which leaves some design decisions insufficiently justified.

Significance:

Strengths.

The work addresses an important and practical challenge in deploying vision-language-action systems on real robotic platforms. Many recent VLA systems implicitly assume synchronous reasoning and control, while real robotic systems often operate under strict control frequencies and limited onboard compute resources. By explicitly modeling reasoning latency and allowing the control policy to adapt to delayed semantic information, the paper highlights a systems-level issue that is likely to arise in many real-world deployments. The combination of dynamic simulation experiments and real robot evaluation also suggests that the proposed approach has practical relevance for embodied AI and robotic navigation applications.

Weaknesses.

At the same time, the scope of the contribution remains somewhat specialized. The proposed framework focuses specifically on navigation under reasoning latency, and the paper does not provide evidence that the same design would generalize to other embodied tasks such as manipulation or complex multi-step tool use. Furthermore, the evaluation benchmark used in the paper is largely constructed by the authors, which makes it somewhat difficult to judge how well the results would transfer to widely used community benchmarks.

Originality:

Strengths.

The main originality of the paper lies in framing the interaction between semantic reasoning and control as a latency-aware problem and designing a system interface that explicitly exposes delayed semantic information to the control policy. The delayed semantic-control interface, together with the latency-consistent training procedure that injects reasoning delays during imitation learning and reinforcement learning, represents a thoughtful system-level design that adapts existing components to a realistic robotics setting. The work therefore contributes a useful perspective on how vision-language reasoning modules can be integrated with real-time control policies in embodied systems.

Weaknesses.

The underlying model components themselves are largely based on existing techniques, including standard vision-language backbones, transformer-based action policies, and PPO-style reinforcement learning. As a result, the novelty primarily lies in the system integration and problem formulation rather than in fundamentally new model architectures or learning algorithms.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
I would appreciate clarification on the following points.

1.The proposed system relies on a relatively small vision-language backbone (InternVL3-1B). It would be helpful to understand whether the latency-aware design remains effective when paired with larger or more capable VLMs. Have the authors evaluated, or do they expect similar benefits when using stronger vision-language models?

2.The comparison set mainly includes navigation policies and several vision-language navigation systems, but does not include stronger embodied VLA models such as RT-2, PaLM-E style systems, or other recent language-conditioned robot policies. Could the authors clarify how TIC-VLA is expected to compare with these systems, or discuss any practical reasons why such comparisons were not included?

3.The real-world evaluation demonstrates promising results, but the number of trials appears relatively small. Could the authors provide more details on the number of runs per task and the variance of the results, and comment on whether larger-scale real-world evaluations show similar trends?

4.The action expert uses a transformer architecture with six cross-attention layers to integrate visual tokens, semantic features, and latency metadata. Could the authors comment on how sensitive the performance is to this architectural choice, and whether shallower or deeper policies were considered during development?

5.The delayed semantic-control interface relies on ego-motion offsets to reinterpret stale semantic information. In dynamic environments where objects move independently of the robot (e.g., pedestrians suddenly changing direction), how robust is this mechanism in practice, and are there scenarios where delayed semantics can still lead to incorrect decisions?
reviews.limitations: No. The paper does not explicitly discuss the limitations of the proposed approach. It would be helpful for the authors to acknowledge several potential limitations, such as the reliance on a relatively small vision-language backbone, the limited scale of the real-world experiments, and the uncertainty of how well the latency-aware design generalizes to other embodied tasks beyond navigation.
reviews.final_justification: The rebuttal adequately addressed my main concerns and improved my confidence in the paper. In particular, the added backbone analysis, stronger navigation-oriented comparisons, and architecture ablation make the empirical support more convincing, while the clarification on the limited scale of the real-world evaluation is reasonable and improves the presentation of the work. Although the novelty remains mainly in the system design and problem formulation, I still find the paper technically solid, practically meaningful, and well motivated for the problem it targets. Overall, the rebuttal reinforces my original assessment, and I maintain my score and recommendation.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and constructive suggestions. We are encouraged that the reviewer found the paper technically solid and appreciated the practical motivation. Below, we provide point-by-point responses.

**1. Scalability to larger VLM backbones**

We agree that an important question is whether the benefit of our latency-aware design extends to stronger VLMs. To examine this, we include results in the supplementary material (Table 11) using a larger VLM, Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The results show a clear trade-off: although Qwen2.5-VL-3B is a stronger model, it introduces higher inference latency, which worsens reasoning-action misalignment and consequently degrades navigation performance. In contrast, InternVL3-1B achieves the balance between reasoning capability and inference speed.

These results support our motivation: stronger semantic reasoning alone is not sufficient if the added latency breaks closed-loop control. We believe that improving VLM inference speed is also important.

**2. Comparisons with stronger VLA models** 

We agree that stronger comparisons help better position our work. Models such as RT-2 and PaLM-E were primarily designed for manipulation, and applying them to navigation would require substantial adaptation, making it difficult to ensure fairness and reproducibility.

To address this concern in a setting more aligned with our task, we include two recent navigation VLA models, OmniVLA [1] and MobileVLA [2]. We follow their open-source implementations and fine-tune/evaluate them under the same settings. As shown below, TIC-VLA outperforms these VLA models across reported metrics, which strengthens the empirical support for our approach.

|Method|Nav Error↓|Success Rate↑|SPL↑|Collision Rate↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|OmniVLA [1]|16.53|31.76|28.33|49.41|
|MobileVLA [2]|16.09|32.94|30.31|45.88|
|TIC-VLA (no RL)|**10.85**|**47.06**|**42.41**|**34.12**|

[1] OmniVLA: An Omni-Modal Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation (ICRA 2026)

[2] MobileVLA-R1: Reinforcing Vision-Language-Action for Mobile Robots

**3. Real-world evaluation scale and variance**

We agree that the real-world evaluation is limited in scale, and we appreciate the opportunity to clarify this. For each real-world task, we conducted five trials and report the average success rate, with task-wise results provided in Table 8 of the supplementary material. The results show that latency-aware design improves deployability under realistic asynchronous inference.

We agree that a larger-scale real-world evaluation would strengthen the empirical evidence. However, one key challenge is that real-world dynamic scenes, especially those involving humans, are difficult to standardize across repeated runs. For this reason, we use large-scale simulation as our primary controlled evaluation, and position the real-robot experiments mainly as evidence of feasibility and transfer under practical deployment conditions. In the revision, we will state the scale of the real-world evaluation explicitly as a limitation.

**4. Sensitivity to the action expert architecture**

We agree that the architectural choice should be better justified. To address this, we conducted an ablation on the number of cross-attention layers in the Transformer action expert without RL fine-tuning.

The results show that the 6-layer design achieves the best performance. A smaller variant (3 layers) shows a comparable but slightly weaker performance, while a deeper variant (12 layers) increases model complexity without improving the performance metrics.

|Layers|Nav Error ↓|Success Rate ↑|SPL ↑|Collision Rate ↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|3| 10.98|45.88|41.39|35.29|
|6 (ours)|**10.85**|**47.06**|**42.41**|**34.12**|
|12|10.73|44.71|40.77|37.64|

**5. Handling dynamic objects under delayed semantics**

We agree that ego-motion compensation alone cannot handle independently moving agents. When object motion is independent of the robot, delayed semantic information may no longer match the current scene. Our approach mitigates this in three ways: (1) the policy is trained with dynamic agents during training, exposing it to such behaviors; (2) the action policy conditions on current observations, allowing immediate reaction to discrepancies with stale semantics; and (3) latency and ego-motion metadata enable the policy to implicitly assess the freshness of semantic inputs.

However, we do not claim that this mechanism fully resolves the problem. In highly dynamic or unpredictable scenarios, delayed semantics can still lead to incorrect decisions. We will clarify this limitation more explicitly.

**6. Discussion of limitations**

Thank you for pointing this out. We will add a dedicated limitations section in the revised paper. Key points include: (1) the system is not yet fully optimized for runtime efficiency; (2) real-world evaluation remains limited in scale; and (3) generalization beyond navigation (e.g., manipulation) remains an open question.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. We appreciate the positive assessment of the paper’s motivation, technical completeness, and empirical validation. Below we provide point-by-point responses.

**1. Stronger baseline comparison**

We agree that the baseline comparison should be strengthened. To address this concern, we have added two recent and stronger navigation-VLA baselines that are better aligned with our action space and deployment setting: OmniVLA [1] and MobileVLA [2]. We fine-tune and evaluate both methods using their open-source implementations under the same setting as TIC-VLA.

As shown below, TIC-VLA outperforms these strong navigation VLA baselines across all metrics. These results strengthen the empirical claim that the gains are not only against prior VLN baselines, but also against more competitive recent navigation-VLA methods.

|Method|Nav Error↓|Success Rate↑|SPL↑|Collision Rate↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|OmniVLA [1]|16.53|31.76|28.33|49.41|
|MobileVLA [2]|16.09|32.94|30.31|45.88|
|TIC-VLA (no RL)|**10.85**|**47.06**|**42.41**|**34.12**|

[1] OmniVLA: An Omni-Modal Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation (ICRA 2026)

[2] MobileVLA-R1: Reinforcing Vision-Language-Action for Mobile Robots

**2. Benchmark scale and diversity**

We agree that benchmark scale and diversity are important. Rather than focusing only on building a larger or more general benchmark, we design DynaNav to target a key but underexplored problem: maintaining effective control under delayed reasoning in VLA systems.

We need to clarify that while DynaNav contains four high-level scene types, its diversity is not limited to four fixed templates. Each category includes varied layouts, visibility conditions, and human motion patterns, and the human-populated setting further introduces diversity through different motion trajectories, dynamic occupancy, and changing local interactions. The benchmark captures a broader range of navigation situations.

However, we acknowledge that the current scale is still limited for broader claims. In the revision, we will clarify the intended scope of DynaNav as a targeted benchmark for realistic VLA navigation, and we aim to expand scene diversity and benchmark scale in future work.

**3. Better articulation of novelty relative to prior work**

We appreciate this suggestion and agree that the novelty relative to prior asynchronous or dual-system VLA methods should be articulated more sharply.

Our contribution is not simply the use of asynchronous reasoning, but three specific technical contributions: (1) a delayed semantic-control interface that explicitly exposes delayed semantic states, latency metadata, and ego-motion offsets to the action policy; (2) a latency-consistent training pipeline that aligns policy training with deployment-time delay, rather than training synchronously and deploying asynchronously; and (3) a benchmark and evaluation setting designed specifically to study this failure mode in dynamic navigation. 

We will revise the paper to more clearly separate these contributions from the broader asynchronous formulation in prior work.

**4. Generalization to unseen latency distributions**

Thank you for raising this important point. During both IL and RL fine-tuning, we inject randomized latency from 0 to 10 seconds so that the policy is trained under a range of delays rather than a single fixed latency. This range covers the latencies observed in both our simulation and real-world deployment.

We agree that this does not establish robustness to arbitrary out-of-distribution latency patterns, such as extreme delay spikes beyond the training range. In such cases, performance is expected to degrade as semantic feedback becomes significantly stale. Our claim is therefore intentionally limited to robustness within the practical latency regime encountered in deployment. This assumption is appropriate in our setting because the system runs onboard without network-dependent latency, making delay relatively stable in practice.

**5. Performance increase from 1s to 2s latency in Figure 5**

Thank you for catching this. We agree that this trend was not explained sufficiently. The increase from 1s to 2s latency is not a meaningful trend. Before RL fine-tuning, performance at these two latency levels is essentially unchanged. After RL fine-tuning, the small increase corresponds to only one additional successful episode out of 85 trials, so it should be interpreted as a statistical fluctuation. We will revise the text to state this explicitly.

**6. Examples of sudden dynamic changes**

We agree that abrupt environmental changes, such as humans suddenly appearing nearby, are important for evaluating reactive robustness. Our supplementary videos already include such cases, but we agree that the paper should present these cases more concretely. In the revision, we will add representative qualitative examples involving more challenging dynamic events.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thank you for the supportive and constructive feedback. We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the importance of the problem and the clarity of our framework. Below, we respond point by point.

**1. Failure case analysis**

We agree that failure analysis is important. Following your suggestion, we conducted a finer-grained analysis of unsuccessful episodes and grouped them into three main failure modes: (1) getting stuck after a collision; (2) failing to reach the goal within the time limit, where the agent gets close to the goal but does not reach it; and (3) misinterpreting the goal or instruction, leading to incorrect navigation. 

|Outcome / Reason|TIC-VLA (no RL)|TIC-VLA|
|--|--|--|
|Stuck after collision|23.53%|17.65%|
|Failed to reach navigation goal / timeout| 16.47%|15.29%|
|Misinterpretation of goal or instruction|12.94%|11.76%|
|Success|47.06%|55.29%|

This analysis shows that RL fine-tuning yields the largest reduction in collision-related failures, indicating improved robustness in closed-loop interaction. However, timeout and instruction-related failures remain prevalent, indicating that the main remaining bottlenecks are long-horizon planning and semantic grounding. We will include this analysis in the revision.

**2. Dependency on VLM reasoning accuracy**

We agree that this is a limitation. Because TIC-VLA uses delayed high-level semantics from the VLM, incorrect or stale semantic outputs can propagate downstream and lead to navigation errors.  For this reason, TIC-VLA is designed not to rely on delayed semantics alone: the policy also conditions on current observations, which can help correct some outdated or imperfect high-level information. In addition, latency-consistent training improves robustness to delayed inputs during deployment.

However, these designs do not fully resolve the issue. If the VLM produces a fundamentally incorrect interpretation of the goal or scene, the downstream policy may still inherit this error. We will make this limitation more explicit in the revision and expand the discussion of future directions.

**3. Sensitivity to odometry drift**

We agree that odometry drift is a critical practical concern. To improve robustness, we apply dropout to both state inputs and ego-motion offsets during training, so that the action policy does not overfit to perfectly accurate motion estimates. In addition, following your suggestion, we conducted robustness tests in simulation by injecting Gaussian noise into translation and rotation measurements proportional to distance traveled at each step and accumulated over time. 

The results show that TIC-VLA remains robust under typical/moderate drift, with almost no degradation in navigation performance. Under the severe stress-test condition, performance declines more noticeably, but the method remains functional rather than failing catastrophically.

|Drift Level|Gaussian Noise (trans, rot)|Nav Error ↓|Success Rate ↑|SPL ↑|Collision Rate ↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|--|
|None|--|10.55|55.29|50.29|28.24|
|Typical|(0.02 m/m, 1°/m)|10.66|55.29|50.12|29.41|
|Severe|(0.05 m/m, 5°/m)|11.87|43.53|38.41|35.29|

**4. Real-world performance in crowded environments**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that evaluation in highly crowded real-world settings is important. However, such experiments are difficult to conduct in a controlled and reproducible way: pedestrians may avoid the robot, behave inconsistently across runs, or intentionally interfere, which makes fair comparison across methods challenging.

For this reason, we use simulation as the primary testbed for systematic evaluation under extreme crowd densities, where pedestrian count, behavior, and initial conditions can be controlled and reproduced across trials. We will revise the paper to make the scope of our real-world validation more explicit. Expanding real-world evaluation to more crowded and dynamic settings is an important direction for future work.

**5. Rationale for the 3-second action prediction horizon**

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. The 3-second prediction horizon was chosen to balance short-term responsiveness and longer-horizon planning. A shorter horizon makes the policy more reactive, but provides limited foresight. A longer horizon offers more planning context, but makes short-term action prediction less accurate.

Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we evaluated 1-second and 5-second prediction horizons in TIC-VLA models without RL fine-tuning. The 3-second horizon provides the best balance and achieves the strongest performance in core navigation metrics. The 1-second horizon is slightly more reactive and achieves the lowest collision rate, but its success rate and SPL are lower. We will include these ablations in the revised paper.

|Horizon|Nav Error ↓|Success Rate ↑|SPL ↑|Collision Rate ↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|1s|12.23|42.35|38.72|**32.94**|
|3s (ours)|**10.85**|**47.06**|**42.41**|34.12|
|5s|11.77|40.00|36.46|35.29|

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
Thank you for your supportive and constructive review. We appreciate your recognition of the practical importance of the problem, the clarity of our framework, and the breadth of our experiments. Below, we respond point by point.

**1. Train-test mismatch in imitation learning**

We agree this is a valid concern. In our pipeline, IL is used to learn a latency-aware action expert under clean supervision: given delayed semantics and latency metadata, how should the robot act? We use ground-truth reasoning traces to avoid entangling action learning with errors from the reasoning model. Using model-generated reasoning at this stage would make policy learning less stable and increase training cost by an order of magnitude due to autoregressive generation.

We also agree that this introduces a train-test mismatch if using IL alone. We **mitigate this in the RL fine-tuning stage**, where the policy is trained in closed loop using its own delayed generated VLM semantics. This exposes the policy to the same types of signals encountered at deployment, thereby better aligning training and testing conditions. 

**2. Stronger empirical evidence**

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and agree that the stronger empirical evidence is important. To address the reviewer’s concern, we repeated the main benchmark evaluation for the key methods with 3 random seeds and report mean ± std below. 

The results show **consistent relative trends across seeds**, and the variance is moderate and does not change the overall conclusions. These results provide additional evidence that the gains are not due to a single run. We will add multi-seed benchmark results to the revised paper to strengthen the empirical evidence.

|Method|Nav Error↓|Success Rate↑|SPL↑|Collision Rate↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|NavDP (goal)|**8.58**±0.63|53.33±2.45|**51.73**±3.07|29.80±0.68|
|DualVLN|16.86±0.82|30.98±1.80|27.95±1.61|47.84±2.45|
|TIC-VLA (no RL)|11.36±0.59|46.27±2.45|41.9±2.34|34.90±0.68|
|TIC-VLA|10.06 ± 0.53|**55.69**±2.95|51.29±3.06|**28.2**±1.18|

**3. Comparison with non-language and asynchronous baselines**

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that the margin over NavDP is relatively small on some metrics. Our intent in including NavDP is to provide a strong reference point, but it is important to note that this comparison is not direct: NavDP is a privileged goal-conditioned policy that receives continuously updated target coordinates relative to the robot, whereas TIC-VLA receives only a natural-language instruction at the start and must infer, ground, and maintain the goal over time. Achieving comparable performance to such a privileged baseline is thus meaningful.

We also agree that stronger asynchronous baselines are important. While our ablations do not fully replace a standalone baseline, they help isolate the effect of key design components. In Table 2, removing latency-aware modeling degrades performance, and in Table 9, removing ego-motion compensation leads to consistent drops across all metrics. This suggests that asynchronous execution alone is not sufficient, and explicit latency modeling and compensation are both important. We also include DualVLN as an asynchronous language-guided baseline.

To further strengthen the comparison, we add two recent VLA navigation baselines with continuous setting, OmniVLA [1] and MobileVLA [2]. We follow their open-source implementations and evaluate them under the same settings. As shown below, TIC-VLA consistently outperforms these stronger language-guided baselines that are more closely matched to our problem setting, supporting the effectiveness of our approach.

|Method|Nav Error↓|Success Rate↑|SPL↑|Collision Rate↓|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|OmniVLA [1]|16.53|31.76|28.33|49.41|
|MobileVLA [2]|16.09|32.94|30.31|45.88|
|TIC-VLA (no RL)|**10.85**|**47.06**|**42.41**|**34.12**|

[1] OmniVLA: An Omni-Modal Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation (ICRA 2026)

[2] MobileVLA-R1: Reinforcing Vision-Language-Action for Mobile Robots

**4. Safety interpretation and collision rate in Table 4**

We thank the reviewer for this observation and agree our interpretation may have been unclear. In the non-reasoning setting, the lower collision rate is primarily associated with reduced activity: the agent tends to move less, make slower progress, and fail more often. In other words, **fewer collisions in this case do not necessarily indicate safer navigation**, but rather a more conservative or partially inactive policy.

By contrast, enabling reasoning improves goal completion and navigation progress. This increased activity can slightly increase the collision rate, but it leads to a substantial improvement in task success. This reflects a tradeoff between activity and safety rather than degraded safety. We will revise the paper to clarify this point.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
In this paper, the authors propose TIC-VLA, a latency-aware framework for language-guided robot navigation that addresses the temporal mismatch between slow vision-language reasoning and fast reactive control. The architecture is dual-system: a slow VLM emits delayed semantic features while a fast action policy consumes current observations together with delayed semantics, latency metadata, and ego-motion offsets that compensate for robot motion during the reasoning interval. The central design choice is to treat reasoning latency as a first-class input to the action policy.Training proceeds in three stages: VLM supervised fine-tuning, imitation learning with injected reasoning delays, and online reinforcement learning under asynchronous inference so that the policy learns to expect and handle delays it encou ters in deployment. The paper introduces DynaNav, a physics-based dynamic-navigation benchmark with human participants, and reports results on DynaNav and on a real Unitree Go2 quadruped under multi-second VLM inference latency.

The paper received positive reviews across the board: one weak accept (R-zeMP) and three accepts (R-5RZg, R-jChU, R-wj1w). Reviewers agreed that latency-as-modeling-issue is well-motivated and that the delayed semantic-control interface is clean. Some concerns pointed out were a train-test mismatch between IL with oracle reasoning and asynchronous deployment (R-zeMP), limited DynaNav and real-world scale (R-zeMP, R-jChU, R-wj1w), narrow margin over the privileged NavDP baseline (R-zeMP), odometry-drift and VLM grounding robustness (R-5RZg), failure-case analysis (R-5RZg), novelty boundaries against prior dual-system work (R-jChU), and scalability to larger VLM backbones (R-wj1w).

The authors presented a rebuttal covering several parts: multi-seed DynaNav numbers, two recent navigation-VLA baselines (OmniVLA, MobileVLA) where TIC-VLA outperforms by clear margins, architecture and horizon ablations, odometry-drift stress tests showing graceful degradation, a failure-mode breakdown showing RL fine-tuning primarily reduces collision-related failures, an oracle-IL justification (avoiding reasoning-error entanglement during action learning, with RL closing the loop on model-generated reasoning), and a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone comparison showing gains from a stronger VLM are eaten by added inference latency, which reinforces the latency-aware framing. All four reviewers marked their concerns as fully resolved and confirmed positive scores; R-jChU explicitly raised their score.

The technical contribution is useful: an explicit, deployable framing of reasoning latency as a modeling problem, paired with a coherent training pipeline and real-robot deployment evidence. Some limitations remain on DynaNav scale, real-world trial count, and the narrow margin over privileged NavDP. I recommend acceptance, and encourage the authors to incorporate the multi-seed results, OmniVLA/MobileVLA comparisons, failure-mode analysis, drift robustness, ablations, and backbone-scaling discussion into the main text, while highlighting cuirrent limitations more explicitly.

our_title: Expanding the Capabilities of Reinforcement Learning via Text Feedback

match.matched_title: Expanding the Capabilities of Reinforcement Learning via Text Feedback

submission.title: Expanding the Capabilities of Reinforcement Learning via Text Feedback
submission.abstract: The success of RL for LLM post-training stems from an unreasonably uninformative source: a single bit of information per rollout as binary reward or preference label. At the other extreme, distillation offers dense supervision but requires demonstrations, which are costly and difficult to scale. We study natural language feedback as an intermediate signal: richer than scalar rewards, yet cheaper than complete demonstrations. Textual feedback is a natural mode of human interaction and is already abundant in many real-world settings, where users, tools, and automated judges routinely critique LLM outputs. Towards leveraging text feedback at scale, we formalize a multi-turn RL setup where text feedback is available during training but not at inference. Therefore, models must learn to internalize the feedback in order to improve their test-time single-turn performance. To do this, we propose two methods: Self Distillation, which trains the single-turn policy to match its own feedback-conditioned second-turn generations; and Feedback Modeling, which predicts the feedback as an auxiliary objective.  We provide theoretical analysis on both methods, and empirically evaluate on reasoning puzzles, competition math, and creative writing tasks. Our results show that both methods consistently outperform strong baselines across benchmarks, highlighting the potential of RL with an additional source of rich supervision at scale.
submission.tldr: Achieving best of both worlds between RL and distillation with RL from text feedback.
submission.lay_summary:
When training AI language models to improve their responses, the standard approach gives the model only a simple thumbs-up or thumbs-down after each attempt — a single bit of information that says nothing about what went wrong or how to fix it. At the other extreme, providing full corrected solutions is expensive and hard to scale.

We study a middle ground: training with written critiques — the kind of feedback a teacher might give a student, such as "you made an error in step 3" or "your argument missed a key constraint." This text feedback is richer than a simple score, yet far cheaper than writing out a complete solution.

The challenge is that such feedback is available during training but typically not when the model is actually used. We develop two methods that help the model internalize critiques so it learns to avoid mistakes on its own, without needing feedback at test time. One method treats the model's own corrected responses as demonstrations to learn from; the other trains the model to predict what a critic would say, sharpening its internal error awareness.

Across reasoning, math, and creative writing tasks, both methods substantially outperform standard training approaches.

reviews.summary: Motivated by the limited information in reward- or preference-based post-training and scalability challenges of demonstration-based distillation, the manuscript proposes two methods for leveraging natural language feedback. Prior work has explored multi-turn strategies, where models update their answers based on feedback received after earlier turns. While this improves performance when feedback is available, it typically does not improve first-turn performance in absence of detailed feedback. One proposed method is based on self-distillation via an unbiased estimate of the advantage of correcting the initial prediction by instead providing the updated answer generated after observing feedback. Several stability and efficiency measures are explored, with a baseline of average first-turn rewards providing both more stable convergence and improved final performance compared to measures like clipping importance ratios. The other proposed method is based on feedback modeling, where instead of explicitly correcting predictions, the model is asked to predict the feedback it would receive. This provides a dense learning signal that helps with representation learning, as it targets relevant directions in parameters space that are often missed by the sparse reward signal. Experimental evaluation shows that both methods outperform strong baselines by a considerable margin. Extensive ablation studies show the impact of several design choices. An experiment on test-time scaling with self-critiquing shows that the proposed feedback modeling auxiliary task also adds significant improvements at test time.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
## Soundness
The motivation is sound and the theoretical treatment is extensive and well organized. While I did not thoroughly verify every proof, I did not find any mistakes. The theoretical analysis matches the trends observed in empirical results. The only lack in rigour, which this work shares with most LLM papers due to the prohibitive computational cost, is that there is no estimation of the multi-run variability in performance.

## Presentation
The manuscript is well organized and seems polished. I only have a few minor suggestions:
* “Intuition that reward-only RL provides near-rank-1 updates”: I suggest adding a citation here
* I would format the best result in each benchmark in bold (Table 1).
* A short comment on how hyperparameters were chosen would be useful.

## Significance
The proposed methods are addressing the critical question of how to incorporate rich natural language feedback that is only available during RL post-training to improve first-turn performance. Prior methods largely focused on improvements in multi-turn settings, i.e., evaluating how models improve their response after observing feedback on their  initial attempt. If these promising results generalize across more benchmarks, this could be a very impactful contribution.

## Originality
The work proposes to aim for better first-turn performance even when learning from feedback. To my knowledge the two presented methods are novel and show a promising avenue for future research.
reviews.key_questions_for_authors:
1. I know it is a general problem with LLM experimentation due to the high computational cost, but I expect there to be significant variance in post-training. Can you comment on variability between runs, how hyperparameters were selected for each model (including baselines)? 
2. Could you comment on why you specifically chose Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 to simulate feedback provider and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the main model?
reviews.final_justification: My initial evaluation was already very positive and the additional insights provided in the rebuttal reinforced my assessment.

reviews.summary: This paper studies how LLMs can learn effectively from natural language feedback during post-training. It identifies a mismatch between multi-turn RL objectives used during training and the single-turn performance objective. The paper also shows that improving multi-turn reward does not automatically translate into better first-turn responses. To address this, the paper proposes **Self Distillation**, which uses improved second-turn performances, generated after receiving feedback, to directly train the first-turn policy. The method includes importance weightaged estimator and introduces a first-turn reward baseline to prevent gradient collapse when the second-turn performance becomes high. They also introduce **Feedback modeling**, which trains the model to predict textual feedback itself. Empirically, the paper evaluates the proposed methods across reasoning and code generation tasks. Results show **Self Distillation** improves performance over reward-only RL baselines, and that the feedback modeling further enhances performance through self refinement.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:
The distinction between multi-turn and single-turn objectives is clearly formalized. The unbiased importance weighted estimator is well-motivated. The theoretical analysis of Feedback modeling is another strength. Although the results rely on a local linearized assumption, the claims provide a plausible explanation for why textual feedback offers richer supervision than scalar rewards. Empirical results are solid and support the claim. Comparison to GRPO is appropriate. 

**Weaknesses**:
The experiments assume relatively high-quality feedback often produced by a judge model. The robustness of the method to weak feedback is not evaluated. Test time scaling is somewhat limited. Most results focus on two-turn refinement, it would be useful to know whether gains continue or become unstable over longer refinements.

reviews.summary:
This paper tackles the limitation of RL post-training for LLMs where the supervision signal is often a sparse scalar reward. A reward of 0 provides little information about why an output is wrong, making learning inefficient when the base model struggles. The authors propose leveraging natural language critiques as an intermediate supervision signal. They formalize a multi-turn training setup where the model produces an answer, receives critique, and revises, but evaluation focuses on improving single-turn performance where critique is unavailable at test time.

Training uses two sources of signal:

1. Standard RL objective (scalar reward: verifiable for reasoning/math, judge-based for writing).

2. Feedback-based auxiliary learning, via either:

-  Self Distillation: distill the model’s own critique-conditioned second-turn response into the first-turn policy

- Feedback Modeling: train the model to predict the critique text as an auxiliary loss.

They evaluate across reasoning, math, and creative writing benchmarks and include extensive ablations.
reviews.strengths_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths** 

(1) The paper is clearly written, the motivation is easy to follow.

(2) The framing of training-time feedback, test-time single-turn performance is well-motivated and nontrivial.

(3) The Self Distillation design is thoughtful, in particular, the discussion of second-turn mean baselines and “gradient-signal collapse” is insightful and practically relevant.

(4) Results are strong across multiple domains, and the paper includes meaningful ablations isolating key choices.

(5) The qualitative examples in the appendix help interpret what kinds of errors critiques correct and how improvements propagate to the first turn.

**Weaknesses**

(1) Experiments use Qwen3-235B as the feedback provider for training a Llama-3.1-8B learner. Since the paper shows correctness-only feedback is much weaker, the effectiveness may rely heavily on the judge’s capability. An ablation on judge size would strengthen the claim that the method is broadly useful. It would also be valuable to discuss alternatives such as a learned judge (e.g., RL-Tango [1]).

(2) Given access to a 235B model, a natural baseline is to generate (i) improved second-turn solutions or (ii) full solutions/reasoning traces with the judge and then perform standard SFT/distillation on the student (possibly with filtering by verifiable reward). Without this, it is hard to disentangle gains from the proposed RL-from-feedback objectives vs. simply distilling from a strong teacher, since we have an access to it anyway.

(3) All results use the same learner (Llama-3.1-8B) and the same judge family (Qwen3-235B). It remains unclear whether gains persist with different learners or different judges (smaller or different families). Even one additional pairing would improve confidence.


**References** 

[1] Zha, Kaiwen, et al. "Rl tango: Reinforcing generator and verifier together for language reasoning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.15034 (2025).
reviews.key_questions_for_authors: see weaknesses
reviews.final_justification: This paper studies how to improve LLM post-training with natural language feedback rather than relying solely on sparse scalar rewards, and one of its main strengths is how effectively it leverages this richer supervision signal. My main reservation was the reliance on a very large judge model, which I still view as a meaningful limitation. That said, I found the paper interesting and ultimately worthy of acceptance, as the authors provided convincing rebuttal evidence that the approach remains beneficial even with weaker judges. The added cross-model generalization experiments further increased my confidence. Overall, the rebuttal addressed my central concerns and strengthened my positive assessment.

rebuttals.author: Authors
rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the careful and constructive review. We are glad the reviewer found the paper clearly written, the framing well-motivated, and the Self Distillation design (including gradient-signal collapse analysis) insightful. We address each concern below.
>*An ablation on judge size would strengthen the claim that the method is broadly useful. It would also be valuable to discuss alternatives such as a learned judge (e.g., RL-Tango [1]).*

We have added experiments using a smaller, less capable model as the judge, simulating the kind of noisy, imperfect feedback one would expect from non-expert human annotators or lightweight automated graders in practice. We show the results on knights and knaves (with the same learner model) below:

|Judge Model|Self Distillation|Feedback Modeling|GRPO|
|-|-|-|-|
|Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (in the paper)|0.802|0.880|0.352|
|Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct|0.661|0.750|-|
|Qwen3-4B-Instruct|0.609|0.758|-|

We observe that both of **our methods (especially feedback modeling) are robust to the weaker feedback providers** (we use the model from the same model family to show a clean hierarchy), as the performance still greatly improves upon GRPO even with a much weaker model to simulate the feedback provider.

Regarding RL-Tango: we thank the reviewer for the reference. RL-Tango studies jointly training a generator and verifier, which is complementary to our setting where the feedback provider is external. We will include a discussion in the revised paper.

>*A natural baseline is to generate (i) improved second-turn solutions or (ii) full solutions/reasoning traces with the judge and then perform standard SFT/distillation*

We want to clarify that **Qwen3-235B is not used as a teacher, it is used to simulate a feedback provider**. That is, the larger model is part of the learning environment, so we can not fully control the generation of the larger models (e.g., generating demonstrations or obtaining logits for distillation).

Concretely, given the student's attempt, it produces a natural language critique identifying errors and suggesting improvements. It never generates correct solutions or reasoning traces. This mirrors how feedback works in practice: a compiler returns error messages, a unit test reports which cases fail, and a human marks what went wrong during a chat; none of these produce demonstrations. The 235B model is simply a convenient stand-in for these real-world feedback sources in a controlled experimental setting. Distilling from it would be analogous to distilling from a unit test framework: it conflates the feedback provider with a solution provider, which is not the setting we wish to model in our paper. Another analogy one can draw is in RLHF/alignment; sometimes people use LLM-as-a-judge to simulate human preference [1,2], but distilling from the judge LLM is not a fair baseline.

That said, the reviewer's suggestion could help contextualize the gap between learning from feedback and learning from demonstrations. We show the comparison below:

|  |GRPO|Self Distillation|Feedback Modeling|Distillation|Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct|
|-|-|-|-|-|-|
| Knights and Knaves |0.352|0.802|0.880|0.862|0.984|

We observe that distillation performs slightly better than self-distillation, and feedback modeling actually achieves the same performance as distillation. While we do not believe this result can generalize to arbitrary setting, we believe this is a very positive result showing RLTF in some cases can be as performative as distillation, which is way more expensive and less practical. 

>*All results use the same learner (Llama-3.1-8B) and the same judge family (Qwen3-235B)...Even one additional pairing would improve confidence.*

We agree that showing generalization across learner–judge pairings is important. We have added experiments using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct as the learner, and GPT-OSS-120B to simulate the feedback provider. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct is the cheapest Qwen model on tinker and we also want to cover the case of MoE models. We choose GPT-OSS-120B so we can test robustness to arbitrary model combinations. We choose knight swap because the current reasoning tasks are easy enough for the student model (without any training). We summarize the results below:

| |GRPO Multi Turn|Self Distillation|Feedback Modeling|
|-|-|-|-|
|Knight Swap|0.225|0.305 (+37.3%)|0.365 (+62.2%)| 

These results confirm that our methods generalize beyond the Llama family. We remark that we constructed the same number of prompts in knight swap as in other reasoning environment, but at the end of training (1 epoch), the GRPO performance has saturated but both of our methods are still climbing, so we expect *the gap will be even larger under additional training*, but that is beyond our current resource limit.  

[1] Zheng et al. (2023). "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena”.

[2] Bai et al. (2022). “Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback”.

|-|-|-|-|

These results confirm that our methods generalize beyond the Llama family. >*Since you are using a larger model during the training, could you provide the performance of on-ploicy distillation which using the Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as teacher model.*

We want to clarify that **Qwen3-235B is not used as a teacher, it is used to simulate a feedback provider**. That is, the larger model is part of the learning environment, so we can not fully control the generation of the larger models (e.g., generating demonstrations or obtaining logits for distillation).

Distilling from it would be analogous to distilling from a unit test framework: it conflates the feedback provider with a solution provider, which is not the setting we wish to model in our paper. Another analogy one can draw is in RLHF/alignment; sometimes people use LLM-as-a-judge to simulate human preference [2,3], but distilling from the judge LLM is not a fair baseline.

That said, to contextualize the gap between learning from feedback and learning from demonstrations, we include an off-policy distillation baseline using Qwen3-235B as a teacher (on-policy distillation is not applicable as the teacher and student use different tokenizers, workarounds exist [1] but it is beyond the scope of this rebuttal):
|  | GRPO | Self Distillation | Feedback Modeling | Distillation | Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct |
|-|-|-|-|-|-|
| Knights and Knaves | 0.352 | 0.802  | 0.880 | 0.862 | 0.984 |

We observe that distillation performs slightly better than self-distillation, and feedback modeling actually achieves the same performance as distillation. While we do not believe this result can generalize to arbitrary setting, we believe this is a very positive result showing RLTF in some cases can be as performative as distillation, which is way more expensive and less practical. 

Finally, we also conduct experiments where we use a weaker model to simulate the feedback provider, and we think that might be complementary to the above results. Due to character limitation we refer the reviewer to the second table in our response to reviewer XNey.

>*Could you provide the training cost(time and memory requirment) compared to previous method, since your method looks like quite slow because some non-paralllel step.*

Our methods introduce negligible additional cost over multi-turn GRPO, which is a baseline in our experiments. The overhead is limited to computing one additional loss term on already-collected data, which is negligible relative to the cost of generation. To provide a concrete example, on knights and knaves, multi-turn GRPO took 38.5 hours, self-distillation took 42 hours, and feedback modeling took 44 hours, but note that these are subject to variability on the tinker side. 

More broadly, a key motivation of our work is that text feedback is already abundant in practice. Our methods extract more learning signal from this existing data at essentially zero marginal cost.

rebuttals.rebuttal:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful review. We are glad the reviewer found the single-turn vs. multi-turn formalization clear, the importance-weighted estimator well-motivated, and the theoretical analysis of Feedback Modeling a strength. We address both concerns below.

>*The experiments assume relatively high-quality feedback often produced by a judge model. The robustness of the method to weak feedback is not evaluated.*

We have added experiments using a smaller, less capable model as the judge, simulating the kind of noisy, imperfect feedback one would expect from non-expert human annotators or lightweight automated graders in practice. We perform experiments on the knights and knaves environment, keep the same learner model, and test a few different judge models and record the results below

| Judge Model  | Self Distillation | Feedback Modeling | GRPO  |
|-|-|-|-|
| Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (in the paper) | 0.802  | 0.880 | 0.352 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct | 0.661 | 0.750 | - |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct | 0.609 | 0.758 | - |

We observe that **both of our methods (especially feedback modeling) are robust to the weaker feedback providers** (we use the model from the same model family to show a clean hierarchy), as the performance still greatly improves upon GRPO even with a much weaker model to simulate the feedback provider.

>*Test time scaling is somewhat limited. Most results focus on two-turn refinement, it would be useful to know whether gains continue or become unstable over longer refinements.*

While our main experiments focus on the two-turn setting (where the gap between multi-turn RL and single-turn performance is most clearly isolated), we have added three-turn training (which is the longest horizon under our experiment constraints) and evaluation results:

|  | 2-turn Self Distillation | 2-turn Feedback Modeling | 3-turn Self Distillation | 3-turn Feedback Modeling |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| Knights and Knaves | 0.802  | 0.880 | 0.835 | 0.871 |
| Math500 (DAPO) | 0.548 | 0.567 | 0.568 | 0.577 |

Concretely, in the three turn setting, for self-distillation, we use the same self-distillation objective to distill both $\pi(y_2 \mid x_2)$ and $\pi(y_1 \mid x_1)$ into $\pi(\cdot \mid x_0)$ at the same time, and the extension of feedback modeling is more obvious. We observe improvement on self-improvement on both reasoning tasks and math, and feedback modeling on math as well. We do not observe improvement on feedback modeling on reasoning as the original results already achieve very high accuracy. We also want to document an interesting observation that during the three-turn setting, only distilling the final round teacher $\pi(y_2 \mid x_2)$ induces instability in the training, which we think is worth future investigation on the best style of progressive distillation.

We note that the test-time scaling results in Section 6.4 (Figure 4) also provide some evidence on this question from the inference side: Feedback Modeling enables multiple rounds of self-critique at test time. The new 3-turn training results complement this by showing the behavior on the training side as well.

decision.title: Paper Decision
decision.comment:
This paper studies LLM learning using text feedback which is available at train time but not inference. This problem has been studied before (e.g., Cheng et al. 2023) and its importance stems from the fact that common alternatives like RL learn from scalar reward which is weak, and imitation learning which is expensive and costly. The paper proposes two approaches: one of which is self-distillation where the model mimics its own output conditioned on the feedback, and the second which learns to predict feedback as an auxiliary tasks. This approach seems intuitive and authors have evaluated on a range of tasks and provided additional theoretical analysis.

All reviewers lean towards acceptance. They overall found the approach well-motivated, clearly-written and generally found the results to be strong. Specially, given that text feedback can lead to more sample-efficient learning and improve LLM agents, I think this paper can make a good impact. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.
